experimental_note: This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of introducing Li vacancies via tetravalent substitution (Li1.6Mn0.8Zr0.2Cl4) to determine whether vacancy concentration alone remedies the abnormally low conductivity of Li2MnCl4 or if higher-valence dopants drive ordering/secondary phases that suppress mobility relative to 3+ dopants. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.6Mn0.8Zr0.2Cl4 synthesized at 400 °C refines as single-phase spinel (Fd-3m, Rwp 6.48%) but exhibits multiple unindexed peaks, and its room-temperature conductivity (9.23e-06 S/cm) increases by ~10× over Li2MnCl4 (8.81e-07 S/cm) yet remains below Li1.6Mn0.9V0.2Cl4 (2.04e-05 S/cm) and Li1.4Mn0.8Ta0.2Cl4 at 400 °C (2.15e-05 S/cm), and well short of the 1e-4 decision threshold—indicating vacancy creation improves σ but Zr4+ doping does not deliver the high mobility seen with some 3+ dopants, consistent with the need to manage ordering/phase deviations beyond vacancy level alone.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Nb5+-driven octahedral/Li-vacancy ordering in Li1.4Fe0.8Nb0.2Cl4 (manifested by low-angle superstructure features near ~15° 2θ) suppressing Li-ion mobility, and that modest Mn2+ substitution on Fe at 450 °C would frustrate this ordering and restore conductivity at fixed Li deficiency. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.4Fe0.7Mn0.1Nb0.2Cl4 (450 °C) refines as spinel (Fd-3m; weight fraction 1.0; Rwp=4.84%), exhibits weaker unmodeled low-angle peaks at 15.06° and 15.37° 2θ (relative intensity 0.17 each vs a prior ~14.94° feature of ~0.48, i.e., >50% reduction), and achieves a room-temperature ionic conductivity of 2.03e-05 S/cm, meeting the ≥1e-5 S/cm decision threshold. Residual low-angle features indicate some remaining unmodeled ordering or structural deviation, but the conductivity recovery aligns with reduced ordering-driven transport suppression.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Cr3+-driven octahedral-site/Li-vacancy ordering and defect association in Li1.5Mg0.5Cr0.5Cl4 that suppress Li mobility; lowering the Cr3+ fraction (Li1.8Cr0.2Mg0.8Cl4, 450 °C) was expected to yield a cleaner spinel pattern and raise σ_RT by ≥2 orders of magnitude. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.8Cr0.2Mg0.8Cl4 shows σ_RT = 3.74e-07 S/cm (≥2 orders above Li1.5Mg0.5Cr0.5Cl4 at 1.25e-09 S/cm) and the Li2CrCl4 reference phase is reduced (0.0117 vs 0.05). However, XRD still indicates notable heterogeneity: spinel (Fd-3m) is 0.8311 with 0.1572 LiCl present, Rwp increased to 12.33% (vs 10.43%), and strong missing peaks remain (e.g., 15.42° with relative intensity 0.53), indicating unresolved structural/phase complexity rather than a “cleaner spinel.” Conductivity also remains below the ≥1e-6 S/cm target and below Li2MgCl4 (2.91e-06–4.2e-06 S/cm).

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Cr3+-induced octahedral-site/Li-vacancy ordering and defect associates (and possible Li2CrCl4-like secondary phases) in Li1.5Mg0.5Cr0.5Cl4 that suppress Li-ion mobility, with the prediction that lowering Cr content would minimize such ordering/associates and restore conductivity toward Li2MgCl4. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.9Cr0.1Mg0.9Cl4 synthesized at 450 °C shows a majority spinel phase (Fd-3m, 0.9158) with only LiCl (Fm-3m, 0.0842) as an identified secondary phase and no Li2CrCl4, and delivers 6.38e-07 S/cm—higher than the Cr-rich composition but still below Li2MgCl4 (2.91e-06 to 4.2e-06) and the ≥1e-6 S/cm target; the XRD fit (Rwp = 9.55%) with one missing peak at 36.51° and extra calculated peaks (e.g., 14.91°) indicates residual structural/phase mismatch, so reducing Cr improves but does not fully resolve the low-conductivity anomaly.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Zn2+ content disrupting inverse spinel formation in Li2-yM1±xCl4 at 450 °C, promoting segregation into nonspinel LiCl/MCl2 and suppressing Li+ transport, and that lowering the Zn fraction should restore the spinel framework and increase conductivity. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li2Co0.9Zn0.1Cl4 refined as spinel (Fd-3m) with 1.0 weight fraction and Rwp 3.33% (with some missing/extra peaks indicating model/sample mismatches), and its room-temperature ionic conductivity is 4.04e-07 S/cm—higher than Li2Co0.5Zn0.5Cl4 (4.88e-08 S/cm) but still below the Co/Mg and Co/Mn analogues (2.8e-06–7.57e-06 S/cm).

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Zn2+ destabilizing the inverse spinel in Li2Co0.5Zn0.5Cl4 at 450 °C, and that introducing Y3+ (with reduced Zn) to create Li vacancies can stabilize the spinel framework and improve room-temperature ionic conductivity. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.8Co0.7Y0.2Zn0.1Cl4 synthesized at 450 °C shows a majority spinel (Fd-3m) phase (0.7678) with a secondary Li3YCl6 (P-3m1) phase (0.2322), a good refinement (Rwp = 4.83%), and an increased room-temperature ionic conductivity of 2e-06 S/cm compared to Li2Co0.5Zn0.5Cl4 (4.88e-08 S/cm); however, the presence of the Li3YCl6 secondary phase and missing/extra peaks indicate the product is not single-phase spinel and the ≥1e-5 S/cm target was not achieved.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of light V substitution (~15% in Li2−yMn1−xVxCl4) optimizing Li-vacancy concentration and cation/Li disorder to maximize ionic conductivity, with higher V (≥20%) reducing mobility via vacancy clustering and/or cation ordering. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.6Mn0.9V0.2Cl4 (400 °C) is single-phase spinel (Fd-3m; weight fraction 1.0; Rwp 4.36%; no extra peaks; one very weak missing peak at 99.48° 2θ) and shows σRT = 2.04e-05 S/cm, lower than Li1.65Mn0.95V0.15Cl4 (2.59e-05 S/cm) yet higher than Li2MnCl4 (5.95e-06 S/cm), Li2FeCl4 (1.14e-05 S/cm), and Li1.5Mn0.5V0.5Cl4 (2.86e-06 S/cm), consistent with an optimum near ~15% V; however, XRD provides no clear evidence for ordering or vacancy clustering as the cause of the conductivity decrease.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Ta5+ substitution near ~20% in Li2−yFe1−xTaxCl4 optimizing the Li‑vacancy concentration and Li/M disorder in the inverse spinel (Fd‑3m), thereby maximizing room‑temperature ionic conductivity; lowering Ta to 15% (with higher Li content) should reduce σ compared to Li1.4Fe0.8Ta0.2Cl4 at the same synthesis temperature. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.55Fe0.85Ta0.15Cl4 (400 °C) refines as spinel (Fd‑3m) with Rwp = 4.66% (single spinel phase in the model) and shows σRT = 4.32e-06 S/cm, which is >10× lower than Li1.4Fe0.8Ta0.2Cl4 at 400 °C (4.57e-05 S/cm), meeting the predefined decision rule and supporting an optimum near x ≈ 0.20.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of adding 10% Mg2+ on the Fe site in Li1.4Fe0.8Ta0.2Cl4 (forming Li1.4Fe0.7Mg0.1Ta0.2Cl4 at 400 °C) to frustrate cation ordering while preserving the Ta5+-driven Li-vacancy level, thereby increasing Li/M disorder and raising room-temperature ionic conductivity beyond the Ta-only benchmark (≥4.57e-05 S/cm) with a predominantly spinel phase. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as the XRD refinement reports spinel (Fd-3m) at 1.0 weight fraction with Rwp 5.99% but includes multiple missing and extra peaks (indicating differences from the reference model), and the measured room-temperature ionic conductivity is 2.02e-06 S/cm—well below Li1.4Fe0.8Ta0.2Cl4 at 400 °C (4.57e-05 S/cm); thus, although the >50% spinel fraction criterion is met, the conductivity criterion is not.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of unusually high conductivity in Li1.5Mn0.5Sc0.5Cl4 arising from the synergy of very high Li-vacancy concentration and frustrated Li/M ordering, with an added contribution from percolation between two closely related spinel domains at x≈0.5. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.6Mn0.6Sc0.4Cl4 (400 °C) refines as single-phase spinel (Fd-3m; weight fraction 1.0; Rwp = 8.14%) with three weak unindexed peaks and shows σ_RT = 1.57e-05 S/cm—lower than Li1.5Mn0.5Sc0.5Cl4 (4.63e-05 S/cm) yet higher than Li2MnCl4 (5.95e-06 S/cm). The loss of the two-spinel-like refinement signature coincides with a drop in conductivity, consistent with a domain-related contribution to the abnormal σ at x≈0.5, while the remaining enhancement vs. Li2MnCl4 indicates that vacancy/disorder alone raises σ but does not reproduce the abnormal level under these conditions.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of higher-temperature synthesis driving greater cation ordering (monitored by stronger low-angle ~15° 2θ features) that reduces Li+ conductivity, and that co-doping at fixed Li deficiency (using Sc and Ta on the octahedral sublattice) at 400 °C would frustrate such ordering and retain or improve σ relative to Li1.4Mn0.8Ta0.2Cl4 (400 °C). The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.4Mn0.7Sc0.15Ta0.15Cl4 (400 °C) shows a stronger unindexed low-angle peak at 14.94° 2θ with relative intensity 0.39 (vs 0.15 at 15.14° for Li1.4Mn0.8Ta0.2Cl4 at 400 °C) and a lower room-temperature ionic conductivity of 1.58e-05 S/cm (vs 2.15e-05 S/cm), despite a high spinel (Fd-3m) fraction of 0.9506 with 0.0494 LiCl and an Rwp of 5.56%.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of the abnormally high conductivity in Li1.5Fe0.5Cr0.5Cl4 being dominated by electronic conduction from mixed-valent Fe2+/Fe3+ centers and/or FeClx networks rather than true Li+ transport. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.6Cr0.5Fe0.5Cl4 synthesized at 400 °C refines as spinel-only (Fd-3m, Rwp = 7.56%) with no FeClx-type phases included in the model, and its room-temperature conductivity is 1.51e-08 S/cm—>3 orders of magnitude lower than the 3.53e-05 S/cm outlier in Li1.5Fe0.5Cr0.5Cl4. Although several missing/extra peaks indicate minor unidentified features, the large collapse in σ for a spinel sample without FeClx phases is consistent with suppression of electronic pathways and does not require invoking a hidden Li-rich superionic phase.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of slight LiCl exsolution during synthesis driving the spinel matrix slightly Li-deficient, thereby maximizing mobile Li-vacancy concentration and Li/M disorder; nominally single-phase batches are closer to stoichiometric/partially ordered states with reduced vacancy density and lower conductivity. The hypothesis is not supported (inconclusive) by the experiment outcome as Li1.34Fe0.78Ta0.22Cl4 synthesized at 400 °C did not form the intended Fd-3m spinel—XRD is best matched to Li6FeCl8 (Fm-3m, 95.97 wt%) plus TaCl4 (C12/m1, 4.03 wt%) with additional unindexed features (Rwp 5.15%), and the room-temperature ionic conductivity is 7.72e-07 S/cm, well below both Li1.4Fe0.8Ta0.2Cl4 batches (4.57e-05 S/cm with ~8.4 wt% LiCl and 2.49e-06 S/cm single-phase). Because the spinel matrix did not form, the test did not isolate vacancy effects within the target framework, so the data do not confirm the proposed exsolution/vacancy mechanism.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of unusually high conductivity in Li1.5Mn0.5Sc0.5Cl4 arising from very high Li-vacancy concentration, suppressed Li/M octahedral ordering, and microstructural percolation between two closely related spinel domains. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as the 450 °C sample refines predominantly to a single spinel (Fd-3m, 0.9754) with minor ScCl (R-3m, 0.0246), shows no missing or extra peaks (no evidence of superlattice features), and exhibits higher room-temperature conductivity (6.43e-05 S/cm) than the 400 °C sample (4.63e-05 S/cm) that previously indexed as two spinel-like references; this indicates that two-domain percolation is not required and is consistent with disorder/high-vacancy-driven transport, but the extent of Li/M disorder and ionic transference are not directly confirmed by the current data.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of the abnormally high conductivity in Li1.5Fe0.5Cr0.5Cl4 being dominated by electronic conduction from mixed-valent Fe chlorides/FeClx networks rather than intrinsic Li+ superionic transport in the inverse spinel. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.5Cr0.5Mg0.5Cl4 (450 °C) refines as spinel (Fd-3m) with 1.0 weight fraction (Rwp = 13.19%, with some missing and extra peaks) and exhibits low room-temperature conductivity (1.48e-07 S/cm), satisfying the predefined decision rule (spinel fraction >50% with σ ≤ 1e-6 S/cm) and matching the low-σ values of the spinel-rich Li1.5Fe0.5Cr0.5Cl4 syntheses (1.58e-08 and 2.17e-07 S/cm), indicating the Fe-containing outlier’s high σ (3.53e-05 S/cm) is unlikely due to intrinsic Li+ conduction.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Co2+ stabilizing an orthorhombic Li2CoCl4-like (Cmmm) framework at 450 °C in Li2Co0.5Fe0.5Cl4 that suppresses spinel formation and lowers σRT, and that introducing Mn2+ at fixed Co content (Li2Co0.5Fe0.25Mn0.25Cl4) would disrupt this ordering, eliminate Cmmm signatures, stabilize spinel, and raise σRT toward ≥1e-5 S/cm. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li2Co0.5Fe0.25Mn0.25Cl4 synthesized at 450 °C refines as single-phase spinel (Fd-3m, 1.0 weight fraction, Rwp=3.89%) with no Cmmm phase detected (minor missing/extra peaks only), but its σRT=2.3e-06 S/cm remains comparable to Li2Co0.5Fe0.5Cl4 (2.8e-06 S/cm) and well below spinel benchmarks Li2Mg0.5Fe0.5Cl4 (1.04e-05 S/cm), Li2Mn0.5Fe0.5Cl4 (2.07e-05 S/cm), and Li2FeCl4 (1.14e-05 S/cm), indicating spinel stabilization without the expected conductivity increase.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Ni2+-driven Li/M cation and Li-vacancy ordering in Li2Fe0.8Ni0.2Cl4 suppressing Li-ion transport, and that 10% Mn2+ co-substitution would frustrate such ordering, reduce unindexed XRD features, and recover σRT toward ≥1e-5 S/cm. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li2Fe0.7Mn0.1Ni0.2Cl4 (450 °C) indexes as spinel (Fd-3m, Rwp=5.32%) and achieves σRT=7.63e-06 S/cm (~13× higher than Li2Fe0.8Ni0.2Cl4 and closer to Li2FeCl4=1.14e-05), and the specific missing peaks near ~35.5° and ~50.8° observed in Li2Fe0.8Ni0.2Cl4 are absent; however, numerous other missing peaks and new extra peaks persist, and the higher synthesis temperature (450 °C vs 400 °C) is a confounding variable, so the conductivity recovery cannot be attributed solely to Mn co-substitution.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of V dopant segregation as Li6VCl8 with concurrent FeCl2 formation under 400 °C/Ni-crucible conditions that depletes Li from the spinel and depresses ionic conductivity, and that a charge-balanced V3+-compatible target at higher temperature would suppress these impurities and increase σ. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.85Fe0.85V0.15Cl4 (450 °C) shows 91.17 wt% spinel (Fd-3m) with only LiCl (8.83 wt%) and no FeCl2 or Li6VCl8 detected by XRD (Rwp=3.47%; two low-intensity unindexed peaks), and achieves σRT=9.87e-06 S/cm (~60× higher than Li1.6Fe0.9V0.2Cl4), meeting the ≥90% spinel/no-FeCl2/Li6VCl8 criterion and approaching the 1e-5 S/cm target.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of limited In3+ solubility in the Fe-based inverse spinel at 450 °C leading to exsolution of a highly conducting Li–In chloride (e.g., Li6In2+xCl12) in Li1.8Fe0.8In0.2Cl4, which elevates σRT; reducing In to ≤0.1 should yield single-phase spinel and lower σRT to the intrinsic spinel level. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.9Fe0.9In0.1Cl4 synthesized at 450 °C refines as 100 wt% spinel (Fd-3m, Rwp=3.17%) with only two low-intensity unindexed peaks and no Li–In chloride phases included in the fitted model, and shows σRT=6.4e-06 S/cm—lower than the multiphase Li1.8Fe0.8In0.2Cl4 (2.15e-05 S/cm) and comparable to single-phase aliovalent-doped spinels (7.46e-06, 4.98e-06, 2.95e-06).

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of an ordering–conductivity anti-correlation in Li1.4Mn0.8Ta0.2Cl4: higher synthesis temperature strengthens low-angle (~15° 2θ) superlattice features from Li/M octahedral ordering that reduce Li+ conductivity, while lower temperature suppresses this ordering and improves σ without losing the spinel framework. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as the 350 °C product remains predominantly spinel (Fd-3m, 0.9841), shows no ~15° 2θ missing peak, and exhibits σ = 1.19e-05 S/cm—higher than the 450 °C sample (5.16e-06 S/cm); however, σ does not surpass the 400 °C value (2.15e-05 S/cm), so the expected further increase was not achieved.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of electronic leakage via mixed-valent Fe (Fe2+/Fe3+) and/or a hidden Sc–Li chloride percolation pathway causing the anomalously high conductivity in Li1.5Fe0.5Sc0.5Cl4. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as the 350 °C re-synthesis refined to a single spinel (Fd-3m) phase (weight fraction 1.0; Rwp 7.11%; no FeCl3 detected by XRD; only low-intensity missing peaks) and the room-temperature conductivity increased to 2.71e-05 S/cm (vs 1.37e-05 S/cm at 400 °C), failing the predefined ≥5× drop criterion expected for electronic leakage; additionally, no Li3ScCl6/Li6Sc2Cl12-like phase was observed by XRD, so any hidden Sc–Li chloride contribution remains unconfirmed. Overall, the persistence/increase of σ alongside the absence of FeCl3 is more consistent with ionic transport associated with the spinel framework rather than dominant electronic leakage.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of cation ordering (antisite-poor, subtly symmetry-lowered variant) and/or higher grain-boundary resistance causing the abnormally low ionic conductivity in Li2MnCl4, with the expectation that lower synthesis temperature would enhance ordering (low-angle superlattice peaks near ~15–16° 2θ) and further suppress σ. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as the 350 °C Li2MnCl4 sample is mixed-phase (spinel (Fd-3m) 0.85 + MnCl2 (R-3m) 0.15, Rwp 7.16%), shows no low-angle superlattice reflections (missing peaks only at 35.2°, 59.65°, 82.29°; extra at 82.03°), yet has a lower σRT (3.77e-07 S/cm) than both 400 °C counterparts (5.95e-06 and 8.81e-07 S/cm); because the XRD indicates an impurity and lacks ordering signatures, this result does not validate cation ordering nor isolate microstructure as the cause of the original abnormality.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Co2+ stabilizing a cation-ordered orthorhombic Li2CoCl4-like (Cmmm) framework at 450 °C that suppresses inverse spinel (Fd-3m) formation and depresses σ; raising synthesis temperature should promote Li/M disorder, stabilize spinel, and increase σRT toward ~1e-5 S/cm. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as Li2Co0.5Fe0.5Cl4 synthesized at 500 °C refines as spinel (Fd-3m, 1.0 weight fraction, Rwp 2.59%) with no detected Cmmm or LiCl (only two low-intensity missing peaks at 24.78° and 39.42°), yet σRT is 1.42e-06 S/cm—lower than the 450 °C sample (2.8e-06 S/cm) and well below spinel analogues Li2Mg0.5Fe0.5Cl4 (1.04e-05 S/cm), Li2Mn0.5Fe0.5Cl4 (2.07e-05 S/cm), and Li2FeCl4 (1.14e-05 S/cm)—indicating that eliminating the Cmmm phase alone does not recover high conductivity in this composition under these conditions.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Ni2+ in Li2Fe0.8Ni0.2Cl4 inducing Li/M octahedral and Li-vacancy ordering within an average spinel (Fd-3m) framework that suppresses Li-ion transport, and that higher synthesis temperature should increase disorder, suppress the prior missing peaks near ~35.5 and ~50.8 two-theta, and raise σRT toward ~1e-5 S/cm. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as the 500 °C synthesis yields single-phase spinel with improved Rwp (3.86% vs 5.69% at 400 °C), the earlier missing peaks near ~35.5 and ~50.8 two-theta are no longer observed (only weaker low-angle missing peaks at 17.26 and 24.55 two-theta remain), and σRT increases from 5.83e-07 S/cm to 3.67e-06 S/cm (~6×). However, the conductivity gain does not reach the ≥10× target and remains below Li2FeCl4 (1.14e-05 S/cm) and Li2Mn0.5Fe0.5Cl4 (2.07e-05 S/cm), indicating incomplete recovery of the desired disordered, high-conductivity state.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of temperature-driven suppression of the Cmmm cation–vacancy ordering in Li1.6Fe0.8Mn0.4Cl4 (which previously formed a Li3.66Fe2.17Cl8-like Cmmm phase with low σRT at 400 °C), expecting that higher synthesis temperature would stabilize the disordered inverse spinel (Fd-3m) and raise σRT to ≥1e-05 S/cm. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as synthesis at 500 °C yields XRD indexed entirely as spinel (Fd-3m, 1.0 weight fraction, Rwp=3.54% with two weak unindexed peaks) and increases σRT from 4.58e-07 S/cm to 2.97e-05 S/cm, meeting the predefined success criteria.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of heavy divalent substitution (x=+0.4) with Li deficiency in Li1.6Fe0.8Mn0.4Cl4 driving cooperative cation–vacancy ordering into a Cmmm-type framework (Li3.66Fe2.17Cl8-like) that suppresses Li mobility, and that reducing M excess to x=+0.1 (Li1.8Fe0.9Mn0.2Cl4) at elevated temperature will re-stabilize an Fd-3m spinel and raise σRT to ≥1e-5 S/cm. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.8Fe0.9Mn0.2Cl4 synthesized at 500 °C indexes as spinel (Fd-3m, reported 1.0 weight fraction, Rwp=3.15%) with only two minor unindexed peaks and exhibits σRT=1.44e-05 S/cm, meeting the predefined success criteria and contrasting the Li1.6Fe0.8Mn0.4Cl4 outcome (Cmmm, 4.58e-07 S/cm); however, without a high‑temperature re-test of Li1.6Fe0.8Mn0.4Cl4, kinetic contributions cannot be fully excluded.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of limited In3+ solubility in the Fe-based inverse spinel at 450 °C causing exsolution of a highly conducting Li–In chloride secondary phase (e.g., Li6In2+xCl12) that percolates and dominates the measured ionic conductivity; increasing the synthesis temperature to 500 °C should dissolve the Li–In chloride, produce ≥95 wt% spinel, and lower σRT toward intrinsic spinel values. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as the 500 °C Li1.8Fe0.8In0.2Cl4 sample shows 85.02 wt% spinel (Fd-3m) and 14.98 wt% LiCl (Fm-3m) with no Li–In chloride detected by XRD (Rwp 3.34%), yet the room-temperature ionic conductivity increases to 2.72e-05 S/cm (vs 2.15e-05 S/cm at 450 °C) and remains higher than Li2FeCl4 (1.14e-05 S/cm) and Sc/Y/Zr analogs (~3e-06–7e-06 S/cm); thus elevated conductivity persists without detectable Li–In chloride and the predicted ≥95 wt% spinel and σ reduction did not occur.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of co-doping a Mn-based inverse spinel chloride with V3+ (~15%) and Hf4+ (~10%) to fix Li at 1.65 (~0.35 Li vacancies/f.u.), frustrate Li/M octahedral ordering, maintain a dominant Fd-3m spinel fraction, and thereby exceed the room-temperature ionic conductivity of Mn–V-only analogs. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.65Hf0.1Mn0.75V0.15Cl4 forms predominantly spinel (Fd-3m, 86.59% with LiCl 13.41%, Rwp 6.22%) but shows unindexed low-angle peaks (~10.98° and 15.17° 2θ) consistent with residual ordering/distortions, and its room-temperature ionic conductivity (8.17e-06 S/cm) is lower than Mn–V benchmarks (~2.6e-05 and ~1.8e-05 S/cm); thus, while the spinel fraction target was met, Hf4+ co-doping did not enhance transport under these synthesis conditions.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of co-doping the inverse-spinel Li2−yMnCl4 framework with ~15% V3+ and ~5% Nb5+ to create ~0.3 Li vacancies, disperse/frustrate Li/M ordering, preserve a cubic spinel lattice, and thus achieve room-temperature ionic conductivity surpassing Mn–V single-doped analogues. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.7Mn0.8Nb0.05V0.15Cl4 synthesized at 400 °C formed a two-phase mixture (spinel Fd-3m: 0.7942; Li6VCl8 Fm-3m: 0.2058; Rwp 7.78%) with extra/missing peaks indicating structural mismatch, and exhibited a room-temperature ionic conductivity of 9.98e-07 S/cm, below the intended benchmarks.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of co-doping the Mn inverse spinel chloride host with In3+ and Ta5+ at moderate levels in Li1.6In0.1Mn0.8Ta0.1Cl4 to retain a high Li-vacancy concentration, preserve a predominantly Fd-3m spinel framework while suppressing cation ordering, and thereby increase room-temperature ionic conductivity beyond single-dopant baselines via enhanced site disorder and configurational entropy. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as XRD refines to a single spinel (Fd-3m) phase at 1.0 weight fraction with Rwp 7.81% (consistent with a maintained spinel framework and no major segregated phases), but several unindexed peaks (e.g., 34.39° with relative intensity 0.6) and a calculated extra low-angle peak at 14.52° indicate deviations from an ideal disordered spinel (possible subtle ordering/distortion or minor undetected phases), while the room-temperature ionic conductivity of 1.27e-05 S/cm shows a modest gain over the In-only baseline (~9e-06 S/cm) without clear synergistic improvement over single-dopant benchmarks.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of using 10% Ta5+ substitution for Co2+ in Li1.7Co0.9Ta0.1Cl4 to create ~0.30 Li vacancies, promote octahedral-site disorder in an inverse spinel chloride framework, and thereby achieve a spinel-dominant phase with enhanced room-temperature Li+ conductivity over undoped divalent systems. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as XRD at 400 °C shows a mainly spinel (Fd-3m) phase (0.8653) but with a notable Li2CoCl4 (Cmmm) minority phase (0.1347), along with multiple unindexed and extra reflections (including a strong extra peak at 15.47°) indicating structural deviations or additional phases; despite a good refinement (Rwp = 2.46%), the measured room-temperature ionic conductivity is very low (6.71e-08 S/cm), contradicting the expected conductivity enhancement.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of heterovalent Sc3+ substitution on a Ni2+-based inverse spinel chloride (Li1.75Ni0.75Sc0.25Cl4) to create y = 0.25 Li vacancies and promote Li/M disorder, thereby retaining a spinel framework (>50 wt%) and achieving ~1e-4 S/cm room-temperature Li+ conductivity. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as XRD indicates a dominant spinel (Fd-3m) structural phase at 77.65 wt% with a NiCl2 (R-3m) impurity at 22.35 wt% (Rwp = 8.17%), and minor missing/extra peaks suggest deviations from the ideal reference; however, the measured room-temperature ionic conductivity is 9.15e-07 S/cm—well below the target—indicating that the achieved vacancy/disorder state and phase purity under the 500 °C synthesis did not deliver the anticipated high conductivity.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Zr4+ aliovalent doping into a Zn2+ inverse spinel chloride host to generate ~0.30 Li vacancies (y = 2x for x = 0.15), promote extensive octahedral cation disorder, and enable 8a–16c–8a Li+ percolation, thereby stabilizing an inverse spinel majority phase with high room-temperature ionic conductivity. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as XRD identifies a Li2ZnCl4 (Pnma) phase at 1.0 weight fraction (Rwp 6.78%) rather than an inverse spinel, with several unindexed peaks suggesting additional minor phases, and the measured room-temperature ionic conductivity is 2.88e-08 S/cm, far below the targeted superionic regime.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of stabilizing a disordered inverse-spinel chloride (Fd-3m) Li2−yM1±xCl4 framework via Hf4+ substitution on a Zn2+ host in Li1.6Hf0.2Zn0.8Cl4, creating moderate Li vacancies and heterogeneous M-site fields to lower Li+ migration barriers and enhance room-temperature ionic conductivity relative to prior 4+ cases. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as the XRD is indexed entirely as Li2ZnCl4 (Pnma, 1.0 weight fraction; Rwp 7.38%) rather than an inverse-spinel phase, with numerous missing/extra peaks indicating additional unidentified (likely Hf-containing) phases, and the measured room-temperature ionic conductivity is very low (2.51e-08 S/cm), far below the anticipated improvement.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of stabilizing a disordered inverse spinel Li2–yM1±xCl4 framework at Li=1.4 by co-doping the octahedral M-sublattice with Zn2+, Sc3+, and Hf4+ (average M charge ~+2.6) to frustrate cation/Li-vacancy ordering while keeping Cl-only chemistry, aiming for Fd-3m (or lightly symmetry-lowered) structure and high room-temperature ionic conductivity comparable to the best Fe–Ta case. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.4Hf0.2Sc0.2Zn0.6Cl4 synthesized at 300 °C shows XRD best matched to Li3ScCl6 (C12/m1) at 100 wt% with Rwp = 12.58% and many missing/extra peaks (no evidence of an inverse spinel), and the room-temperature ionic conductivity is low (3.22e-06 S/cm), far below the targeted high conductivity.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Y3+-driven formation of a Li3YCl6 grain-boundary network that explains the abnormal high conductivity observed in Li1.8Cr0.6Fe0.2Y0.2Cl4. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.8Mg0.8Y0.2Cl4 (450 °C) contains predominantly spinel (Fd-3m, 0.9286) with a minor Li3YCl6 (P-3m1, 0.0714) fraction and exhibits σ_RT = 1.06e-05 S/cm—higher than Li2CrCl4-rich baselines (e.g., Li2CrCl4: 2.72e-07 S/cm; Li1.4Cr0.6Fe0.2Ta0.2Cl4: 5.96e-06 S/cm) and comparable to Y–Cl–containing references (Li1.5Mg0.5Y0.5Cl4: 1.49e-05 S/cm; Li1.5Co0.5Y0.5Cl4: 2.3e-05 S/cm). The explicit detection of Li3YCl6 alongside elevated conductivity supports a correlation between Li3YCl6 presence and enhanced transport, but the small Li3YCl6 fraction and σ well below ≥1e-4 S/cm do not demonstrate that a Li3YCl6 boundary network dominates conduction in this sample.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Y3+-induced formation of Li3YCl6 (or related Y–Cl) secondary phases that create percolative grain-boundary pathways and thereby explain the anomalously high ionic conductivity observed in Li1.8Cr0.6Fe0.2Y0.2Cl4 despite its Li2CrCl4-indexed XRD. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.7Mg0.7Y0.3Cl4 (450 °C) shows explicit two-phase XRD with spinel (Fd-3m) 0.7496 and Li3YCl6 (P-3m1) 0.2504 (Rwp = 8.35%), and achieves σRT = 1.29e-05 S/cm—much higher than Li2CrCl4-rich references (Li2CrCl4: 2.72e-07 S/cm; Li1.4Cr1.2Cl4: 7.95e-08 S/cm) and comparable to Li3YCl6-containing samples (Li1.5Mg0.5Y0.5Cl4: 1.49e-05 S/cm; Li1.5Co0.5Y0.5Cl4: 2.3e-05 S/cm). While direct σ scaling versus a z=0.2 Mg–Y baseline is not available, the observed Li3YCl6 fraction together with elevated conductivity aligns with the boundary-phase percolation hypothesis rather than a purely intrinsic spinel mechanism.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of the elevated 5.62e-06 S/cm observed in Li1.6Fe0.9Cr0.2Cl4 arising from electronic conduction through FeCl2 rather than true Li-ion transport in an inverse spinel. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.8Fe0.8Cr0.2Cl4 synthesized at 450 °C indexes as spinel (Fd-3m) with the chosen model (weight fraction 1.0, Rwp 4.85%) with two unindexed reflections, and shows σ_RT = 4.27e-06 S/cm—within the typical single-phase spinel range seen in related compositions (e.g., Li2FeCl4 1.14e-05; Li1.6Fe0.9Y0.2Cl4 7.46e-06; Li1.6Fe0.9Sc0.2Cl4 4.98e-06; Li1.6Fe0.8Zr0.2Cl4 2.95e-06). This contrasts with the original Li1.6Fe0.9Cr0.2Cl4 product (FeCl2 + LiCl by XRD) that nevertheless gave 5.62e-06 S/cm, consistent with the prior value being influenced by electronic pathways in the FeCl2-containing mixture rather than enhanced Li-ion transport in spinel; note that t_ion was not measured here.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Cr3+ causing element-specific suppression of Li mobility in inverse spinel chlorides by stabilizing octahedral-site and Li-vacancy ordering and forming defect-associated Cr–VLi pairs that hinder 3D Li migration, which explains the abnormally low σ_RT observed in Li1.5Co0.5Cr0.5Cl4. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.4Mn0.4V0.6Cl4 (Cr-free) synthesized at 400 °C indexes as spinel (Fd-3m; Rwp = 5.95%) with no extra peaks and some low-intensity missing peaks, and exhibits σ_RT = 4.18e-06 S/cm—comparable to Li1.5Mn0.5V0.5Cl4 (4.58e-06 S/cm) and several orders of magnitude higher than the Cr-containing Li1.5Co0.5Cr0.5Cl4 (7.35e-09 S/cm) and Li1.5Mg0.5Cr0.5Cl4 (1.25e-09 S/cm). This indicates that poor conductivity is not inherent to the spinel framework or vacancy level, consistent with Cr-specific suppression; however, the anticipated conductivity increase from higher vacancy content (y = 0.6) was not realized, and the test does not vary Cr within the abnormal Co/Cr system, so the evidence is supportive but indirect.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of high Co2+ content at 400 °C stabilizing a Cmmm cation/vacancy-ordered phase (Li3.66Fe2.17Cl8-like) in Li1.6Fe0.8Co0.4Cl4, and that lowering Co to ~0.2 at the same temperature would recover the Fd-3m spinel and raise ionic conductivity. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.6Fe1.0Co0.2Cl4 synthesized at 400 °C shows spinel (Fd-3m) as the majority XRD-matched phase (0.8247) with no Cmmm phase reported, alongside minor LiCl (0.0923) and FeCl2 (0.083); Rwp = 2.57%. The room-temperature ionic conductivity (2.75e-06 S/cm) is ~13× higher than that of Li1.6Fe0.8Co0.4Cl4 (2.15e-07 S/cm) and falls within the range observed for related Li1.6Fe-based spinels. Missing/extra peaks are noted but do not contradict spinel dominance in this sample.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Nb5+ co-doping in Li1.7Mn0.8Nb0.05V0.15Cl4 reducing V solubility in the inverse spinel, driving Li6VCl8 formation and low-angle superlattice features that suppress Li+ transport; lowering Nb to 0.03 while keeping Li≈1.70 and V≈0.15 should suppress Li6VCl8 and superlattice peaks and restore higher conductivity. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.7Mn0.85Nb0.03V0.15Cl4 (400 °C) shows 100 wt% spinel (Fd-3m) with Rwp 5.42%, no extra or missing peaks (no ~29.8° 2θ Li6VCl8 or ~15° 2θ superlattice features), and σRT = 1.63e-05 S/cm—meeting the predefined success criteria and significantly higher than the original Li1.7Mn0.8Nb0.05V0.15Cl4 (9.98e-07 S/cm).

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Cr in Li1.5Mn0.5Cr0.5Cl4 forming Cr chlorometallates (Li5CrCl8, CrCl3) at 400 °C instead of entering the spinel, which depresses spinel fraction and blocks Li+ transport; reducing Cr to 20% and matching Li vacancies (Li1.8Mn0.8Cr0.2Cl4) should suppress these secondary phases, yield a predominantly single-phase spinel, and increase conductivity. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.8Mn0.8Cr0.2Cl4 (synthesized at 400 °C) shows no Li5CrCl8/CrCl3 among the refined phases and a higher σ (1.88e-06 S/cm vs. 6.76e-08 S/cm for Li1.5Mn0.5Cr0.5Cl4), but the product remains biphasic with 80.42 wt% spinel and 19.58 wt% LiCl and exhibits missing peaks at 15.39° and 34.71°, so the ≥90 wt% spinel and ≥1e-05 S/cm targets were not met.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of the abnormal 5.62e-06 S/cm in Li1.6Fe0.9Cr0.2Cl4 at 400 °C arising from failure to form the inverse spinel (producing a FeCl2/LiCl mixture with electronic pathways), and that raising the synthesis temperature to drive single-phase spinel formation would reduce the apparent conductivity into the typical spinel ionic range. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.6Fe0.9Cr0.2Cl4 synthesized at 500 °C converts to single-phase spinel (Fd-3m, 1.0; Rwp 3.93%), indicating the 400 °C non-spinel result was kinetically limited, while the room-temperature conductivity is 1.21e-05 S/cm—comparable to historical single-phase spinels (e.g., Li2FeCl4 1.14e-05 S/cm) and not lower than the FeCl2/LiCl mixture (5.62e-06 S/cm), so the specific claim that the prior value was dominated by electronic conduction through FeCl2 is not confirmed.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Ni crucible chlorination causing Ni/Cl loss and off-stoichiometry that prevented spinel formation in Li2Fe0.7Mn0.1Ni0.2Cl4 at 450 °C. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as resynthesis at 500 °C yielded a single-phase spinel (Fd-3m, 1.0 weight fraction; Rwp 5.45%) with no missing peaks and only minor extra peaks, and a room-temperature ionic conductivity of 5.0e-06 S/cm, consistent in magnitude with related spinel samples (e.g., Li2Fe0.8Ni0.2Cl4 at 500 °C: 3.67e-06 S/cm) and contrasting the prior MnCl2 + LiCl result; however, because crucible/Cl buffering is unspecified and the temperature changed, this support is suggestive rather than definitive.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of chlorination of the Ni crucible consuming Ni and Cl (forming NiCl2) in the Li2Fe0.7Mn0.1Ni0.2Cl4 synthesis, shifting stoichiometry and preventing inverse spinel formation; using a nonreactive crucible or sealed ampoule (and buffering Cl activity) should restore spinel formation with ~1e-05 S/cm conductivity. The hypothesis is indirectly supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.9Fe0.45Mn0.45Sc0.1Cl4 synthesized at 500 °C shows 100% spinel (Fd-3m; Rwp 3.86%) with no missing or extra peaks and a room-temperature ionic conductivity of 1.47e-05 S/cm, matching the expected range; however, because the tested composition differs from Li2Fe0.7Mn0.1Ni0.2Cl4, the crucible type was not documented, and the synthesis temperature differs from the original, the result does not conclusively isolate Ni-crucible chlorination as the root cause of the original abnormality.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of high Co2+ content at 400 °C stabilizing a Cmmm-ordered Li3.66Fe2.17Cl8-type phase in Li1.6Fe0.8Co0.4Cl4, suppressing the inverse spinel (Fd-3m) and lowering ionic conductivity; increasing the synthesis temperature to 500 °C should suppress the Cmmm phase, recover the spinel, and raise σ. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.6Fe0.8Co0.4Cl4 synthesized at 500 °C shows 95.4% spinel (Fd-3m) with 4.6% FeCl2 and no Cmmm phase in the XRD fit (Rwp = 3.86%), and the room-temperature ionic conductivity increases from 2.15e-07 S/cm (400 °C sample) to 3.34e-06 S/cm, satisfying the decision rule (spinel fraction >0.5 and σ increase).

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of long‑range Co/Fe ordering in Li2Co0.5Fe0.5Cl4 at 500 °C suppressing Li-site disorder/percolation (lowering σ), and that introducing ~10% Sc3+ to create Li vacancies (Li1.9Co0.45Fe0.45Sc0.1Cl4) would disrupt the ordering (loss of superlattice-like peaks near ~24.8° and ~39.4° 2θ) and raise σ by ≥10×. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.9Co0.45Fe0.45Sc0.1Cl4 (500 °C) is single-phase spinel (Fd-3m, Rwp 3.14%) with no missing (unindexed) peaks—specifically, the superlattice-like reflections at 24.78° and 39.42° seen for Li2Co0.5Fe0.5Cl4 (500 °C) are absent—while σ increases to 4.8e-06 S/cm, a ~3.4× improvement over 1.42e-06 S/cm but below the ≥10× target; an extra calculated peak at 15.33° indicates minor model–sample differences without contradicting the disappearance of the prior superlattice features.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of long‑range Co/Fe cation ordering in Li2Co0.5Fe0.5Cl4 at 500 °C suppressing Li-site disorder and percolation, and that introducing slight heterovalent dopant (Sc3+) to create Li vacancies would disrupt this ordering (disappearance of the previously observed unindexed peaks near ~24.8° and ~39.4° 2θ) and raise ionic conductivity. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.95Co0.475Fe0.475Sc0.05Cl4 (500 °C) is predominantly spinel (Fd-3m, 0.9802) with minor ScCl (R-3m, 0.0198), retains an unindexed peak at ~24.55° and shows another at ~50.4° while the ~39.4° feature reported for Li2Co0.5Fe0.5Cl4 (500 °C) is not reported, and its room-temperature conductivity increases to 3.17e-06 S/cm from 1.42e-06 S/cm for Li2Co0.5Fe0.5Cl4; however, conductivity remains below Li2FeCl4 (1.14e-05 S/cm), Li2Mg0.5Fe0.5Cl4 (1.04e-05 S/cm), and Li2Mn0.5Fe0.5Cl4 (2.07e-05 S/cm), indicating that any disruption of ordering is incomplete under these conditions.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of low conductivity in Li1.7Mn0.8Nb0.05V0.15Cl4 arising from V segregation into Li6VCl8 and associated low-angle cation-ordering features in the spinel, and that lowering the synthesis temperature would suppress Li6VCl8 and retain a more disordered, vacancy-rich spinel to restore higher ionic conductivity. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as XRD at 350 °C shows predominantly spinel (Fd-3m, 0.9559 wt) with no Li6VCl8 detected (only minor LiCl, 0.0254 wt, and Nb3Cl8, 0.0187 wt) and a good refinement (Rwp 4.85%), while the room-temperature ionic conductivity increases to 1.59e-05 S/cm from 9.98e-07 S/cm at 400 °C. A residual low-angle extra peak near ~14.7° 2θ persists, indicating some deviation from the ideal spinel model, but the elimination of Li6VCl8 alongside the conductivity recovery meets the predefined success criteria (≥90 wt% spinel and σ approaching/above 1e-5 S/cm), supporting the hypothesis with minor caveats.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of reducing In3+ content (to x=0.05) and lowering the synthesis temperature to 350 °C will suppress diversion into Li6In2−xCl12 and restore the inverse spinel (Fd-3m) with room-temperature ionic conductivity ≥1e-5 S/cm, addressing the prior abnormal formation of Li6In2.12Cl12 for Li1.6In0.1Mn0.8Ta0.1Cl4 at 400 °C. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.65Mn0.85In0.05Ta0.10Cl4 synthesized at 350 °C indexes exclusively to spinel (Fd-3m, 1.0 weight fraction, Rwp 7.41%) with no Li6In2−xCl12 phase reported, indicating successful structural suppression of the In-rich framework; however, several missing peaks and one extra calculated peak point to unmodeled features, and the room-temperature ionic conductivity is 6.09e-06 S/cm, below the 1e-5 S/cm target, so the conductivity criterion is not met.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of In3+-driven stabilization of Li6In2−xCl12-type halide frameworks at 400 °C, enhanced by co-present Ta5+, which diverts In/Ta co-doped compositions away from the inverse spinel; reducing In/Ta contents and synthesis temperature should suppress Li6In2−xCl12 and favor spinel. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.80Mn0.90In0.05Ta0.05Cl4 synthesized at 350 °C indexes predominantly to spinel (Fd-3m, 0.9099) with minor LiCl (Fm-3m, 0.0901), Rwp 5.04%, and no Li6In2−xCl12 is detected; the room-temperature ionic conductivity is 5.44e-06 S/cm, comparable to spinel references. This contrasts the original Li1.6In0.1Mn0.8Ta0.1Cl4 (400 °C), which indexed 100 wt% to Li6In2.12Cl12. Note that two unindexed peaks are present and both composition and temperature were changed concurrently, so the individual contributions of In, Ta, and temperature are not isolated.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Cr in Li1.5Mn0.5Cr0.5Cl4 stabilizing as Cr3+ and forming Li5CrCl8/CrCl3 at 400 °C, which causes phase separation and very low conductivity; using CrCl2 at 350 °C with slightly reduced LiCl and limiting Cr to 20% (Li2Mn0.8Cr0.2Cl4) should force Cr2+ substitution, suppress Li5CrCl8/CrCl3, deliver ≥90 wt% spinel, and raise conductivity into the ≥1e-06–1e-05 S/cm range. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as XRD for Li2Mn0.8Cr0.2Cl4 at 350 °C still contains substantial Li5CrCl8 (0.2626) with only 0.7374 spinel (Rwp 7.15%), failing the ≥90 wt% spinel/no-Li5CrCl8 criterion (CrCl3 not detected), and the room-temperature conductivity is 3.69e-07 S/cm—well below the targeted range and lower than Li2Cr0.5Mn0.5Cl4 (6.92e-06 S/cm), with only a modest increase relative to the original abnormal Li1.5Mn0.5Cr0.5Cl4 (6.76e-08 S/cm).

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of a Mn2+-rich inverse spinel chloride with Li ≈ 1.5, lightly co-doped by V3+ and Nb5+, to create Li-vacancy percolation and frustrate octahedral cation ordering, yielding a spinel-dominant structure and elevated room-temperature ionic conductivity (∼10^-5–10^-4 S/cm). The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.5Mn0.7V0.2Nb0.1Cl4 synthesized at 400 °C is predominantly spinel (spinel (Fd-3m) 97.19 wt% with minor Nb3Cl8 (R3m) 2.81 wt%, Rwp 5.15%), but several unindexed peaks indicate minor additional phases or structural deviations, and the measured ionic conductivity (7.5e-06 S/cm) falls below the targeted range; thus, while the intended spinel framework and vacancy/disorder strategy largely formed, the ionic transport did not reach the anticipated level, likely limited by residual impurity or incomplete dopant incorporation/ordering effects.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of using Mn2+ as the dominant divalent cation with moderate Y3+ (0.2) plus a small Ta5+ addition (0.1) in Li1.5Mn0.7Y0.2Ta0.1Cl4 to set Li = 1.5, thereby introducing Li vacancies and cation-size/valence disorder that suppresses ordering and yields a spinel-dominant inverse spinel chloride with room-temperature ionic conductivity ≥1e-5 S/cm. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as XRD after 400 °C synthesis shows a dominant spinel (Fd-3m) phase (0.7481 wt fraction) with a secondary Li3YCl6 (P-3m1) phase (0.2519 wt fraction) and good refinement quality (Rwp 5.59%) with only minor unindexed/extra peaks, and the measured room-temperature ionic conductivity is 2.08e-05 S/cm; the ~25 wt% Li3YCl6 indicates some Y segregation that could be reduced with further optimization.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of using a metal‑rich inverse spinel topology in Li1.2Mn0.9Nb0.2Cl4 (x=+0.1) to generate a high Li‑vacancy density via Nb5+ while preserving Mn‑dominated disorder (avoiding ordering), thereby opening alternative 3D Li percolation pathways and increasing room‑temperature ionic conductivity. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as XRD at 400 °C refines to a spinel (Fd‑3m) structural model (1.0 weight fraction, Rwp=6.07%) but shows unindexed observed peaks at 34.47°, 34.84°, and 50.21° and a calculated low‑angle peak at 14.68° not present, indicating structural deviations or minor unidentified phases/ordering; moreover, the measured ionic conductivity is 3.93e-06 S/cm at 25 °C, well below the targeted high‑conductivity regime.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of using a Mn2+-rich inverse spinel host with modest aliovalent V3+ substitution (Li1.9Mn0.9V0.1Cl4) to create charge-balanced Li vacancies and Li/M disorder, yielding a high-fraction Fd-3m spinel and enhanced room-temperature ionic conductivity while minimizing V–Cl secondary phases. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as XRD shows a predominant spinel (Fd-3m) phase at 0.9199 wt fraction with a minor Li6VCl8 (Fm-3m) impurity at 0.0801 and a good fit (Rwp = 6.14%), with several small unindexed peaks; the room-temperature ionic conductivity is 8.88e-06 S/cm, near the targeted ~1e-5 S/cm, but the presence of Li6VCl8 indicates V segregation at the 400 °C synthesis temperature, contrary to the goal of fully suppressing secondary phases.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of introducing a modest (10%) highly polarizable trivalent dopant (Bi3+) into the Fe-based inverse spinel chloride (Li1.9Fe0.9Bi0.1Cl4) to tune Li-vacancy concentration, soften the lattice, widen Li+ migration bottlenecks, and obtain a single-phase Fd-3m material with equal or improved room-temperature ionic conductivity relative to the In-doped analog. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as XRD after synthesis at 400 °C shows a predominant spinel (Fd-3m) phase (0.8842) alongside a LiCl (Fm-3m) secondary phase (0.1158) and several unindexed peaks, indicating incomplete single-phase formation or additional minor phases, and the measured conductivity is 1.49e-07 S/cm at 25 °C—below the mid-10^-6 S/cm benchmark of the In-doped reference.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of the abnormal ~3.09e-05 S/cm conductivity in Li1.8Cr0.6Fe0.2Y0.2Cl4 arising either from undetected nanocrystalline/amorphous Li3YCl6 or from partial electronic conduction via Cr2+-containing chlorides (CrCl2/Li2CrCl4). The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as substituting Cr2+ with Mg2+ in Li1.8Mg0.6Fe0.2Y0.2Cl4 (500 °C) yields an XRD pattern dominated by spinel (Fd-3m, 0.9005) with minor Li3YCl6 (P-3m1, 0.0995) and a lower room-temperature conductivity of 9.46e-06 S/cm versus 3.09e-05 S/cm for the Cr-containing sample, consistent with suppression of an electronic-leakage pathway and not supporting hidden Li3YCl6 as the primary cause; confirmation of electronic contribution would require dedicated DC polarization measurements.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of the unexpectedly high σRT in Li1.6Fe0.9Y0.2Cl4 originating from mixed electronic conduction via FeCl2 and/or a nanoscale Li–Y chloride phase; enforcing a charge-balanced inverse spinel (Li1.8Fe0.8Y0.2Cl4) should suppress FeCl2 and lower σ into a spinel-like range if that hypothesis is correct. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.8Fe0.8Y0.2Cl4 synthesized at 500 °C refined to an Fd-3m spinel model at 100 wt% (Rwp 4.44%) with several missing (unindexed) peaks and showed σRT = 3.82e-05 S/cm—higher than both Li2FeCl4 (1.14e-05 S/cm) and the abnormal Li1.6Fe0.9Y0.2Cl4 (7.46e-06 S/cm)—indicating that high conductivity persists without detected FeCl2; while the missing peaks suggest possible minor unidentified features, a separate Li–Y chloride phase is not required to account for the observed high conductivity in this spinel sample.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of mixed electronic conduction via a micro-percolating FeCl2 network and/or an XRD-invisible Li–Y chloride at grain boundaries causing the anomalously high room-temperature conductivity in Li1.6Fe0.9Y0.2Cl4. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.8Mg0.8Y0.2Cl4 synthesized at 500 °C refined to 87.23 wt% spinel (Fd-3m) plus 12.77 wt% Li3YCl6 (P-3m1) and achieved σRT = 1.1e-05 S/cm—comparable to the spinel-rich Li2FeCl4 (1.14e-05 S/cm)—showing that high conductivity persists without Fe/FeCl2 and is consistent with predominantly ionic transport from the inverse-spinel framework, potentially aided by the Li–Y chloride minority phase.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of the anomalous 5.62e-06 S/cm in Li1.6Fe0.9Cr0.2Cl4 at 400 °C being dominated by electronic conduction through FeCl2/CrCl3 pathways, and that forming a vacancy-/disorder-optimized inverse spinel at 500 °C (Li1.5Fe0.8Cr0.3Cl4) would eliminate FeCl2/CrCl3 and raise σRT to ≥1e-4 S/cm. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.5Fe0.8Cr0.3Cl4 (500 °C) refined with a single spinel (Fd-3m) model at 1.0 weight fraction (Rwp 4.76%) and no FeCl2/CrCl3 phases identified, while σRT = 1.11e-05 S/cm—within the expected spinel range (~1e-6–1e-5) but below the ≥1e-4 S/cm target; the missing/extra peaks indicate model/sample mismatch (and possible minor unidentified features), and without transference-number or microstructural measurements the electronic-conduction origin of the 400 °C value in Li1.6Fe0.9Cr0.2Cl4 remains unconfirmed.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of low-temperature synthesis and Zn2+ tetrahedral preference preventing inverse-spinel formation in Li2Fe0.5Zn0.5Cl4, leading to FeCl2/Cmmm phases and ultralow σRT; raising the synthesis temperature (≈450–500 °C) should produce Fd-3m spinel and increase σRT toward ~1e-5–2e-5 S/cm like Mg/Mn analogues. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li2Fe0.5Zn0.5Cl4 synthesized at 500 °C refines as spinel (Fd-3m, 1.0 weight fraction, Rwp 5.99%) and σRT increases to 3.05e-06 S/cm from 1e-08 S/cm, meeting the phase criterion (≥50 wt% spinel) but not the conductivity target; multiple missing/extra peaks indicate deviations from the reference model, consistent with residual structural differences that may limit σRT relative to Mg/Mn analogues (≈1e-5–2e-5 S/cm).

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of the elevated σRT observed for Li2Fe0.7Mn0.1Ni0.2Cl4 arising from micropercolating impurity networks/Maxwell–Wagner effects rather than intrinsic inverse spinel Li-ion transport, with the expectation that re-balancing cations to favor spinel would return σRT to the typical spinel regime. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li2Fe0.85Ni0.10Mn0.05Cl4 synthesized at 500 °C shows a majority spinel (Fd-3m, 0.7635) with secondary Li2FeCl4 (Imma, 0.1727) and MnCl2 (R-3m, 0.0638), Rwp=4.14%, and σRT=1.29e-05 S/cm—consistent with spinel references (e.g., Li2FeCl4: 1.14e-05; Li1.8Fe0.9Mn0.2Cl4: 1.44e-05) and well below ≥1e-4 S/cm, indicating the abnormal σ in decomposed Li2Fe0.7Mn0.1Ni0.2Cl4 is unlikely to reflect intrinsic spinel transport. However, the predefined success criterion of ≥80 wt% Fd-3m with suppressed missing/extra peaks was not fully met, leaving some uncertainty about the exact origin of the elevated σ in the decomposed mixture.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of reducing In3+ to trace levels while maintaining moderate Ta5+ (Li1.50Mn0.80Ta0.15In0.05Cl4) will retain an inverse spinel (Fd-3m) and avoid layered Li–In phases, while vacancy/disorder tuning delivers σ ≥ 2e-05 S/cm—exceeding Ta-only cases. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as XRD indexes entirely to spinel (Fd-3m, 1.0 wt fraction, Rwp 7.09%) with no Li6In2+xCl12 phase detected and no observed unindexed ~15° 2θ feature (the 14.9° entry is an extra peak in the calculated pattern), but several unindexed observed peaks remain (30.08°, 34.73°, 49.61°), and the room-temperature ionic conductivity is 9.4e-06 S/cm—below the ≥2e-05 S/cm target and not higher than the Ta-only benchmark at 400 °C (2.15e-05 S/cm).

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of ZrCl4 volatilization at 450 °C driving Li1.6Mg0.8Zr0.2Cl4 toward a LiCl-rich bulk while trace, underdetected inverse spinel microdomains persist and dominate ionic transport; stabilizing a spinel phase at lower temperature by Fe2+ co-doping (Li1.6Fe0.2Mg0.6Zr0.2Cl4) should yield a spinel-majority pattern and higher σ than LiCl-only baselines, thereby linking the anomalous σ to spinel-derived transport rather than LiCl. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.6Fe0.2Mg0.6Zr0.2Cl4 synthesized at 400 °C shows a single spinel (Fd-3m) phase (weight fraction 1.0, Rwp 8.55%, no extra peaks) and an ionic conductivity of 1.96e-06 S/cm, which exceeds LiCl-only samples (e.g., Li2Ca0.2Mg0.6Sn0.2Cl4: 2.97e-07; Li1.8Bi0.2Ca0.2Mg0.6Cl4: 1.11e-07) and the 400 °C Li1.6Mg0.8Zr0.2Cl4 spinel/ZrCl2 mixture (3.32e-08), consistent with spinel-controlled transport; however, the potential electronic contribution from ZrCl2 and sealed-ampoule retention of Zr were not assessed in this test.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of low synthesis temperature (250 °C) freezing cation ordering in Li2Zn0.5Mg0.5Cl4, which suppresses Li+ transport, and that raising the synthesis temperature would increase Li/M-site disorder in the inverse spinel (Fd-3m) framework and improve room-temperature ionic conductivity. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as the 400 °C sample retains >50% spinel (Fd-3m, 0.5995), shows a markedly improved Rwp (7.43% vs 14.68% at 250 °C) with fewer missing peaks, and exhibits ~19× higher σ_RT (1.88e-07 S/cm vs ~1e-08 S/cm). However, XRD indicates substantial secondary phases (Li2ZnCl4, Pnma: 0.3296; ZnCl2 polymorphs totaling 0.071), and the conductivity remains well below the ≥1e-6 S/cm target and related Co-based spinels, indicating temperature-induced disorder alone is insufficient and, per the decision rule, further vacancy engineering (aliovalent doping) is needed to reach the desired performance.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Zn2+ and Mg2+ co-occupancy stabilizing a cation-ordered, near-normal inverse spinel in Li2Zn0.5Mg0.5Cl4 that limits Li-vacancies and octahedral Li participation; introducing Sc3+ in Li1.85Zn0.425Mg0.425Sc0.15Cl4 at 400 °C should create Li vacancies (y = 0.15), increase M-site disorder, retain ≥50% Fd-3m spinel, and raise σRT toward ≥1e-4 S/cm. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as XRD indexes solely to Li3ScCl6 (C12/m1, 1.0 weight fraction) with no detected Fd-3m spinel, Rwp 7.12% with numerous missing/extra peaks, and the measured room-temperature ionic conductivity is 8.1e-07 S/cm—below the 1e-6 failure threshold and far below the 1e-4 success target—indicating the vacancy/disorder strategy with Sc3+ at 400 °C did not retain the inverse spinel framework or achieve the desired conductivity improvement.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Cr3+ driving octahedral-site preference and cation ordering in Li1.8Mn0.8Cr0.2Cl4, which suppresses Li+ mobility, and that reducing Cr to 5% while co-doping V3+ (Li1.8Mn0.8Cr0.05V0.15Cl4) at the same Li-vacancy level will frustrate ordering (suppress low-angle superlattice reflections) and restore σRT to >1e-5 S/cm. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.8Mn0.8Cr0.05V0.15Cl4 (400 °C) is single-phase spinel (Fd-3m, Rwp 5.16%) and shows markedly reduced low-angle/unindexed features (missing peaks at 15.26° with relative intensity 0.07 and 34.84° with 0.06, versus Li1.8Mn0.8Cr0.2Cl4’s 15.39° at 0.32 and multiple features near 30–35° and 50°), but the room-temperature ionic conductivity only increases modestly to 2.48e-06 S/cm—remaining well below the >1e-5 S/cm target and far under V- or Ta-doped analogs—indicating suppression of ordering signatures alone did not sufficiently enhance conductivity.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Cr3+ in Li1.8Mn0.8Cr0.2Cl4 favoring octahedral coordination and inducing Li/M cation ordering and vacancy clustering at y=0.2, thereby raising Li+ migration barriers; reducing Cr to 10% and lowering the vacancy level (Li1.9Mn0.9Cr0.1Cl4) was expected to weaken ordering signatures and increase σRT. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.9Mn0.9Cr0.1Cl4 (400 °C) is predominantly spinel (Fd-3m, 0.865) with LiCl (Fm-3m, 0.135), shows diminished low-angle (~15° 2θ) features relative to Li1.8Mn0.8Cr0.2Cl4 but retains missing peaks near 30.54°, 34.56°, and 49.76°, and its σRT (1.98e-06 S/cm) remains essentially unchanged versus Li1.8Mn0.8Cr0.2Cl4 (1.88e-06 S/cm), failing to reach ≥1e-5 S/cm; this indicates that lowering Cr content and vacancies does not recover high mobility, consistent with an intrinsic Cr octahedral-site preference suppressing Li+ transport, while vacancy clustering at y=0.2 is not the primary driver.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of replacing Hf4+ with Zr4+ to reduce chloride complexation/volatility, keep V3+ in the spinel framework (avoid Li6VCl8/HfCl4 formation), stabilize octahedral-site disorder, and thereby enhance Li+ mobility relative to the abnormal Li1.65Hf0.1Mn0.75V0.15Cl4 case. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.6Mn0.875Zr0.05V0.15Cl4 synthesized at 400 °C is indexed by XRD as spinel (Fd-3m) with 1.0 weight fraction (Rwp 5.62%) and no identified Li6VCl8 or molecular chloride phases, though several missing peaks remain; however, the room-temperature ionic conductivity is 7.34e-06 S/cm, which is below the stated success threshold (≥1e-4 S/cm) and lower than related Mn–V spinels (e.g., Li1.6Mn0.9V0.2Cl4 at 2.04e-05 S/cm), indicating phase stabilization without the anticipated conductivity enhancement.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of high ionic conductivity arising from a percolative Li3YCl6 grain-boundary network plus Y3+-induced Li-vacancy disorder in an inverse spinel matrix, with conductivity expected to scale with Li3YCl6 connectivity while retaining a spinel-majority bulk. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.6Mg0.6Y0.4Cl4 at 450 °C shows a substantial increase in the Li3YCl6 (P-3m1) fraction (0.5297) compared to z=0.2 (0.0711) and z=0.3 (0.2237), accompanied by a marked rise in room-temperature conductivity to 2.52e-05 S/cm (vs 1.06e-05 and 1.29e-05), indicating a positive σ–Li3YCl6 content correlation; however, the spinel (Fd-3m) fraction drops below 50% (0.4703), failing the predefined criterion of maintaining a spinel-majority bulk, so while σ scales with increased Li3YCl6, the specific spinel-bulk boundary-percolation mechanism is not confirmed.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of high room-temperature conductivity in Li2−y M1±x Cl4 spinels arising from a percolative Li3YCl6 grain-boundary network plus Y3+-induced Li-vacancy/disorder, rather than vacancy content alone. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.6Mg1.2Cl4 (450 °C) shows only a spinel (Fd-3m) phase by XRD (weight fraction 1.0; no Li3YCl6 detected, though several missing peaks indicate some unindexed features) and a lower σ (4.55e-06 S/cm) compared to Y-containing analogues Li1.8Mg0.8Y0.2Cl4 (1.06e-05 S/cm) and Li1.7Mg0.7Y0.3Cl4 (1.29e-05 S/cm), aligning instead with spinel-rich peers (~2.2–6.1e-06 S/cm). This indicates that matching Li-vacancy content without Li3YCl6-like boundary phases does not reproduce the higher conductivity, consistent with the proposed boundary-percolation mechanism.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Y3+-induced formation of Li3YCl6 boundary phases and Li-vacancy disorder in the inverse spinel Li2−y M1±x Cl4 framework leading to monotonic increases in room-temperature ionic conductivity with increasing Y content while maintaining a spinel-majority microstructure. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.67Mg0.67Y0.33Cl4 (450 °C) shows spinel (Fd-3m) 0.6554 and Li3YCl6 (P-3m1) 0.3446—higher Li3YCl6 fraction than Li1.7Mg0.7Y0.3Cl4 (0.2237) and Li1.8Mg0.8Y0.2Cl4 (0.0711)—with σ = 2.33e-05 S/cm, exceeding σ for Li1.7Mg0.7Y0.3Cl4 (1.29e-05 S/cm) and Li1.8Mg0.8Y0.2Cl4 (1.06e-05 S/cm), while retaining spinel ≥0.5; however, the increase is moderate and remains below 1e-4 S/cm, indicating partial progress toward the targeted percolation-enhanced conductivity.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of combining Mg/Mn with limited Y3+ and Nb5+ in an inverse spinel Li2−yM1±xCl4 to create a robust Li-vacancy network and octahedral-site disorder that stabilizes a predominantly spinel phase and raises room-temperature Li+ conductivity to ~1e-5 S/cm without Li3YCl6 phase dominance. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.5Mg0.55Mn0.15Y0.2Nb0.1Cl4 formed mostly spinel (Fd-3m, 0.8002 wt) with minority Li3YCl6 (P-3m1, 0.1998 wt), achieved near-1e-5 S/cm conductivity (8.89e-06 S/cm) with good refinement (Rwp 7.16%), though several small unindexed peaks indicate additional minor phases or ordering and the product was not single-phase.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of using mixed-valent Mg–Y–Nb with slight M deficiency in Li1.75Mg0.7Y0.2Nb0.05Cl4 to destabilize long-range cation/Li-vacancy ordering, maintain an Fd-3m spinel-majority phase with limited Li3YCl6 formation, and thereby increase room-temperature ionic conductivity via a 3D Li-vacancy network. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as XRD shows a spinel (Fd-3m) majority (0.918) with a minor Li3YCl6 (P-3m1) fraction (0.082), but the refinement quality is modest (Rwp 12.10%) with numerous missing peaks indicating additional unidentified phases or structural distortions, and the measured ionic conductivity (1.37e-06 S/cm at 25 °C) is lower than the ~1e-05 to 6e-06 S/cm benchmarks, indicating the intended transport enhancement was not achieved.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of combining Mg to stabilize the inverse spinel framework (Fd-3m), introducing Y3+ to create Li vacancies, and adding a small amount of soft Cu+ to increase lattice polarizability and frustrate cation ordering—together targeting a spinel-majority Li1.7Mg0.9Y0.1Cu0.2Cl4 with reduced Li+ migration barriers and higher room-temperature ionic conductivity. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as no data were collected (the outcome array is empty), providing no XRD evidence of spinel formation or cation disorder and no ionic conductivity measurement to validate the proposed performance gains.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of using a Mg/Mn-based inverse spinel host with low-level Ni2+ and Y3+ doping to introduce a moderate Li-vacancy concentration (Li1.8Mg0.5Mn0.2Ni0.1Y0.2Cl4), maintain the Fd-3m spinel framework, avoid NiCl2 impurity seen in Ni-rich systems, and leverage lattice expansion and cation disorder to increase room-temperature ionic conductivity relative to Mg–Mn analogs. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as XRD at a synthesis temperature of 400 °C refines to a single spinel (Fd-3m) phase (weight fraction 1.0, Rwp 8.03%) with no NiCl2 detected, consistent with the impurity-avoidance and spinel-retention aspects; however, several unindexed low-intensity peaks suggest subtle structural deviations or minor unidentified phases, and the measured ionic conductivity is 3.45e-06 S/cm at 25 °C, slightly below the Mg–Mn benchmark (~5e-06 S/cm), indicating the anticipated conductivity enhancement was not achieved under these conditions.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of co-doping a Mn2+-rich inverse spinel chloride (Li2−yMCl4) with V3+ (0.15) and Hf4+ (0.05) to set y≈0.25 (Li1.75Mn0.80V0.15Hf0.05Cl4), expand the lattice via Mn2+, frustrate Li/M-vacancy ordering, retain the disordered Fd-3m spinel, and thereby achieve higher room-temperature Li-ion conductivity. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as XRD at 400 °C shows a single-phase spinel (Fd-3m) with good refinement (Rwp 4.40%) and no missing/extra peaks—consistent with retaining the target spinel without apparent symmetry-lowering ordering—however the measured room-temperature ionic conductivity is only 6.88e-06 S/cm, which is lower than the anticipated high σRT for the y≈0.25 window, so the conductivity enhancement was not realized.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of tri-valent Y3+ substitution (~20%) into a Mn2+-rich inverse spinel Li2−yM1Cl4 host to create ~0.2 Li vacancies while preserving Fd-3m spinel, with the larger Mn2+-based lattice and Li/M octahedral disorder lowering migration barriers and enhancing room-temperature Li+ conductivity. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as XRD shows the spinel (Fd-3m) phase as the major component (0.8708) but with a significant Li3YCl6 (P-3m1) secondary phase (0.1292) and a missing peak at 34.59°, indicating incomplete Y incorporation and possible additional phases/structural deviations; furthermore, the room-temperature ionic conductivity is 1.99e-05 S/cm, which is well below the expected high-conductivity regime.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of the abnormal high conductivity in Li1.8Cr0.6Fe0.2Y0.2Cl4 arising either from undetected nanocrystalline/amorphous Li3YCl6 or from partial electronic conduction through Cr2+-containing chlorides. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as replacing Cr with Mn/Mg in Li1.6Mn0.4Mg0.2Y0.4Cl4 (450 °C) produced XRD-matched phases spinel (Fd-3m) 0.4903, Li3YCl6 (P-3m1) 0.2479, MgCl2 (P-3m1) 0.1665, and Li13.52Mg9.28Cl32 (Fd-3m) 0.0953 (Rwp 6.29%) and a room-temperature conductivity of 1.44e-05 S/cm—typical of Y3+-containing spinel/Li3YCl6 mixtures (Li1.5Mg0.5Y0.5Cl4 1.49e-05; Li1.5Mn0.5Y0.5Cl4 2.4e-05) and lower than Cr-bearing mixtures (Li1.6Cr0.4Mn0.2Y0.4Cl4 5.24e-05; Li1.8Cr0.6Fe0.2Y0.2Cl4 3.09e-05). This disfavors hidden Li3YCl6 as the sole cause of the abnormal conductivity and is consistent with an electronic contribution in the Cr-containing samples, though direct transference-number measurements would be required for confirmation.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of the abnormal behavior of Li2Fe0.5Zn0.5Cl4 arising from Zn2+ tetrahedral preference and low-temperature (250 °C) synthesis preventing formation of an inverse-spinel (Fd-3m) phase; increasing synthesis temperature to 450 °C and reducing Zn content (with slight Li vacancy introduction) should promote spinel formation and recover σRT toward the ~1e-5 S/cm level observed in Mg/Mn analogues. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.9Fe0.7Zn0.35Cl4 synthesized at 450 °C is indexed as spinel (Fd-3m, 1.0 weight fraction, Rwp 5.23%) with a few missing/extra peaks and exhibits σRT = 1.04e-05 S/cm—~3 orders of magnitude higher than Li2Fe0.5Zn0.5Cl4 (1e-08 S/cm) and comparable to Li2Mg0.5Fe0.5Cl4 (1.04e-05 S/cm) and Li2Mn0.5Fe0.5Cl4 (2.07e-05 S/cm); although it does not reach ≥1e-4 S/cm, the formation of a spinel-indexed phase and restoration of typical conductivity corroborate the hypothesis, while the individual effects of temperature vs. Zn content are not isolated by this single experiment.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of increasing Sc to α = 0.55 in Li1.45Mn0.45Sc0.55Cl4 to raise the Li-vacancy concentration and further frustrate Li/M octahedral ordering, thereby stabilizing a disordered Fd-3m spinel and boosting σ_RT to ≥1e-4 S/cm. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as the 450 °C product is predominantly spinel (Fd-3m, 0.8998) with minor MnCl2 (0.1002), shows only small unmatched XRD features, and delivers σ_RT = 4.17e-05 S/cm—below the ≥1e-4 S/cm target and lower than Li1.5Mn0.5Sc0.5Cl4 at 450 °C (6.43e-05 S/cm)—indicating that raising Sc from 0.5 to 0.55 did not enhance conductivity and, within this dataset, performance appears optimized near α ≈ 0.5.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of introducing aliovalent Sc3+ and V3+ to create Li vacancies (y≈0.5) and disrupt Li/M octahedral ordering—factors proposed to cause the abnormally low conductivity in Li2MnCl4. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.5Mn0.5Sc0.4V0.1Cl4 synthesized at 450 °C refines as single-phase spinel (Fd-3m, 1.0; Rwp 5.45%) with only minor high-angle missing peaks (49.81° and 82.88°) and no reported low-angle superlattice reflections, and achieves σRT = 5.2e-05 S/cm—much higher than Li2MnCl4 (8.81e-07 S/cm) and comparable to prior Sc-doped samples—yet it does not meet the ≥1e-4 S/cm target; microstructure effects were not independently probed here.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Zr4+-driven octahedral/Li-vacancy ordering with concurrent ZrCl2 formation in Li1.6Mg0.8Zr0.2Cl4 suppressing Li+ transport, and that partial Sc3+ co-doping would disrupt these ordering signatures, eliminate ZrCl2, and raise σ to ≥1e-6 S/cm while retaining a spinel-rich phase. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.5Mg0.7Zr0.2Sc0.1Cl4 synthesized at 450 °C shows a single spinel (Fd-3m) phase (1.0) with no ZrCl2 identified, no extra low-angle peaks (only moderate-intensity missing peaks), and a room-temperature ionic conductivity of 3.48e-06 S/cm—substantially higher than Li1.6Mg0.8Zr0.2Cl4 at 400 °C (3.32e-08 S/cm, spinel 0.8888 with ZrCl2 0.1112 and extra low-angle peaks) and higher than the LiCl-dominant Li1.6Mg0.8Zr0.2Cl4 at 450 °C (1.27e-06 S/cm); these results meet the predefined decision rule (≥90% spinel, no ZrCl2, σ ≥1e-6 S/cm).

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of TaCl5 volatility at 450 °C suppressing bulk inverse spinel formation in Li1.4Mg0.8Ta0.2Cl4, with residual disordered spinel microphases contributing to the anomalously high conductivity; Ta-rich, Li-deficient stoichiometry should retain Ta, increase the spinel fraction, improve the XRD fit, and raise σ. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.3Mg0.8Ta0.22Cl4 (450 °C) indexes as spinel (Fd-3m, 1.0) with a lower Rwp (13.53% vs 15.39% for the LiCl-only Li1.4Mg0.8Ta0.2Cl4 at 450 °C), consistent with improved spinel formation, but the room-temperature ionic conductivity (1.61e-06 S/cm) does not surpass the original 1.82e-06 S/cm and remains well below the Fe-stabilized spinel Li1.4Fe0.2Mg0.6Ta0.2Cl4 (6.1e-06 S/cm); persistent missing peaks indicate unresolved features relative to the spinel model. Thus, Ta compensation appears to stabilize the spinel structure at 450 °C, but it did not deliver the expected conductivity improvement.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of using divalent metal excess (x≈+0.1) and corresponding Li deficiency (y≈0.2) in the inverse spinel chloride Li1.8Mn0.7Sn0.4Cl4 to retain Fd-3m spinel disorder while the soft/polarizable Sn2+ and lattice expansion from Mn2+ lower Li+ migration barriers, yielding high room-temperature ionic conductivity (anticipated when synthesized near 500 °C to avoid low-T cation ordering). The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as XRD shows the targeted spinel (Fd-3m) as the majority phase (≈0.8591 weight fraction) with a minor LiCl impurity (≈0.1409), a good refinement (Rwp = 6.18%), and minor missing/extra peaks suggesting structural deviations; however, the room-temperature ionic conductivity is low (3.13e-06 S/cm), well below the expected high-σ regime, and the synthesis at 400 °C (below the proposed ~500 °C) may have limited disorder and contributed to impurity formation, likely suppressing ionic transport.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of engineering an inverse spinel chloride Li1.66Mn0.78V0.16Ta0.06Cl4 with mixed-valence co-doping (Mn2+, V3+, low-level Ta5+) to set y≈0.34 Li vacancies, maintain Fd-3m spinel disorder, frustrate cation ordering, and thereby enable robust 3D Li+ percolation and high room-temperature ionic conductivity. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as XRD shows the target spinel (Fd-3m) as the majority phase (0.8943) but with significant secondary phases Li6VCl8 (Fm-3m, 0.0917) and TaCl4 (C12/m1, 0.014) plus one unindexed low-angle peak, indicating incomplete dopant incorporation/phase segregation; despite the cubic spinel framework, the room-temperature ionic conductivity is low (4.12e-06 S/cm), inconsistent with the expected high-σ disorder–vacancy regime.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of using a Li‑deficient inverse spinel (Li2−yM1±xCl4) with Fe2+ as the divalent host and co‑doping with V3+ (~0.2) and Ta5+ (~0.1) to set ~0.5 Li vacancies per formula unit, preserve disordered Fd‑3m symmetry (minimize cation ordering and low‑angle superlattice features), and thereby achieve room‑temperature Li‑ion conductivity in the 10^-5–10^-4 S/cm range. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.5Fe0.7V0.2Ta0.1Cl4 synthesized at 400 °C is single‑phase spinel (Fd‑3m, 100 wt%) with a good refinement (Rwp 3.75%), no extra calculated peaks, and only a few weak unindexed reflections at 30.32°, 35.06°, and 50.13° (indicating minor deviations but no evident ordering or secondary phases), and it exhibits 1.65e-05 S/cm ionic conductivity at 25 °C, which falls within the predicted performance range.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of reducing Y3+ content while increasing Ta5+ at Li=1.45 in Li1.45Mn0.75Y0.10Ta0.15Cl4 to suppress Li3YCl6 formation, preserve a >90% inverse spinel (Fd-3m) matrix with high Li-vacancy fraction and cation-site disorder, and thereby push room-temperature ionic conductivity toward ≥1e-4 S/cm. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as XRD refines to spinel (Fd-3m) as the sole modeled phase (weight fraction 1.0, Rwp 5.83%), indicating successful suppression of the Li3YCl6 impurity, but several unindexed low- and mid-angle peaks suggest cation ordering/distortions or minor unidentified phases; moreover, the measured ionic conductivity is 5e-06 S/cm, well below the targeted ≥1e-4 S/cm and lower than prior Y-richer compositions, implying that the intended vacancy/disorder tuning at 400 °C did not translate into enhanced Li+ transport.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of combining mixed Mn2+/Ni2+ with aliovalent V3+/Ta5+ at Li≈1.5 in an inverse spinel chloride to frustrate Li/M ordering, suppress superlattice features/impurity formation, and thereby achieve room-temperature ionic conductivity approaching ≥1e-4 S/cm. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as the XRD shows a majority spinel (Fd-3m) phase at 0.7675 with notable secondary phases LiCl (Fm-3m, 0.141) and MnCl2 (R-3m, 0.0916), Rwp (%) = 5.49% with one minor unindexed peak at 52.69°, and the measured ionic conductivity is 7.22e-07 S/cm—orders of magnitude below the target—indicating that the intended disorder-enhanced conduction was not realized under these synthesis conditions for Li1.5Mn0.4Ni0.3V0.2Ta0.1Cl4.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of co-introducing V3+ (~0.2) with a small amount of Nb5+ (0.1) into a Co2+-based inverse spinel chloride host at Li ≈ 1.5 (Li1.5Co0.7V0.2Nb0.1Cl4) to generate charge/size disorder on the 16d sublattice, suppress cation ordering and Li6VCl8 formation, and thereby yield a predominant Fd-3m phase with room-temperature ionic conductivity in the high-10^-5 to ~10^-4 S/cm range. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as XRD shows a single spinel (Fd-3m) phase at 400 °C with a good refinement (Rwp 3.12%) and no Li6VCl8 identified, though several low-intensity missing and extra peaks indicate subtle structural deviations; however, the measured ionic conductivity is 6.06e-07 S/cm at 25 °C, which is well below the targeted conductivity range.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of using a metal-rich inverse spinel Li2−yM1+xCl4 motif with Ni2+ as the backbone and low-level V3+ (Li1.4Ni1.0V0.2Cl4; total M = 1.2) to create Li vacancies and cation disorder that suppresses Li6VCl8, yields a dominant Fd-3m inverse spinel fraction, and increases room-temperature Li+ conductivity.
