The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as XRD shows substantial phase segregation with NiCl2 (R-3m) at 0.5196 weight fraction and spinel (Fd-3m) only 0.4804, along with minor missing/extra peaks (32.86° and 84.2°) indicating model/sample mismatch; no Li6VCl8 is detected, but the large NiCl2 impurity suggests the metal-rich stoichiometry drove NiCl2 formation rather than a single-phase inverse spinel. The room-temperature ionic conductivity is very low (2.1e-08 S/cm at 25 °C), contradicting the targeted enhancement. Under the 500 °C synthesis, the intended vacancy/disorder strategy did not yield a dominant spinel phase nor improved conductivity.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of elevated ionic conductivity in Li1.7Mg0.7Y0.3Cl4 being driven by increased Li3YCl6 boundary-phase connectivity at fixed Y content, with higher synthesis temperature converting residual YCl3 to Li3YCl6 and boosting σ via grain-boundary percolation while maintaining a spinel majority. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as the 500 °C synthesis yields spinel (Fd-3m) 0.7822 and Li3YCl6 (P-3m1) 0.2178 with no detectable YCl3, i.e., the Li3YCl6 fraction did not increase versus 450 °C (0.2237) and the room-temperature ionic conductivity only rose modestly from 1.29e-05 to 1.77e-05 S/cm, well below the ≥1e-4 S/cm decision threshold for percolation-driven enhancement.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of excessive Hf4+ co-doping in Li1.65Hf0.1Mn0.75V0.15Cl4 fracturing inverse spinel stability by partitioning V into Li6VCl8 and Hf into molecular chlorides, and that lowering Hf to ~3% while keeping V3+ at 15% would restore a spinel-dominant phase and room-temperature conductivity. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.65Mn0.89Hf0.03V0.15Cl4 synthesized at 350 °C shows a majority spinel (Fd-3m) fraction (0.8367) with a residual Li6VCl8 impurity (0.1633) and no extra peaks (Rwp 6.12%), indicating improved spinel stability relative to the Hf-rich abnormal case, but the ionic conductivity is low (1.65e-06 S/cm) and several missing peaks persist, so conductivity recovery and full suppression of competing phases were not achieved.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of the Mn–Nb–V inverse spinel being metastable near a narrow stability boundary, with strong sensitivity to Cl chemical potential and precise Nb content; at 400 °C small deviations (e.g., Cl loss or reduction) drive decomposition to MnCl2, so synthesizing at 350–380 °C while keeping Nb in the 0.03–0.07 range and maintaining a Cl reservoir should retain the spinel and, with added Li vacancies, improve Li+ conductivity. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.64Mn0.78Nb0.07V0.15Cl4 synthesized at 350 °C is predominantly spinel (Fd-3m 0.9378) with minor LiCl (Fm-3m 0.0622), good refinement (Rwp 4.39%), and no MnCl2 detected—consistent with temperature/Cl-potential sensitivity and avoidance of the 400 °C decomposition; however, the room-temperature ionic conductivity is 1.02e-05 S/cm, below the ≥3e-05 S/cm target and lower than related Nb=0.03–0.05 compositions (1.59e-05–1.63e-05 S/cm), indicating that increasing Li-vacancy content to Li=1.64 did not enhance conductivity under these conditions.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Cl/F anion-site mixing in Li1.4Fe0.8Ta0.2Cl3.6F0.4 introducing additional configurational disorder that intrinsically enhances Li+ transport, while the F-containing batch also achieving higher phase purity (no LiCl) compared to Li1.4Fe0.8Ta0.2Cl4; a phase-pure Cl-only control at 450 °C isolates the intrinsic Cl/F effect. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.4Fe0.8Ta0.2Cl4 synthesized at 450 °C forms single-phase spinel (Fd-3m, 1.0; Rwp = 3.70%) and shows σRT = 2.35e-05 S/cm—higher than the LiCl-containing 400 °C Cl-only sample (8.96e-06 S/cm) yet still below the F-mixed Li1.4Fe0.8Ta0.2Cl3.6F0.4 at 400 °C (3.03e-05 S/cm), indicating that removing LiCl improves σ but anion-site mixing retains a measurable intrinsic conductivity advantage.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of cation/Li-vacancy ordering in Li1.4Mg0.8Ta0.2Cl4 (stabilized at lower synthesis temperature) suppressing ionic conductivity, and that introducing a small disordering dopant (Sc3+) at constant Li content would frustrate Ta–VLi ordering, reduce low-angle superlattice features, and increase σ. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.4Mg0.8Ta0.17Sc0.05Cl4 (450 °C) refines as spinel (Fd-3m, 1.0) with improved Rwp (9.96% vs 13.77% for Li1.4Mg0.8Ta0.2Cl4 at 450 °C), shows no extra peaks and lacks the prominent low-angle feature (e.g., ~15°) seen in the Ta-only sample, and achieves higher σ_RT (4.31e-06 S/cm) relative to Li1.4Mg0.8Ta0.2Cl4 at 450 °C (1.82e-06 S/cm) and far above the 400 °C sample (6.8e-08 S/cm). Some missing peaks at 34.9°, 50.14°, and 84.14° remain, but overall the reduction of low-angle discrepancies and the conductivity gain are consistent with the ordering-based explanation.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Y3+ being largely outside the inverse-spinel solubility field at high Y in Li1.5Co0.5Y0.5Cl4, driving Li3YCl6 formation and that the abnormal high σRT is dominated by Li3YCl6 rather than the spinel framework. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.9Co0.9Y0.1Cl4 (450 °C) refines as single-phase spinel (Fd-3m, Rwp 2.85%) with no Li3YCl6 phase identified and σRT = 1.87e-06 S/cm—within spinel baselines and ~12× lower than Li1.5Co0.5Y0.5Cl4 (2.3e-05 S/cm). While several low-intensity unindexed peaks are present, they do not establish Li3YCl6 in this sample; overall the data indicate that reducing Y to 10% restores spinel behavior and removes the impurity-dominated high conductivity observed at 50% Y.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of cation/vacancy ordering in Li1.7Co0.9Ta0.1Cl4 (including a Li2CoCl4-like Cmmm impurity and superlattice features around ~15°) causing anomalously low room-temperature ionic conductivity, which should be mitigated by higher-temperature synthesis that increases Li/M site disorder. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as the 450 °C synthesis yields single-phase spinel (Fd-3m, 1.0) with no detected Li2CoCl4 (Cmmm), markedly weaker superlattice-like misfits (e.g., missing peak at ~15.33° with 0.07 relative intensity vs prior extra peak at ~15.47° with 0.61), and a ~9× increase in σ_RT from 6.71e-08 S/cm (400 °C) to 6.12e-07 S/cm, despite some residual missing peaks indicating remaining structural deviations.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of the abnormally low σRT in Li1.9Fe0.9Bi0.1Cl4 arising primarily from BiCl3 volatilization/limited Bi solubility that induces LiCl exsolution, rather than an intrinsic Bi3+ (6s2) lone-pair–driven cation/Li-vacancy ordering that narrows Li-ion pathways; reducing Bi to x=0.05 at 400 °C should produce single-phase inverse spinel with restored σ in the typical 10^-6–10^-5 S/cm range. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.95Fe0.95Bi0.05Cl4 refined to spinel (Fd-3m) at 1.0 weight fraction (Rwp 5.92%) with minor unindexed features and achieved σRT = 7.68e-06 S/cm—much higher than Li1.9Fe0.9Bi0.1Cl4 (1.49e-07 S/cm) and comparable to single-phase references (e.g., Li2FeCl4 = 1.14e-05 S/cm, Li1.9Fe0.9In0.1Cl4 = 6.4e-06 S/cm)—indicating the prior suppression was largely linked to impurity formation/Bi loss rather than an intrinsic ordering effect, though the presence of low-intensity missing/extra peaks means subtle structural deviations cannot be ruled out.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of the elevated conductivity in Li1.5Mn0.7Y0.2Ta0.1Cl4 being dominated by a percolating/connected Li3YCl6 secondary phase rather than intrinsic inverse-spinel transport. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.6Mn0.8Y0.1Ta0.1Cl4 synthesized at 400 °C shows no Li3YCl6 by XRD (spinel (Fd-3m) 0.9468 with minor LiCl (Fm-3m) 0.0532; Rwp 5.58%) and its room-temperature ionic conductivity drops to 1.0e-05 S/cm from 2.08e-05 S/cm in the Li3YCl6-containing sample, consistent with the decision rule that suppressing Li3YCl6 reduces σ toward intrinsic spinel values.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of excess octahedral metal content with high‑valence Nb5+ in Li1.2Mn0.9Nb0.2Cl4 driving Li/M octahedral ordering (manifested by a ~14–16° 2θ superlattice feature) and vacancy clustering that collapse the 3D Li percolation network; reducing metal excess (to M=1.0) and synthesizing at 400 °C in Li1.4Mn0.8Nb0.2Cl4 should suppress ordering and increase σ. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.4Mn0.8Nb0.2Cl4 (400 °C) refines as single‑phase spinel (Fd‑3m, Rwp 5.45%) with no extra low‑angle (~14–16° 2θ) peak and delivers higher σ (2.63e‑05 S/cm) than both the abnormal Li1.2Mn0.9Nb0.2Cl4 (3.93e‑06 S/cm) and the 450 °C Li1.4Mn0.8Nb0.2Cl4 (8.36e‑06 S/cm), consistent with suppressed ordering correlating with improved transport; the presence of several mid‑angle missing peaks indicates residual deviations/unindexed features but does not contradict the observed conductivity increase.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of concurrent Sc3+ and In3+ additions stabilizing Li3MCl6-type (Li3ScCl6) frameworks at the expense of the inverse spinel field, with In3+ seeding Li3MCl6; removing In while retaining Sc3+ (0.2) and charge-neutral Li content (Li=1.8) should favor the Fd-3m spinel at lower temperature. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.8Mg0.8Sc0.2Cl4 synthesized at 400 °C exhibits a majority inverse spinel phase (Fd-3m, 0.7199 weight fraction) with only LiCl (0.21) and MgCl2 (0.0701) impurities, no Li3ScCl6 detected, Rwp=9.78% with no missing peaks and one small extra peak, and σ=6.91e-07 S/cm; this contrasts with the In-containing Li1.6In0.2Mg0.6Sc0.2Cl4 (500 °C) and Li1.85Zn0.425Mg0.425Sc0.15Cl4 (400 °C), both of which crystallized entirely as Li3ScCl6, indicating that removing In suppresses Li3ScCl6 formation and retains the spinel field under comparable synthesis conditions.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of the anomalously low conductivity in Li1.4Mg0.2Ni0.2Y0.6Cl4 arising from Ni-induced blocking—i.e., Li3YCl6 present but isolated by an insulating YCl3/Li2MgCl4 matrix and/or undetected Ni-rich boundary phases—with possible suppression of Li-vacancy mobility by Ni; removing Ni should restore Li3YCl6 connectivity and raise σ to the ~1e-5 S/cm range at 500 °C. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.4Mg0.4Y0.6Cl4 (500 °C) shows Li3YCl6 (P-3m1) as the majority phase (0.7422) with MgCl2 (P-3m1) as the secondary phase (0.2578), an Rwp of 7.89%, and a recovered σRT of 3.97e-05 S/cm—over three orders of magnitude higher than 2.96e-08 S/cm for Li1.4Mg0.2Ni0.2Y0.6Cl4—consistent with removal of Ni-related blocking and not with a fundamental percolation failure at this Li:Y ratio/temperature; minor missing/extra peaks indicate some unmodeled features but do not detract from the overall conclusion.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of vacancy/disorder optimization via Y3+ substitution in inverse spinel Li2−yFe1−xYxCl4: specifically, that increasing to x=y≈0.25 and synthesizing at higher temperature should suppress cation/Li-vacancy ordering, enhance Li/M octahedral disorder, and strengthen the 16d–48f–16c Li+ percolation network to push σRT toward or beyond 1e-4 S/cm while retaining >50% inverse spinel fraction. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.75Fe0.75Y0.25Cl4 synthesized at 500 °C shows a majority spinel (Fd-3m) phase fraction of 0.8135 with Rwp 4.92% and σRT = 4.63e-05 S/cm—higher than Li2FeCl4 (1.14e-05 S/cm) and slightly above Li1.8Fe0.8Y0.2Cl4 (3.82e-05 S/cm)—but it also contains Li3YCl6 (P-3m1) at 0.1865, did not achieve ≥1e-4 S/cm, and exhibits missing peaks at 49.77° and 80.03°, leaving suppression of ordering and attainment of a fully optimized single-phase inverse spinel unconfirmed.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of whether the anomalously high ionic conductivity in Li1.8Fe0.8In0.2Cl4 at 500 °C (despite only spinel + LiCl detected by XRD) originates from intrinsic Li-vacancy/disorder in the inverse spinel (y≈0.2) or from undetected Li–In grain-boundary phases. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.8Fe1.1Cl4 synthesized at 500 °C refines to predominantly spinel (Fd-3m, 0.9515 wt) with only LiCl (0.0485 wt), no FeCl2 detected by XRD (Rwp 4.28%), and exhibits σRT = 4.3e-05 S/cm—higher than single-phase references (Li2FeCl4: 1.14e-05 S/cm; Li1.9Fe0.9In0.1Cl4: 6.4e-06 S/cm) and exceeding Li1.8Fe0.8In0.2Cl4 (2.72e-05 S/cm)—indicating elevated conductivity without any In-containing phase and therefore favoring an intrinsic vacancy/disorder mechanism over Li–In boundary conduction. Minor missing/extra peaks suggest subtle model–sample differences but do not alter this conclusion.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Bi3+ (stereochemically active 6s2 lone pair) promotes cation/Li-vacancy ordering and symmetry lowering in Li1.8Bi0.2Ca0.2Mg0.6Cl4, with Ca2+ further stabilizing this ordered, low-conductivity variant; removing Ca should reduce ordering signatures in XRD and raise σ. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.8Bi0.2Mg0.8Cl4 (500 °C) remains single-phase spinel (Fd-3m, 1.0) but shows markedly fewer/weaker missing peaks than Li1.8Bi0.2Ca0.2Mg0.6Cl4 (missing peaks reduced from 15 to 7; key intensities drop at 34.84° from 0.68 to 0.25 (~63%), at 50.05° from 0.35 to 0.08 (~77%), at 33.58° from 0.20 to 0.05 (~75%), and the 30° region from 0.76 to 0.43 (~43%)), extra peaks disappear (old 14.74°/0.26 → none), Rwp improves (13.43% → 10.49%), and σ increases ~28× (1.11e-07 → 3.12e-06 S/cm), reaching the range of related disordered spinels (e.g., Li2MgCl4 = 3.16e-06 S/cm). These changes meet the ≥5× σ criterion and show ≥50% reductions for multiple missing peaks, indicating Ca2+ had a stabilizing role in the ordered, low-σ state while Bi alone still leaves residual ordering but not enough to suppress conductivity abnormally.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of using a Mn2+-host inverse spinel with mixed Y3+ and In3+ (total M3+ = 0.5) to create ~0.5 Li vacancies in Li1.5Mn0.5Y0.25In0.25Cl4, thereby stabilizing the Fd-3m spinel, suppressing Li3YCl6 formation, and achieving high room-temperature ionic conductivity via a disordered, vacancy-rich Li migration network. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as XRD at 400 °C shows a single-phase spinel (Fd-3m, 1.0 weight fraction) with good refinement quality (Rwp 5.87%), and only minor unindexed/extra peaks suggesting subtle disorder rather than a dominant secondary phase, while the measured σRT = 1.19e-4 S/cm exceeds the targeted high-10^-5 S/cm range, consistent with the proposed vacancy/disorder and lattice-softening mechanisms.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of using a Mn-host inverse spinel chloride, Li1.5Mn0.4V0.25Y0.25Mg0.1Cl4, with ~0.5 fraction of trivalent dopants (V3+ + Y3+) and a small Mg2+ addition to create y≈0.5 Li-vacancy percolation and multi-cation disorder on 16d, suppress cation ordering, reduce Li3YCl6 formation, and yield >50% spinel with room-temperature conductivity in the few×10^-5 S/cm range after 400–450 °C synthesis. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as XRD shows a majority spinel phase (spinel (Fd-3m) 0.805) alongside a minor Li3YCl6 (P-3m1) phase (0.195) with good refinement quality (Rwp 6.42%), though one missing low-angle peak and several extra calculated peaks indicate deviations/disorder relative to the ideal model; the measured σ_RT is 2.64e-05 S/cm at 25 °C, meeting the lower end of the targeted range and modestly improving over the Y-only comparator, but not surpassing the Mn–Sc–V benchmark, and the persistence of a ~20% Li3YCl6 side phase shows Y segregation was reduced but not eliminated.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of configuring an inverse spinel chloride Li1.5Mn0.5Y0.2Bi0.3Cl4 with Σ(M3+)≈0.5 (Y3+ + Bi3+) to achieve L≈1.5 (y≈0.5), thereby creating a vacancy-rich Li sublattice; using Bi3+ to soften the Cl framework via high polarizability; and leveraging mixed Y3+/Bi3+ to frustrate octahedral ordering, stabilize an Fd-3m majority at 400–450 °C, and increase room-temperature ionic conductivity relative to Li1.5Mn0.5Y0.5Cl4. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as XRD at 400 °C shows a majority spinel (Fd-3m) phase at 0.7217 (meeting the >50% target) but with a significant secondary phase Li3YCl6 (P-3m1) at 0.2783 and several unindexed peaks indicating additional minor phases or subtle ordering/distortion; moreover, the room-temperature ionic conductivity (1.49e-05 S/cm) is lower than the referenced Li1.5Mn0.5Y0.5Cl4 (2.4e-05 S/cm), so the anticipated conductivity enhancement was not realized despite achieving a spinel-majority structure.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of engineering an inverse spinel chloride Li1.5Mn0.3Fe0.2Y0.25In0.25Cl4 with L≈1.5 and Σ(3+)≈0.5 (Y3+ + In3+) to introduce Li vacancies and maximize 16d cation disorder via four-cation mixing (Mn2+/Fe2+/Y3+/In3+), thereby suppressing cation ordering and avoiding Li3YCl6 dominance, to yield a spinel-majority microstructure with high-10^-5 S/cm room-temperature ionic conductivity under 400–450 °C processing. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as XRD shows a spinel (Fd-3m) majority phase at 71.3 wt% with a secondary Li6In2.12Cl12 (C12/m1) phase at 28.7 wt% (Rwp = 5.91%), consistent with spinel-majority formation at 400 °C; and the measured ionic conductivity is 0.00014 S/cm (1.4×10^-4 S/cm), exceeding the targeted high-10^-5 range. While several missing/extra peaks indicate subtle structural deviations and the In-rich secondary phase suggests some segregation, the absence of Li3YCl6 and the high conductivity achieved support the proposed disorder/vacancy-driven conduction mechanism.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of combining moderate Li deficiency (Li≈1.8) with aliovalent Y3+ (0.2) and Mn2+ (0.2) co-substitution to stabilize a single-phase inverse spinel (Fd-3m) Li2−yM1Cl4 framework, soften/expand the chloride lattice, frustrate Li/M–vacancy ordering, and thereby deliver room-temperature ionic conductivity ≥1e-5 S/cm. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as XRD for Li1.8Fe0.6Mn0.2Y0.2Cl4 synthesized at 400 °C shows a dominant spinel (Fd-3m) phase (≈85.73 wt%) but with secondary Li3YCl6 (≈8.4 wt%) and LiCl (≈5.87 wt%), plus several unindexed peaks (at 17.49°, 35.49°, 82.4°), indicating incomplete single-phase formation and Y segregation at this lower synthesis temperature, even though the refinement fit is good (Rwp 3.75%) and no extra calculated peaks were observed. Importantly, the measured room-temperature ionic conductivity is 1.83e-05 S/cm, meeting the targeted conductivity range, consistent with the lattice-softening/disorder rationale, but the single-phase Fd-3m objective was not fully achieved under these conditions.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of a Li-vacancy-rich inverse spinel chloride (Li1.6Fe0.5Mn0.3Hf0.2Cl4) where Hf4+ increases lattice softness and stabilizes Fd-3m while Mn2+ promotes Li/M disorder to suppress low-symmetry ordering, targeting a single-phase spinel and σRT ≥ 1e-5 S/cm. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as XRD at 400 °C refines to spinel (Fd-3m, weight fraction 1.0, Rwp=6.15%) with no extra calculated peaks, though several unindexed observed reflections (10.89°, 32.71°, 34.98°, 44.12°) suggest subtle structural deviations or minor unidentified components; the room-temperature ionic conductivity is 9.76e-06 S/cm, close to but slightly below the targeted ≥1e-5 S/cm.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of dual aliovalent doping (Zr4+ + V3+) at Li=1.5 in Li1.5Fe0.7V0.1Zr0.2Cl4 to enhance cation/Li-vacancy disorder in the inverse spinel (Fd-3m), yielding a predominantly single-phase structure and σRT ≥ 1e-5 S/cm compared to Zr-only systems. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as the 400 °C synthesis produced a mostly spinel (Fd-3m) phase (0.9738) with a minor VCl5 impurity (0.0262) and a good refinement (Rwp 3.52%), though a few low-intensity missing peaks suggest subtle unmodeled features; the measured room-temperature ionic conductivity (6.16e-06 S/cm) exceeds Zr-only baselines but falls short of the ≥1e-5 S/cm target and prior dual-doping benchmarks, likely influenced by minor impurity and the lower synthesis temperature than the proposed 450–500 °C.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of leveraging Ta5+-induced Li vacancies together with modest Mn2+ co-doping in Li1.7Fe0.7Mn0.2Ta0.1Cl4 to frustrate Li/M-vacancy ordering, retain a disordered Fd-3m inverse spinel, and thereby deliver room-temperature ionic conductivity at or above ~1e-5 S/cm with Li ≈1.7 optimizing vacancy content. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as XRD after 400 °C synthesis shows a dominant spinel (Fd-3m) phase (0.936) with good refinement (Rwp 3.97%) and only minor MnCl2 and Fe–Cl spinel impurities, consistent with suppressed long-range ordering, while missing/extra peaks indicate subtle structural deviations; the measured σRT of 9.22e-06 S/cm is very close to the target but falls slightly below the ≥1e-5 S/cm goal.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of designing a Li-deficient, M-excess inverse spinel chloride (Li1.4Fe0.8Mn0.3Zr0.1Cl4) where mixed Fe2+/Mn2+/Zr4+ creates Li vacancies and cation disorder to suppress ordering and enable a single-phase Fd-3m spinel with room-temperature ionic conductivity ≥ 1e-5 S/cm. The hypothesis is largely supported by the experiment outcome as XRD shows the dominant spinel (Fd-3m) phase (0.9419) with minor LiCl (Fm-3m) impurity (0.0581) and a good refinement (Rwp (%) = 4.11%), with only weak missing peaks (35.9°, 50.21°, 62.71°) suggesting minor unindexed features; the measured ionic conductivity at 25 °C is 3.31e-05 S/cm, exceeding the target. The minor LiCl and unindexed peaks indicate slight phase impurity/structural deviations that could be reduced with process optimization (e.g., higher synthesis temperature), but the core design goal of achieving a high-conductivity inverse spinel is met.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of transferring the V3+-driven Li-deficiency pattern (Li ≈ 1.6–1.7, V ≈ 0.15) into a mixed Mn2+/Zn2+ inverse spinel host to frustrate Li/M octahedral ordering, maintain a disordered Fd-3m framework at 400 °C without low-angle superlattice features, and thereby increase room-temperature ionic conductivity beyond Mn–V-only baselines. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.65Mn0.70Zn0.25V0.15Cl4 forms predominantly a spinel (Fd-3m) phase (0.8423) but with Li2ZnCl4 and LiCl impurities and a strong extra low-angle peak at 14.61° indicating residual ordering, and the measured room-temperature ionic conductivity is 3.27e-06 S/cm—well below the ~2e-5 S/cm benchmark—so while the spinel framework was largely retained, the structural disorder and conductivity enhancement targeted by Zn co-substitution were not achieved under these synthesis conditions.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of combining Mn2+/Fe2+ co-hosting with V3+ fixed at 0.15 and Li = 1.65 in Li1.65Mn0.70Fe0.25V0.15Cl4 to stabilize a disordered Fd-3m inverse spinel without low-angle superlattice ordering and to achieve ≥1e-5 S/cm via optimized Li-vacancy density and lattice softness. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as XRD refines to a spinel (Fd-3m) model with Rwp = 5.16% and no observed ~15° 2θ superlattice peak (appearing only as an extra calculated peak), consistent with suppressed cation ordering, while the measured room-temperature ionic conductivity is 1.4e-06 S/cm—below the predicted threshold—and several mid/high-angle unindexed peaks indicate subtle structural deviations or minor unidentified features that may be limiting Li+ mobility.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of combining Mg2+ with Mn2+ and V3+ in the inverse spinel chloride Li2−yM1±xCl4 framework, fixing Li ≈ 1.65 and V3+ ≈ 0.15 (y ≈ 0.35) to preserve single-phase Fd-3m at ~400 °C, frustrate Li/M ordering (avoid a strong ~15° superlattice peak), and thereby achieve high room-temperature ionic conductivity (~2e-5 S/cm) via enhanced octahedral-site disorder and a robust 3D Li+ percolation network without introducing high-field-strength 5+ dopants. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as XRD for Li1.65Mn0.65Mg0.30V0.15Cl4 refines to a single-phase spinel (Fd-3m, Rwp = 7.44%), with no pronounced low-angle ordering peak, although several low-intensity missing/extra peaks indicate subtle deviations from the reference model; however, the measured room-temperature ionic conductivity is 2.52e-07 S/cm, far below the targeted ~2e-5 S/cm, so the structural phase expectation is met but the anticipated conductivity enhancement is not realized.

This sample (Li1.65Fe0.95V0.15Cl4) is made in order to test the hypothesis of transferring the Mn–V optimized aliovalent doping and Li-vacancy window (Li ≈ 1.65, V3+ ≈ 0.15) into an Fe2+-based inverse spinel chloride to maintain Fd-3m cation disorder and achieve ≥1e-5 S/cm at 400 °C without inducing ordering or secondary phases. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as XRD shows a single-phase spinel (Fd-3m, 100 wt%) with a good refinement (Rwp 3.40%), consistent with the targeted disordered inverse spinel; however, several unindexed peaks indicate minor structural deviations or trace unidentified features, and the measured room-temperature ionic conductivity (2.12e-06 S/cm) falls well below the ≥1e-5 S/cm target, suggesting that the conductivity enhancement seen in Mn–V systems does not transfer to the Fe host under these synthesis conditions.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of using a small Bi3+ fraction (5%) together with V3+ in a Li-deficient inverse spinel chloride (Li1.60Mn0.90V0.15Bi0.05Cl4) to soften the anion lattice, frustrate Li/M octahedral ordering, yield a predominantly disordered Fd-3m spinel at 350–400 °C, and thereby achieve high room-temperature ionic conductivity while minimizing secondary Bi-chloride phases. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as XRD at 400 °C shows a multiphase product with only 0.4011 weight fraction indexed to an Fd-3m spinel-like phase and significant secondary phases (Li6VCl8, Fm-3m, 0.3198; MnCl2, R-3m, 0.2792), along with several unindexed missing peaks and extra calculated low-angle peaks absent in the data indicating model/sample mismatch. The measured ionic conductivity is low (5.26e-07 S/cm at 25 °C), far below the targeted high-σ regime for disordered spinels, indicating that the intended Bi3+-assisted disorder and predominance of the Fd-3m phase were not realized under these synthesis conditions.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of increasing Li vacancies (y≈0.5) and mixing only divalent cations (Mg2+ and Mn2+) with metal excess (x=0.25) in the Li2−yM1±xCl4 inverse spinel to retain a spinel-majority phase while enhancing Li+ transport via a robust vacancy network and cation-site disorder, without forming Li3MCl6 byproducts. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.5Mg0.8Mn0.45Cl4 forms a majority spinel (Fd-3m) phase (≈77%) with no Li3MCl6 detected (Rwp 7.53%), but notable LiCl and MnCl2 impurities (~23%) and low-angle missing/extra peaks suggest structural deviations/possible ordering, and the room-temperature ionic conductivity (4.83e-07 S/cm) is an order of magnitude lower than benchmark spinel analogs and far below the ≥1e-5–1e-4 S/cm target, indicating the intended conductivity enhancement was not achieved.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of using slight metal excess and multi-cation co-doping (Mn2+, Zr4+, Nb5+) in Li1.35Mg0.7Mn0.3Zr0.1Nb0.05Cl4 to increase Li-vacancies and configurational/charge disorder, thereby stabilizing a single disordered inverse spinel (Fd-3m) without secondary phases and boosting room-temperature ionic conductivity into the 1e-5–1e-4 S/cm range. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as XRD shows a single spinel (Fd-3m) phase at 1.0 weight fraction with a reasonable fit (Rwp 8.63%), but several unindexed missing peaks (including a low-angle feature at 15.32°) indicate residual ordering or minor unidentified contributions; critically, the measured conductivity is 3.16e-06 S/cm, below the targeted 1e-5–1e-4 range, so transport enhancement was not achieved.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of co-doping an inverse spinel chloride Li2−yM1±xCl4 framework with Nb5+ and Hf4+ on a Mg2+ host, plus a small Mn2+ fraction, to induce high octahedral-site disorder and controlled Li vacancies near Li≈1.4, thereby suppressing cation/vacancy ordering and boosting room-temperature ionic conductivity to ≥1e-5–1e-4 S/cm without forming Li3MCl6 boundaries. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as XRD shows a majority inverse spinel (Fd-3m) phase (0.8534 weight fraction) with no extra or missing peaks and no Li3MCl6 detected, but secondary LiCl (0.1338) and Nb3Cl8 (0.0128) impurities are present (Rwp 11.02%), and the measured ionic conductivity at 25 °C is 3.63e-06 S/cm, below the targeted range, indicating the co-doping did not deliver the expected conductivity enhancement under the current synthesis conditions.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of combining Bi3+ and Ta5+ with Mg2+ and Mn2+ in Li1.45Mg0.6Mn0.15Bi0.1Ta0.15Cl4 to raise the octahedral average charge and introduce ~0.55 Li vacancies to enhance multi-cation disorder and lattice softness in an inverse spinel chloride, targeting a spinel-majority Fd-3m phase without Li3MCl6-type byproducts and a room-temperature ionic conductivity ≥1e-5–1e-4 S/cm. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as XRD after synthesis at 400 °C shows a single spinel (Fd-3m) phase (Rwp 7.95%) with no Li3MCl6-type phases detected, though several low-intensity unindexed peaks indicate subtle structural deviations; the measured ionic conductivity is 2.75e-06 S/cm, modestly higher than Ta-only (~≤1e-6 S/cm) but below the targeted ≥1e-5–1e-4 S/cm.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of the abnormally high σRT in Li1.75Fe0.75Y0.25Cl4 primarily arising from the Li3YCl6 secondary phase providing parallel Li-ion pathways when Y3+ exceeds its spinel solubility limit. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.78Fe0.78Y0.22Cl4 synthesized at 500 °C refined to nearly single-phase spinel (Fd-3m, 97.17 wt%, Rwp 4.59%) with only minor LiCl (2.83 wt%) and no Li3YCl6, and delivered σRT = 4.23e-05 S/cm—below the abnormal 4.63e-05 S/cm of the Li3YCl6-containing Li1.75Fe0.75Y0.25Cl4 and only modestly above the single-phase Li1.8Fe0.8Y0.2Cl4 (3.82e-05 S/cm), consistent with the secondary Li3YCl6 phase being responsible for the highest σ. While the planned 525 °C test was not executed, the absence of Li3YCl6 together with the measured σ supports the hypothesis.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of an optimal Li-vacancy fraction (y≈0.2) being responsible for the high σRT in Li1.8Fe1.1Cl4, such that increasing vacancies to y=0.3 in Li1.7Fe1.15Cl4 would induce cation–vacancy ordering/distortion (detectable by deviations from Fd-3m) and reduce σRT. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.7Fe1.15Cl4 (500 °C) refined to spinel (Fd-3m, 1.0 weight fraction, Rwp 3.32%) with no extra peaks and only one missing peak, and showed higher σRT = 6.16e-05 S/cm than Li1.8Fe1.1Cl4 (4.3e-05 S/cm), providing no XRD evidence of ordering and demonstrating that conductivity increased rather than decreased with higher Li vacancy.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of the unusually high σRT in phase-pure Li1.8Fe0.8Y0.2Cl4 arising from the combined effect of an optimal Li-vacancy level from 20% Y3+ with total metal near 1 (x≈0), which avoids metal-excess blocking of Li+ pathways, together with synthesis at 500 °C that suppresses cation/vacancy ordering in the Fd-3m spinel. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.6Fe0.9Y0.2Cl4 synthesized at 500 °C refined to single-phase spinel (Fd-3m, 1.0; Rwp 4.13%) but showed σRT = 1.59e-05 S/cm—higher than its 400 °C counterpart (7.46e-06 S/cm) yet still well below Li1.8Fe0.8Y0.2Cl4 at 500 °C (3.82e-05 S/cm)—indicating that temperature alone does not recover the high σ and that extra metal content (x>0) remains a dominant limiter, consistent with composition-controlled percolation in the inverse spinel chloride framework.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of suppressed conductivity in Li2Fe0.5Zn0.5Cl4 being primarily due to low Li-vacancy concentration combined with Zn2+-driven cation ordering, with the expectation that introducing ~10 mol% Li vacancies at fixed Zn = 0.5 (Li1.9Fe0.525Zn0.525Cl4) would raise σRT toward ≥1e-05 S/cm while retaining the inverse-spinel framework. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.9Fe0.525Zn0.525Cl4 synthesized at 500 °C shows a spinel-dominant pattern with a minor Li2ZnCl4 phase (spinel (Fd-3m) 0.9007; Li2ZnCl4 (Fd-3m) 0.0993; Rwp 5.56%) and σRT = 1.99e-06 S/cm—lower than the baseline Li2Fe0.5Zn0.5Cl4 at 500 °C (3.05e-06 S/cm) and far below the ≥1e-05 S/cm target—indicating that adding Li vacancies under these conditions did not improve conductivity.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of a 1:1-specific cation ordering transition at 500 °C in Li1.5Mn0.5Sc0.5Cl4 that suppresses low-angle Fd-3m reflections and collapses the Li conduction network, whereas moving off the 1:1 Mn:Sc ratio (Li1.6Mn0.6Sc0.4Cl4) should frustrate long-range order and prevent the conductivity drop. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.6Mn0.6Sc0.4Cl4 synthesized at 500 °C refines predominantly as spinel (Fd-3m 0.913) with minor LiCl (Fm-3m 0.087), shows no low-angle extra_peaks (only a single high-angle missing peak at 82.57°), and exhibits σRT=3.45e-05 S/cm—higher than its 400 °C value (1.57e-05 S/cm) and far above the collapsed σRT of Li1.5Mn0.5Sc0.5Cl4 at 500 °C (2.2e-06 S/cm)—indicating the severe σ drop at 500 °C is not a generic high-temperature effect and is consistent with an ordering effect specific to the 1:1 composition.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Nb5+-induced Li-vacancy association/cation ordering and/or incomplete reaction at 400 °C causing the abnormally low conductivity in Li1.75Mg0.7Y0.2Nb0.05Cl4, with the prediction that synthesizing the same composition at 500 °C would improve XRD fit (lower Rwp, fewer missing peaks) and increase σ by ≥5× toward ~1e-05 S/cm. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.75Mg0.7Y0.2Nb0.05Cl4 at 500 °C shows an improved refinement (Rwp 7.40% vs 12.10% at 400 °C; missing peaks reduced from many to two low-intensity peaks; no extra peaks), a higher matched Li3YCl6 fraction (0.2454 vs 0.082) with spinel reduced (0.7546 vs 0.918), and σ increased from 1.37e-06 to 1.5e-05 S/cm (~11×), placing it within the ~1e-05–2e-05 S/cm range observed for Y-doped references at similar Li3YCl6 fractions (e.g., Li1.7Mg0.7Y0.3Cl4 at 500 °C: 0.2178 Li3YCl6, 1.77e-05 S/cm; Li1.8Mg0.6Fe0.2Y0.2Cl4 at 500 °C: 0.0995 Li3YCl6, 9.46e-06 S/cm).

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Li1.5Co0.5Cr0.5Cl4 synthesized at 400 °C having depressed room-temperature ionic conductivity due to cation and Li-vacancy ordering (lower symmetry than Fd-3m) and that synthesis at 500 °C would increase configurational disorder within the inverse spinel framework, reduce unindexed reflections compared to the Fd-3m model, and increase σRT. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.5Co0.5Cr0.5Cl4 made at 500 °C refines as spinel (Fd-3m, 1.0 weight fraction; Rwp 4.50%) but still exhibits numerous missing peaks and an extra calculated peak, while the room-temperature ionic conductivity rises from 7.35e-09 S/cm (400 °C) to 7.33e-07 S/cm (500 °C), i.e., an ~2-order-of-magnitude increase.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of vacancy/disorder-optimized inverse spinel at y≈0.5 being the primary driver of the abnormally high conductivity in Li1.5Mn0.5Sc0.5Cl4, such that Li1.5Mn0.5V0.5Cl4 synthesized at 450 °C would also show Fd-3m spinel and similarly high σRT. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.5Mn0.5V0.5Cl4 (450 °C) refines to spinel (Fd-3m, Rwp 7.65%) but shows several unindexed missing peaks and exhibits σRT = 4.67e-06 S/cm—far below Li1.5Mn0.5Sc0.5Cl4 at 450 °C (6.43e-05 S/cm) and the ≥6e-05 S/cm criterion—indicating that keeping y≈0.5 alone did not reproduce the high conductivity and that trivalent identity and/or structural differences reflected by the missing peaks influence transport.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of ultralow σ in Li1.5Mg0.5Cr0.5Cl4 at 400 °C arising from Cr-driven effects (incomplete reaction yielding Cr-containing secondary phases and Cr3+-induced Li-vacancy ordering/defect association), rather than from the high Li-vacancy fraction (y=0.5) itself. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.5Mg1.25Cl4 (450 °C) refines as spinel (Fd-3m, 1.0) with Rwp = 12.67%, and achieves 1.78e-06 S/cm at 25 °C—about 12× higher than Li1.5Cr0.5Mg0.5Cl4 at 450 °C (1.48e-07 S/cm) and >6 orders above Li1.5Mg0.5Cr0.5Cl4 at 400 °C (1.0e-12 S/cm), approaching Li2MgCl4 (3.16e-06 S/cm). Although a low-angle extra reflection (~15.32°) and several unindexed peaks persist, the substantial σ increase without Cr while maintaining y = 0.5 indicates the 400 °C anomaly is primarily Cr-specific (secondary phases/ordering) rather than an intrinsic consequence of high vacancy content.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of the abnormally low σ in Li1.2Mn0.9Nb0.2Cl4 (400 °C) arising from Li/M octahedral ordering and symmetry lowering driven by excess octahedral metal (M=1.1), with the expectation that lowering the synthesis temperature to 350 °C would kinetically suppress ordering, attenuate the ~14.68° 2θ superlattice peak, and increase σRT by ≥3×. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as the 350 °C product is multiphase (spinel (Fd-3m) 0.6897 and MnCl2 (R-3m) 0.3103; Rwp 6.31%), shows no reported extra low-angle peak but retains several missing peaks, and exhibits a σRT of 3.95e-07 S/cm—~10× lower than the 400 °C value of 3.93e-06 S/cm. The attenuation of the ~14.68° feature is not accompanied by a conductivity increase and, given the substantial MnCl2 impurity, does not provide evidence that lowering temperature alleviates the abnormal low σ; any suppression of ordering cannot be confirmed from this dataset.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of incomplete reaction at 250 °C leaving a high LiCl fraction (and some MnCl2), which suppresses the percolating spinel network and yields abnormally low σ in Li2Zn0.5Mn0.5Cl4; synthesizing at 400 °C should increase the spinel fraction, reduce LiCl/MnCl2, lessen model–data mismatches, and raise σRT by ≥10×. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as the 400 °C product shows 0.821 spinel (Fd-3m) + 0.179 Li2ZnCl4 (Fd-3m) with no LiCl or MnCl2 detected by the fit, a reduction in mis-indexed features (missing peaks: 11 vs 21; extra peaks: 3 vs 11), and σRT increases from 1e-08 S/cm to 4.16e-07 S/cm (~40×). However, the spinel fraction remains <0.9 and a secondary Fd-3m phase (Li2ZnCl4) plus a strong low-angle extra peak at ~14.67° persist, indicating the mixed-metal spinel is not fully realized under these conditions even though impurity-driven suppression of conductivity at 250 °C has been alleviated.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of a composite-conduction boost: that the abnormally high σ at 400 °C in Li1.5Mn0.3Fe0.2Y0.25In0.25Cl4 arises from a Li3InCl6-type secondary phase coexisting with a vacancy-rich inverse spinel, and that reducing this secondary phase at 450 °C would lower σRT by ≥25%; if σRT remained ≥1.2e-04 S/cm despite suppressing the secondary phase, the high σ would be intrinsic to the disordered spinel. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as the 450 °C product shows a comparable or higher Li3MCl6-type fraction (spinel (Fd-3m) 0.6516, Li3YCl6 (P-3m1) 0.3484) relative to the 400 °C result (spinel 0.713, Li6In2.12Cl12 0.287) rather than a reduction, yet σRT drops from 1.4e-04 S/cm to 6.18e-05 S/cm (>25% decrease). Because the secondary phase was not suppressed, the planned decision rule cannot be applied; the observed σ decrease with a persistent Li3MCl6-type phase does not support the specific composite-enhancement hypothesis tested here.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Nb5+-driven Li-vacancy/cation ordering in Li1.4Fe0.8Nb0.2Cl4 at low synthesis temperature suppressing Li+ transport, and that synthesizing at 450 °C would disrupt this ordering, reduce XRD misfit/impurities, and restore σRT to ≥1e-05 S/cm. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as the 450 °C sample refines as single-phase spinel (Fd-3m, 1.0; Rwp = 4.65%) with no LiCl and no extra peaks, only weak missing features at 10.98°, 14.23°, 32.81°, and 44.21°, and σRT increases from 1.0e-08 S/cm (400 °C) to 2.75e-05 S/cm—meeting the predefined threshold and aligning with related high-conductivity benchmarks.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of abnormally low σ in Li2Fe0.5Zn0.5Cl4 at 250 °C arising from a Zn2+-biased cation distribution and a low-temperature Fe-rich Cmmm secondary phase that suppress Li-vacancy/disorder; introducing Li vacancies at fixed Fe:Zn via M-excess (x=0.1) and synthesizing at 450 °C should yield a more disordered spinel with minimal secondary phases and σ ≥ 1e-05 S/cm. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.8Fe0.55Zn0.55Cl4 (450 °C) shows mixed phases—spinel (Fd-3m) 0.8617 and Li2ZnCl4 (Pnma) 0.1383—with Rwp 5.07% and several missing/one extra peak, and exhibits σ = 2.52e-06 S/cm, below the ≥1e-05 S/cm target and even slightly lower than Li2Fe0.5Zn0.5Cl4 at 500 °C (3.05e-06 S/cm). This indicates that Li-vacancy introduction at fixed Fe:Zn did not achieve the expected conductivity or phase purity, consistent with the decision-rule refutation that vacancies alone are insufficient under these conditions.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Li3YCl6-driven percolation dominating the abnormally high conductivity in Li1.5Mn0.7Y0.2Ta0.1Cl4—i.e., at fixed composition, σRT should positively correlate with the Li3YCl6 (P-3m1) weight fraction. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as synthesizing Li1.5Mn0.7Y0.2Ta0.1Cl4 at 450 °C reduced the Li3YCl6 fraction from 0.2519 to 0.1441 (spinel increased from 0.7481 to 0.8559), yet the room-temperature ionic conductivity increased slightly from 2.08e-05 to 2.27e-05 S/cm, which contradicts the predicted positive correlation between Li3YCl6 content and σ.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Mg2+-induced cation-site preference/ordering or inhomogeneity causing the abnormally low σ of Li1.65Mn0.65Mg0.30V0.15Cl4 at 400 °C, with higher-temperature (450 °C) synthesis expected to improve agreement with the disordered Fd-3m spinel model and raise σ by ≥10×. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as the 450 °C product shows a much improved XRD refinement (Rwp 4.55% vs 7.44%) with no missing/extra peaks and σRT increases from 2.52e-07 S/cm to 1.32e-05 S/cm (~52×), approaching the V-doped Mg-free references; the sample is predominantly spinel (Fd-3m) 0.907 with minor LiCl (Fm-3m) 0.0509 and MnCl2 (R-3m) 0.0422 present.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Li3YCl6 being the high-conductivity phase responsible for the elevated σRT in Li1.5Co0.5Y0.5Cl4, where XRD showed a dominant Li3YCl6 fraction. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li3YCl6 synthesized at 450 °C is identified by XRD as Li3YCl6 (P-3m1, 1.0 weight fraction, Rwp 8.44% with some missing/extra peaks) and exhibits σRT = 1.25e-04 S/cm—~5× higher than Li1.5Co0.5Y0.5Cl4 (2.3e-05 S/cm) and orders of magnitude above spinel baselines—consistent with Li3YCl6 dominating the composite’s ionic transport.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Ni-driven secondary-phase blocking causing loss of Li3YCl6 percolation in Li1.4Mg0.2Ni0.2Y0.6Cl4 when Li:Y < 3; enforcing Li:Y = 3 at fixed Ni (Li1.5Mg0.3Ni0.2Y0.5Cl4) should suppress YCl3 and restore connectivity/σ. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.5Mg0.3Ni0.2Y0.5Cl4 (500 °C) shows Li3YCl6 (P-3m1) 0.6438 with no YCl3 detected, alongside spinel (Fd-3m) 0.2375 and NiCl2 (R-3m) 0.1187 (Rwp 6.49%), and exhibits σRT = 6.45e-05 S/cm—>3 orders of magnitude higher than 2.96e-08 S/cm for Li1.4Mg0.2Ni0.2Y0.6Cl4 and within the targeted ~1e-5–1e-4 S/cm range—consistent with restored Li3YCl6 connectivity rather than intrinsic Ni-induced suppression of Li transport.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of the unusually high σ in Li1.7Fe1.15Cl4 originating from an optimal Li-vacancy fraction near y≈0.30 in the inverse spinel (Fd-3m), such that further vacancy increase to y=0.40 (Li1.6Fe1.2Cl4) would pass the optimum, induce ordering/secondary phases detectable by XRD, and lower σ. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.6Fe1.2Cl4 (500 °C) refines as single-phase spinel (Fd-3m, 1.0 wt; Rwp 2.93%) with three weak unindexed reflections and no extra peaks, and exhibits σRT = 3.69e-05 S/cm—lower than Li1.7Fe1.15Cl4 (6.16e-05 S/cm) and Li1.8Fe1.1Cl4 (4.3e-05 S/cm)—which is consistent with a conductivity maximum near y≈0.30, but does not provide clear XRD evidence for long-range ordering or secondary phases at y=0.40.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of temperature-trapped cation/vacancy ordering and/or incomplete cation mixing in Li1.6Fe0.9V0.2Cl4 at 400 C causing abnormally low ionic conductivity, and that synthesizing the same composition at 500 C would complete the reaction and improve the spinel framework sufficiently to raise σ toward ~1e-5 S/cm. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.6Fe0.9V0.2Cl4 synthesized at 500 C refines as single-phase spinel (Fd-3m 1.0 vs 0.9873 previously, LiCl removed; Rwp 3.45%; missing peaks reduced from three to two with similar/lower intensities) and σ_RT increases from 6.5e-07 to 3.22e-05 S/cm (>1 order-of-magnitude increase, exceeding the ≥5e-06 criterion and within the ~1e-5 S/cm range observed for related spinels).

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Ca co-doping with Bi in Li1.8Bi0.2Ca0.2Mg0.6Cl4 promotes cation/Li-vacancy ordering that deviates from cubic Fd-3m (seen as many unindexed XRD reflections), suppressing σ, and that increasing synthesis temperature to 500 °C will increase disorder, reduce missing-peak signatures/improve Rwp, and raise σRT by ≥5× toward ~10^-6 S/cm. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as σRT increases ~10× (1.11e-07 → 1.15e-06 S/cm), meeting the ≥5× criterion, and several previously strong missing peaks weaken substantially (e.g., 34.84°/0.68 → 34.28°/0.09 ~87% drop; 50.05°/0.35 → 50.28°/0.08 ~77% drop; 36.21°/0.32 → 36.32°/0.09 ~72% drop), but the total count of missing peaks increases (15 → 19), Rwp improves only slightly (13.43% → 13.27%), and an extra calculated peak remains with higher intensity (14.74°/0.26 → 15.01°/0.59), indicating significant structural deviations persist. Overall, higher-temperature synthesis improves conductivity and weakens key ordering-like reflections, consistent with increased disorder, but does not eliminate the deviations, suggesting Ca may still stabilize residual order.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of high-Zn2+-induced cation ordering in Li2Co0.5Zn0.5Cl4 (manifested by a strong extra low-angle peak near 15° in XRD) suppressing Li-ion conductivity at 450 °C, and that synthesizing the same composition at higher temperature (500 °C) would reduce the ordering (weaker ~15° feature) and increase σRT. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as the 500 °C product remains single-phase spinel (Fd-3m, 1.0) with persistent strong extra low-angle peak at 14.98° (relative intensity 1.0) and numerous missing peaks, and its room-temperature ionic conductivity is 1.32e-08 S/cm—essentially unchanged from the 450 °C sample (1e-08 S/cm).

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of vacancy-limited conductivity and residual cation/vacancy ordering causing the low σRT in Li2Co0.5Fe0.5Cl4 at 500 °C, and that increasing Li-vacancy concentration via higher Sc3+ substitution to Li1.85Co0.425Fe0.425Sc0.15Cl4 at 500 °C would disrupt the ordering (notably eliminating the ~24.8° and ~39.4° unindexed features) and raise σRT beyond the 10% Sc sample. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.85Co0.425Fe0.425Sc0.15Cl4 (500 °C) is single-phase spinel (Fd-3m, Rwp 3.69%), the specific unindexed peaks seen in the undoped 500 °C sample at ~24.78° and ~39.42° are not reported, but new unindexed peaks appear at 18.23°, 36.07°, 50.73°, and 74.58°; critically, σRT increases to 1.17e-05 S/cm, exceeding both Li1.9Co0.45Fe0.45Sc0.1Cl4 (4.8e-06 S/cm) and Li2Co0.5Fe0.5Cl4 (1.42e-06 S/cm), consistent with vacancy-enabled conductivity improvement while structural deviations from the simple Fd-3m model persist.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of a Li3YCl6 secondary phase boosting σ in Li1.8Mg0.8Y0.2Cl4 by lowering intergranular resistance; suppressing Li3YCl6 at lower synthesis temperature (400 °C) should reduce σ toward spinel-only baselines. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.8Mg0.8Y0.2Cl4 (400 °C) shows no Li3YCl6 detected by XRD (spinel (Fd-3m) 0.7537, LiCl (Fm-3m) 0.1615, MgCl2 (R-3m) 0.0848; Rwp = 9.11%; multiple missing peaks) and σRT drops to 1.61e-06 S/cm, far below the same composition at 450–500 °C (≈1.06e-05–1.10e-05 S/cm with 0.0714–0.1277 Li3YCl6) and even below spinel-only baselines (Li2MgCl4: 3.16e-06 S/cm; Li1.6Mg1.2Cl4: 4.55e-06 S/cm; Li1.4Fe0.2Mg0.6Ta0.2Cl4: 6.1e-06 S/cm). While the 400 °C sample contains LiCl and MgCl2, the marked σ decrease concurrent with the absence of Li3YCl6 is consistent with the boundary-phase hypothesis.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Zr4+-driven octahedral/Li-vacancy ordering together with ~21% MgCl2 formation suppressing σ in Li1.6Mg0.8Zr0.2Cl4 at 400 °C, and that Sc3+ co-doping at the same 400 °C (Li1.5Mg0.7Zr0.2Sc0.1Cl4) would frustrate ordering and reduce MgCl2 to yield a spinel-dominant pattern with fewer unindexed features and σRT ≥ 1e-6 S/cm. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.5Mg0.7Zr0.2Sc0.1Cl4 synthesized at 400 °C did not form a spinel: XRD refines to Li6.02Sc2Cl12 (C12/m1) at 1.0 weight fraction with numerous unmodeled features (6 missing and 10 extra peaks), and no MgCl2 was identified; although σRT = 3.03e-06 S/cm meets the conductivity threshold, the required structural criterion (≥90% spinel with reduced unindexed features) was not met, so the improved σ cannot be attributed to the intended spinel-ordering disruption mechanism.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Nb5+-induced Li-vacancy association/cation ordering at 400 °C causing the abnormally low σ in Li1.75Mg0.7Y0.2Nb0.05Cl4, with the prediction that reducing Nb to Li1.875Mg0.7Y0.2Nb0.025Cl4 at the same temperature would lessen ordering signatures (fewer missing peaks, lower Rwp) and raise σ toward ~1e-05 S/cm. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.875Mg0.7Y0.2Nb0.025Cl4 (400 °C) shows only a modest Rwp improvement (12.10% → 9.17%, 2.93% absolute; below the ≥3% criterion), a similar count of missing peaks (17 vs 17), and σRT increases to 4.41e-06 S/cm (~3.2×, below the ≥5× target); additionally, the phase assemblage shifts to spinel (Fd-3m) 0.7782 + LiCl (Fm-3m) 0.2218 rather than the spinel + Li3YCl6 mixture seen in the abnormal 400 °C sample, so the predefined decision thresholds for supporting the Nb-driven ordering/trapping hypothesis are not met.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of low-temperature cation/Li-vacancy ordering in Li1.4Mg0.8Ta0.2Cl4 suppressing ionic conductivity, and that a small Sc3+ co-substitution at fixed Li content (Li1.4Mg0.8Ta0.17Sc0.05Cl4) would frustrate this ordering at 400 °C, leading to fewer XRD misfit features and higher σRT. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.4Mg0.8Ta0.17Sc0.05Cl4 (400 °C) shows σRT = 6.75e-07 S/cm (~10× above Li1.4Mg0.8Ta0.2Cl4 at 400 °C, 6.8e-08 S/cm), but the XRD does not present a cleaner single-phase spinel: it refines to spinel (Fd-3m) 0.7115 plus Li3ScCl6 (C12/m1) 0.2885 with Rwp = 13.15% and numerous missing peaks (e.g., at 15.39°, 29.69°), so the structural criterion (reduced misfit features) is not met. The substantial Li3ScCl6 fraction confounds attribution of the σ increase to frustrated ordering within the spinel, making the mechanism test inconclusive.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of abnormal low σ in Li1.5Co0.5Cr0.5Cl4 at 400 °C arising from long-range cation/Li-vacancy ordering within the inverse spinel, and that introducing a small amount of Zn2+ at fixed Li and Cr content (Li1.5Co0.4Zn0.1Cr0.5Cl4) would frustrate such ordering at 400 °C, yielding higher σRT and fewer/smaller unindexed reflections relative to the undoped 400 °C sample. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.5Co0.4Zn0.1Cr0.5Cl4 synthesized at 400 °C exhibits σRT=8.17e-08 S/cm (≈11× higher than Li1.5Co0.5Cr0.5Cl4 at 400 °C: 7.35e-09 S/cm), moving toward the ≥1e-7 S/cm target; however, XRD shows a multi-phase mixture (spinel (Fd-3m) 0.523, Li2CoCl4 (Cmmm) 0.3496, CrCl3 (C12/m1) 0.0638, LiCl (Fm-3m) 0.0635; Rwp=3.12%) with persistent unindexed features (5 missing peaks and 2 extra peaks), so the conductivity increase and changes in unindexed reflections cannot be unambiguously attributed to reduced ordering within the spinel phase alone.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of using a Mn2+-host inverse spinel with y=0.5 Li vacancies and multi-valent 16d mixing (Mn2+/Bi3+/Ta5+) in Li1.5Mn0.6Bi0.35Ta0.05Cl4 to soften the chloride framework, frustrate cation ordering, retain an inverse-spinel structure (Fd-3m or lightly symmetry-lowered), and thereby achieve high room-temperature Li+ conductivity. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as XRD at 300 °C indexes nominally to a spinel (Fd-3m) phase (100 wt%) but with a relatively high Rwp of 11.07% and many unindexed peaks (notably strong low-angle features around 15.5–15.9°), indicating unidentified secondary phases or symmetry-lowered ordering, and the room-temperature ionic conductivity is only 1.61e-06 S/cm—well below the ≥10^-5–10^-4 S/cm levels targeted from prior y≈0.5 Mn-based spinels.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of co-doping Bi3+ and V3+ into the inverse spinel Li–Mn chloride framework at Li=1.5 (Li1.5Mn0.5Bi0.3V0.2Cl4) to maximize octahedral-site disorder and vacancy concentration, retain a single-phase spinel, and thereby increase room-temperature Li+ conductivity relative to single-dopant benchmarks. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as the measured conductivity is 1.05e-05 S/cm (higher than the V-only analog, 3.67e-06 S/cm, and near the Bi+Y case, 1.49e-05 S/cm), but XRD shows a multiphase product—~63.95% Li2MnCl4 (Fd-3m) plus ~36.05% Li6VCl8 (Fm-3m) with additional missing/extra peaks—indicating phase separation and likely incomplete incorporation of Bi/V into a single spinel phase.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of introducing stereoactive Sn2+ into the inverse spinel Li2−yM1±xCl4 framework (x=0) with a small amount of Nb5+ to set y≈0.3, aiming for vacancy-enabled transport plus Li/M disorder and local distortions to enhance 3D Li+ conduction in Li1.7Mg0.35Sn0.55Nb0.1Cl4. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as XRD shows a multiphase product dominated by LiCl (Fm-3m, 56.3 wt%) with only 43.7 wt% spinel-like phase (Fd-3m) and several unindexed peaks (Rwp 8.65%), indicating substantial secondary phase formation, and the measured room-temperature ionic conductivity is 6.11e-07 S/cm—an order of magnitude lower than the Nb5+-doped Mg baseline (~5.8e-06 S/cm) and lower than other heavy-cation cases—suggesting the intended high-conductivity spinel did not form as a clean, percolating phase under these conditions.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of using In3+ (0.3) and Zr4+ (0.1) co-doping on an Mg2+-based inverse spinel to keep y≈0.5 in Li2−yM1±xCl4, avoid Y-driven Li3YCl6 formation, disrupt Li/M ordering, and thereby realize a spinel-dominant, high-σ Li+ conductor. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.5Mg0.6In0.3Zr0.1Cl4 synthesized at 400 °C refines as single-phase spinel (Fd-3m, 100 wt%), indicating successful spinel stabilization without Li3YCl6, but the refinement has Rwp = 11.66% with several missing peaks and a strong extra peak at 15.31°, suggesting structural deviation/ordering or a minor unidentified phase; the room-temperature ionic conductivity is 1.03e-05 S/cm, which is modest and below the targeted ~1e-4 S/cm, thus not delivering the anticipated high conductivity despite the desired phase outcome.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of using heterovalent co-doping on the Mn-based inverse spinel chloride host—Li1.5Mn0.65In0.25Zr0.05Ta0.05Cl4—to maintain y≈0.5 Li-vacancies while mixing 3+/4+/5+ cations on 16d to frustrate Li/M ordering, stabilize a disordered spinel (avoiding Y-driven Li3YCl6), and thereby raise room-temperature ionic conductivity toward the top values (~1e-4 S/cm). The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as XRD shows the target spinel (Fd-3m) as the major phase (96.16%) with a minor ZrCl4 impurity (3.84%) and no Y-based phases, consistent with spinel formation and intended Y-free chemistry; however, the room-temperature conductivity is 1.82e-05 S/cm—significantly below the benchmarked high-σ compositions (6.4e-05 to 1.4e-04 S/cm)—and the presence of ZrCl4 plus a few missing peaks suggests limited solubility and/or subtle structural deviations, indicating that the 4+/5+ co-doping did not enhance conductivity under these conditions.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of placing Li vacancies near y ≈ 0.3 while co‑doping the inverse spinel chloride with Zr4+ and Cu+ (Li1.7Fe0.7Zr0.2Cu0.1Cl4) to increase configurational disorder, suppress Li/M ordering, and thereby raise room‑temperature Li+ conductivity without adding excess metal (total M = 1). The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as the 400 °C synthesis yields a phase that indexes as spinel (Fd-3m) with good refinement (Rwp = 4.64%) but shows several unindexed low‑intensity peaks suggestive of minor secondary phases or subtle ordering, and the measured room‑temperature ionic conductivity is 5.06e-06 S/cm—only marginally higher than the Zr‑only analogue (~2.95e-06 S/cm) and well below the best y ≈ 0.2–0.3 compositions (≈3–6e-05 S/cm), indicating that the intended co‑doping disorder effect did not substantially enhance transport.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of using Cu+ co-doping at y ≈ 0.3 in the inverse-spinel Li2−yM1Cl4 framework to frustrate Nb5+-driven Li/M ordering and thereby raise room-temperature ionic conductivity into the 10^-5–10^-4 S/cm range, here implemented as Li1.7Fe0.7Nb0.15Cu0.15Cl4 with total M = 1. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as the product is predominantly spinel (Fd-3m, 0.9529) with a small Nb3Cl8 (R3m) impurity (0.0471) and good refinement quality (Rwp = 4.70%), but the room-temperature ionic conductivity is 4.09e-06 S/cm—higher than Nb-only analogs (~1e-08 S/cm) yet below the targeted 10^-5–10^-4 S/cm. The minor Nb3Cl8 impurity and slight missing/extra peaks suggest incomplete Nb/Cu incorporation or residual ordering, which likely limits conductivity despite successful spinel formation.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of transferring the metal‑excess/high‑vacancy (y ≈ 0.2) design from Fe-based spinels to a Mn‑only inverse spinel host (Li1.8Mn1.1Cl4) to realize a disordered cubic Cl sublattice with a percolating Li network and room‑temperature conductivity comparable to Fe‑only high‑σ cases. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as XRD refines as single‑phase spinel (Fd-3m) with good Rwp = 6.40%, indicating the targeted framework forms at 400 °C, but several unindexed observed peaks (15.37°, 30.28°, 34.87°, 49.93°) suggest subtle ordering or minor unidentified features; the measured σRT = 1.75e-05 S/cm is within the 10^-5 S/cm range but falls short of the Fe‑only high‑σ benchmarks (≈4.3–6.16e-05 S/cm), aligning more with the lower end seen in Fe–Mn mixed hosts, implying the high‑σ window is not fully host‑agnostic under these conditions.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of stabilizing a Ni-based inverse spinel chloride, Li1.65Ni0.75Cu0.10Ta0.15Cl4, by co-doping Cu+ and Ta5+ to create y≈0.35 Li vacancies without metal excess, frustrate Li/M ordering (avoid low-angle superlattice), and thus achieve a single-phase Fd-3m spinel with enhanced room-temperature ionic conductivity. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as XRD shows a multiphase product with only ~52% spinel (Fd-3m) and significant LiCl, NiCl2, and TaCl4 impurities (Rwp 5.30% with additional missing peaks), indicating limited solubility/incorporation of the dopants, and the measured ionic conductivity at 25 °C is 1.43e-07 S/cm—well below the ~1e-5 S/cm regime targeted by the vacancy–disorder strategy.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of using a Co2+-based inverse spinel host with a compensated Cu+/Nb5+ pair to keep total M ≈ 1.00 and set moderate Li vacancies (y ≈ 0.35), thereby suppressing cation ordering (weak/absent low-angle superlattice features) and achieving high room-temperature Li-ion conductivity through a disordered Fd-3m framework. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.65Co0.75Cu0.10Nb0.15Cl4 refined predominantly as spinel (Fd-3m, 100 wt%, Rwp 2.45%) but exhibited several low-intensity unindexed low-angle peaks (e.g., 17.41°, 24.69°, 29.29° 2θ), suggesting minor secondary phases and/or cation ordering, and the room-temperature ionic conductivity was very low (7.13e-08 S/cm).

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of introducing Jahn–Teller-active Cu2+ into a Mg–Nb inverse-spinel chloride (Li1.4Mg0.65Cu0.15Nb0.2Cl4) to induce local octahedral distortions and mixed-valence disorder that retain a single Fd-3m spinel phase while increasing room-temperature Li+ conductivity beyond Mg–Nb-only analogs. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as XRD refines as single spinel (Fd-3m, 1.0 weight fraction) but with a relatively high Rwp (14.61%) plus notable extra/missing peaks (extra at 14.93°, missing at 29.69° and 34.84°), indicating deviations from ideal Fd-3m (likely subtle ordering/distortion), and the measured ionic conductivity is 4e-07 S/cm at 25 °C, which is an order of magnitude lower than the Mg–Nb benchmark (~5.81e-06 S/cm) and below the targeted 2–6e-06 S/cm range.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of using mixed-valence doping (replacing Cr3+ with low-level V3+ and adding Nb5+) to keep Li≈1.5 and promote multi-cation disorder on 16d in Li1.5Mg0.7V0.2Nb0.1Cl4, thereby suppressing long-range cation/Li-vacancy ordering and secondary phases to achieve a spinel-only product with σ in the 10^-6 S/cm range. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as XRD shows substantial phase separation with two Fd-3m phases (spinel 0.6879 and Li13.52Mg9.28Cl32 0.3121) and unindexed peaks (15.8°, 63.25°; Rwp=10.93%), indicating additional/unmodeled phases or structural mismatch; the room-temperature ionic conductivity is 3.24e-07 S/cm, below the targeted 2–6e-06 S/cm window.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of co-doping the inverse-spinel chloride Li2−yM1±xCl4 framework with Hf4+ (d0) and low-level Ni2+ to stabilize a (near) single-phase spinel, enhance Li/M disorder via vacancy formation (y≈0.4), and achieve ≥~3e-06 S/cm at room temperature, analogous to Zr4+-based co-doped systems. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as the 400 °C synthesis of Li1.6Mg0.6Ni0.2Hf0.2Cl4 gives an XRD fit modeled as spinel (Fd-3m) at 1.0 weight fraction but with a relatively high Rwp (13.75%) and numerous unindexed missing peaks (up to ~0.47 relative intensity), indicating non-modeled phases and/or symmetry lowering rather than a clean single-phase spinel; the room-temperature ionic conductivity is 8.96e-07 S/cm, below the targeted ≥3e-06 S/cm.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of raising In3+ to 0.4 on an Fe2+-host inverse spinel (Li1.6Fe0.6In0.4Cl4) to retain a spinel-majority matrix while intentionally forming a minor Li3InCl6 boundary network that, together with Li-vacancies, would boost room-temperature ionic conductivity. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as XRD at 400 °C shows a single spinel (Fd-3m) phase (100 wt%, Rwp 5.88%) with no detectable Li3InCl6; several unindexed/extra peaks indicate subtle structural deviations or minor unidentified impurities rather than a distinct Li3InCl6 phase. Nevertheless, the ionic conductivity is 3.24e-05 S/cm, exceeding Fe-spinel baselines and comparable to Y-assisted cases, suggesting the conductivity enhancement likely stems from vacancy/disorder within the spinel rather than the intended Li3InCl6 boundary network.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of applying 20% Y3+ aliovalent substitution in a Ni-based inverse spinel chloride (Li1.8Ni0.8Y0.2Cl4) to set y ≈ 0.2 Li vacancies, promote cation disorder, and achieve high room-temperature ionic conductivity (10^-5–10^-4 S/cm) analogous to Fe-based systems. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as XRD is indexed to a spinel (Fd-3m) framework but shows substantial misfit (Rwp = 11.55% with many missing and extra peaks), suggesting structural deviations/ordering or minor unidentified phases, and the measured room-temperature ionic conductivity is 4.82e-08 S/cm—3–4 orders of magnitude below the target and below the Fe-based Y-doped reference.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of using mixed-valence co-doping (Zr4+ + V3+) in a Ni2+-based inverse spinel chloride to create y≈0.30 Li vacancies while keeping M≈1.0 in Li1.70Ni0.80Zr0.10V0.10Cl4, thereby promoting Li/M disorder, avoiding ordering/segregation, and increasing room-temperature Li+ conductivity. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as XRD refines predominantly to spinel (Fd-3m, Rwp 7.04%) but shows multiple unindexed and model–extra peaks (including low-angle features), suggesting structural deviations or minor secondary phases, and the room-temperature ionic conductivity is very low (5.7e-08 S/cm), indicating no conductivity enhancement despite nominal single-phase spinel indexing.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of co-doping a Ni-based inverse spinel chloride (Li1.60Ni0.80V0.10Ta0.10Cl4) with V3+ and Ta5+ to create y = 0.40 Li vacancies without metal excess, increase cationic disorder (suppress ordering), avoid V/Nb-driven impurity pathways, and thereby achieve higher room-temperature ionic conductivity. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as XRD shows substantial phase segregation—Li6VCl8 (Fm-3m, 35.31%), LiCl (Fm-3m, 27.18%), TaCl4 (C12/m1, 3.86%)—with only ~33.65% spinel (Fd-3m), along with missing/extra peaks indicating additional mismatches. This indicates V largely segregated to Li6VCl8 and Ta did not incorporate effectively into the spinel. The room-temperature ionic conductivity is very low (6.07e-08 S/cm), inconsistent with the targeted enhancement, suggesting the designed vacancy/disorder strategy did not realize a single-phase, highly conducting inverse spinel in this Ni host.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Zn-induced cation distribution/disorder at a high Li-vacancy level (y≈0.4) being responsible for the abnormally high σRT observed in Li1.6Ni0.4V0.4Zn0.2Cl4, such that removing Zn while keeping y and V fixed will reduce conductivity. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.6Ni0.6V0.4Cl4 (450 °C) refines with a majority spinel fraction (spinel (Fd-3m) 0.9043, LiCl (Fm-3m) 0.0957; Rwp 8.88%) and exhibits σRT = 2.26e-07 S/cm, which is >10× lower than the Zn-containing analogue (2.5e-06 S/cm), satisfying the predefined decision rule (majority spinel and σRT ≤ 5e-07).

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of larger average octahedral M2+ radius (by increasing Mn2+ content) in inverse-spinel Li2MCl4 expands the lattice, enlarges Li+ migration bottlenecks, and raises σRT; thus Li2Co0.25Mn0.75Cl4 at 450 °C should show lower-2θ spinel peaks and higher σRT than Li2Co0.5Mn0.5Cl4. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li2Co0.25Mn0.75Cl4 refines as single-phase spinel (Fd-3m, 1.0 weight fraction; Rwp 3.71%) and shows higher σRT (1.18e-05 S/cm) than Li2Co0.5Mn0.5Cl4 (7.57e-06 S/cm), consistent with the predicted Mn-content–σ increase; however, the provided XRD data do not include peak-position comparisons or lattice parameters to verify a lower-2θ shift, and minor missing/extra-peak misfits remain, so lattice expansion cannot be confirmed.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of abnormally high σRT in Li1.5Mn0.5Y0.25In0.25Cl4 arising from high Li-vacancy content and Y3+/In3+-induced octahedral-site disorder that is preferentially retained at 400 °C, with a prediction that annealing at 450 °C would enable partial ordering and/or phase segregation and reduce conductivity. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as the 450 °C sample shows clear phase segregation (spinel (Fd-3m) 0.6976 + Li3YCl6 (P-3m1) 0.3024) and a ≈3× drop in σRT from 1.19e-04 S/cm (400 °C) to 3.98e-05 S/cm, consistent with the predicted reduction in transport upon higher-T treatment.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Fe-driven partial cation/site ordering at 400 °C suppressing Li+ conductivity in Li1.65Mn0.70Fe0.25V0.15Cl4, with the expectation that synthesis at 450 °C would reduce XRD misfit features (fewer/no missing/extra peaks, improved Rwp) and raise σ toward ~1e-5 S/cm. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as the 450 °C product refines as spinel (Fd-3m, 1.0 weight fraction) with improved Rwp (4.14% vs 5.16% at 400 °C) and no missing/extra peaks, and σRT increases from 1.4e-06 to 2.47e-05 S/cm (~18×), reaching the expected conductivity range and aligning with related Mn–V spinels.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Sc3+-induced Li-vacancy–controlled conductivity and concomitant disruption of the extra ordering/distortion seen in undoped Li2Co0.5Fe0.5Cl4 at 500 °C—predicting that raising Sc from 0.15 to 0.20 at 500 °C will keep a spinel-dominant pattern and increase or at least maintain σRT. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.8Co0.4Fe0.4Sc0.2Cl4 (500 °C) refines as single-phase spinel (Fd-3m, 1.0 weight fraction, Rwp 4.78%) with only low-intensity misfit peaks and no secondary phases, and shows σRT = 1.21e-05 S/cm—slightly above Li1.85Co0.425Fe0.425Sc0.15Cl4 (1.17e-05 S/cm) and higher than Li1.9Co0.45Fe0.45Sc0.1Cl4 (4.8e-06 S/cm); additionally, the specific unindexed features reported for undoped Li2Co0.5Fe0.5Cl4 at ~24.78° and ~39.42° are not present here, consistent with the predicted suppression of those ordering-related deviations.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Zn-driven long-range cation ordering in Li2Co0.5Zn0.5Cl4 (signaled by a strong extra low-angle ~15° reflection) suppressing Li+ transport, and that introducing Li vacancies via slight M-excess (x ≈ +0.05; Li1.9Co0.525Zn0.525Cl4) would frustrate the ordering, weaken the ~15° feature, and increase σRT. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.9Co0.525Zn0.525Cl4 (500 °C) refines as spinel (Fd-3m, 1.0) with a much weaker extra low-angle peak at 15.27° (relative intensity 0.31 vs 1.0 at 14.98° in Li2Co0.5Zn0.5Cl4 at 500 °C), fewer model misfits and improved Rwp (5.38% → 4.49%), and σRT increases from 1.32e-08 to 9.98e-08 S/cm (~7.6×). However, the low-angle feature persists and conductivity remains far below Co–Mg/Mn analogues (10^-6–10^-5 S/cm), indicating only partial mitigation of the ordering-linked limitation.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of a 1:1 Mn:Sc–specific octahedral cation arrangement at 500 °C in Li1.5Mn0.5Sc0.5Cl4 that deviates from a simple disordered Fd-3m model, suppresses expected low-angle intensities, and collapses σRT; slight deviation from 1:1 (e.g., Li1.4Mn0.4Sc0.6Cl4) should frustrate this arrangement, eliminate the low-angle model–data mismatch, and restore high conductivity. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.4Mn0.4Sc0.6Cl4 (500 °C) refines as single-phase spinel (Fd-3m, Rwp 9.07%) and shows high σRT = 1.28e-04 S/cm—much higher than Li1.5Mn0.5Sc0.5Cl4 at 500 °C (2.2e-06 S/cm) and above Li1.6Mn0.6Sc0.4Cl4 at 500 °C (3.45e-05 S/cm)—consistent with recovery of conductivity when moving off 1:1; however, the XRD still exhibits low-angle extra_peaks in the calculated Fd-3m model (16.08°, 16.83°, 18.87°, 21.94°) and a low-angle missing peak at 10.07°, so the predicted disappearance of the Fd-3m intensity mismatch is not observed.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of the unusually high σ in Li1.7Fe1.15Cl4 being governed primarily by the Li-vacancy fraction near y≈0.30 (rather than Fe-excess–induced disorder), such that maintaining y≈0.30 without Fe excess in Li1.7Fe0.7Y0.3Cl4 would yield comparable room-temperature conductivity. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.7Fe0.7Y0.3Cl4 (500 °C) exhibits a much lower σRT = 8.68e-06 S/cm than Li1.7Fe1.15Cl4 (6.16e-05 S/cm) and refines as a biphasic mixture with spinel (Fd-3m) 0.8041 and Li3YCl6 (P-3m1) 0.1959 (Rwp 3.51%) with several missing peaks, indicating the targeted single-phase spinel with matched vacancy fraction did not reproduce the high conductivity. While the secondary phase complicates strict attribution, this specific result does not support a vacancy-fraction-only explanation for the abnormal σ in Li1.7Fe1.15Cl4.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of intrinsic high ionic conductivity in Li1.4Fe0.8Mn0.3Zr0.1Cl4 arising from a Li‑vacancy‑rich, disordered inverse spinel (Fd‑3m), rather than from the ~6 wt% LiCl impurity seen at 400 °C; increasing the synthesis temperature to 500 °C should remove LiCl and maintain or improve σRT (≥3e‑05 S/cm). The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as the 500 °C product refines as single‑phase spinel (Fd‑3m, 1.0; Rwp 3.79%) with no LiCl detected, and σRT increases to 5.35e‑05 S/cm (from 3.31e‑05 S/cm at 400 °C), consistent with the high conductivity being intrinsic rather than LiCl‑assisted.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of low-temperature cation/Li-vacancy ordering (and/or subtle symmetry lowering from ideal Fd-3m) in Li1.4Mg0.8Ta0.2Cl4 suppressing Li+ transport at 400 °C, and that increasing synthesis temperature to 500 °C would enhance cation/vacancy disorder, reduce low-angle XRD misfit features, and raise σRT. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.4Mg0.8Ta0.2Cl4 (500 °C) shows markedly improved XRD agreement (spinel (Fd-3m) 0.9486 with only 5.14% LiCl, Rwp = 9.91%, one missing peak at 36.88° and one extra at 30.02°, and no low-angle ~14–15° anomalies seen at 400–450 °C) and a >100× increase in σRT to 7.2e-06 S/cm versus 6.8e-08 S/cm at 400 °C, also exceeding the 450 °C value (1.82e-06 S/cm). Some model–pattern differences remain, but the reduction of low-angle misfits together with the conductivity gain aligns with the ordering-suppression mechanism.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Ca-assisted cation/Li-vacancy ordering in Li1.8Bi0.2Ca0.2Mg0.6Cl4 suppresses conductivity and introduces superstructure reflections relative to ideal Fd-3m; thus, at fixed Bi and 500 °C, reducing Ca content should lessen ordering signatures (fewer/weaker missing peaks, improved Rwp) and increase σRT toward the Ca-free analogue. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.8Bi0.2Ca0.1Mg0.7Cl4 (500 °C) shows fewer missing peaks (3 vs 19 for Li1.8Bi0.2Ca0.2Mg0.6Cl4 at 500 °C) and improved Rwp (9.49% vs 13.27%), with σRT rising to 1.74e-06 S/cm (from 1.15e-06 S/cm), but extra peaks persist (14.81°/0.51) and additional extras appear (28.48°/0.16, 34.86°/0.06), and σRT remains below the Ca-free Li1.8Bi0.2Mg0.8Cl4 value (3.12e-06 S/cm). XRD also indicates a LiCl secondary phase (0.1317 weight fraction), while the spinel phase is 0.8683.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of transferring the high-conductivity motif (Li≈1.5 with mixed Y3+/In3+ on octahedral sites) from Mn-based to a Ni2+-based inverse spinel, expecting suppressed Li/M ordering, avoidance of Y/In-rich side phases, and ~10^-4 S/cm conductivity in Li1.5Ni0.5Y0.25In0.25Cl4. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as XRD shows no inverse-spinel phase and instead a fully accounted three-phase mixture of LiCl (Fm-3m, 43.8 wt%), NiCl2 (R-3m, 40.59 wt%), and Li5.96In1.98Cl12 (C12/m1, 15.61 wt%), with additional unindexed features and Rwp 7.99%. The room-temperature ionic conductivity is 1.17e-06 S/cm, far below the targeted ~10^-4 S/cm, indicating that the intended Ni-host inverse spinel did not form under the 500 °C synthesis and that an In-rich halide side phase persists despite Y/In mixing.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of using mixed Y3+/In3+ substitution with Li≈1.6 and off-commensurate 16d occupancy (Ni2+0.6 vs total M3+0.4) to frustrate Li/M ordering, suppress parasitic Li3YCl6/Li6In2−xCl12 formation, and deliver high room-temperature Li+ conductivity in Li1.6Ni0.6Y0.2In0.2Cl4.
