The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as the XRD shows a multiphase product with only ~76.5 wt% spinel (Fd-3m) and ~23.5 wt% NiCl2 (R-3m), a moderate Rwp of 9.63% with numerous unindexed peaks (including a low-angle feature near 13.5° 2θ that could indicate additional ordering/impurity), indicating incomplete reaction and/or extra phases rather than clean disordering; the measured ionic conductivity is very low at 6.44e-08 S/cm at 25 °C, far from the intended superionic regime.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of low‑temperature Li1.4Fe0.8Nb0.2Cl4 forming a long‑range ordered superstructure (signaled by a strong low‑angle ~15° 2θ feature) that suppresses Li+ transport, and that modest Mn substitution at fixed Li/Nb content (Li1.4Fe0.7Mn0.1Nb0.2Cl4) at 400 °C would frustrate this ordering, markedly reduce the ~15° feature (≥50% drop in relative intensity), and restore σRT to ≥1e-05 S/cm. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.4Fe0.7Mn0.1Nb0.2Cl4 (400 °C) refines as spinel (Fd-3m; 1.0 weight fraction; Rwp=4.68%) and achieves σRT = 1.17e-05 S/cm (recovery from the 1.0e-08 S/cm abnormal baseline), but the unmodeled low‑angle feature near ~15° remains strong (extra peak at 14.87° with relative intensity 0.43 vs ~0.48 in the 400 °C Li1.4Fe0.8Nb0.2Cl4 baseline), i.e., not a ≥50% reduction. Thus, while conductivity is restored, the expected collapse of the low‑angle superstructure signal is not observed, leaving the ordering‑suppression mechanism unconfirmed by XRD at 400 °C.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of introducing a small Bi3+ fraction into a Mn2+-based inverse spinel chloride (Li1.8Mn0.8Bi0.2Cl4) to create Li vacancies while retaining the spinel framework, thereby improving Li+ transport via vacancy-enabled percolation and a softened, polarizable Cl lattice. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as XRD shows a dominant spinel (Fd-3m) phase (0.8364 wt fraction) consistent with retention of the spinel host, but also a notable LiCl impurity (0.1636) and several unindexed peaks indicating secondary phases/limited Bi solubility; the room-temperature ionic conductivity is 5.57e-06 S/cm, which is only moderate and not clearly higher than comparable Mn-containing spinels, suggesting limited transport benefit at this Bi3+ level and synthesis condition.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of using a Mn2+-based inverse-spinel chloride host to better tolerate small Hf4+ substitution (Li1.6Mn0.8Hf0.2Cl4), thereby creating ~0.4 Li vacancies to preserve the Fd-3m framework and promote Li+ transport via increased cation disorder. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as XRD shows a predominantly single-phase spinel (Fd-3m, 100 wt%, Rwp 4.76%) with only one weak unindexed peak at 50.14°, indicating the intended framework forms with minor deviations, while the room-temperature ionic conductivity is 6.76e-06 S/cm—demonstrating only modest transport rather than a strong enhancement.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of introducing a small V3+/Nb5+ co-doping pair into a Mn2+-based inverse spinel chloride (Li2–yM1±xCl4) to set y≈0.4 Li vacancies and increase charge/size disorder on 16d, thereby frustrating Li/M ordering and enhancing 3D Li+ percolation, with the expectation of a mostly single-phase spinel and moderate-to-high room-temperature conductivity superior to a Co-host analogue. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.6Mn0.8V0.1Nb0.1Cl4 forms predominantly spinel (Fd-3m, 93.56 wt%) with minor LiCl (5.11 wt%) and residual NbCl5 (1.33 wt%) and good refinement (Rwp 4.86%, one weak unidentified peak), and exhibits σRT = 7.57e-06 S/cm—within the targeted moderate range and substantially higher than the Co-host benchmark—though the NbCl5 residue and LiCl indicate incomplete dopant incorporation and slight segregation, falling short of a fully single-phase outcome.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of replacing Jahn–Teller-active Cu2+ with soft monovalent Cu+ co-doped with Nb5+ in a Mg2+ inverse spinel host so that Li1.6Mg0.6Cu0.2Nb0.2Cl4 forms a single spinel framework with a vacancy-rich Li sublattice (y≈0.4), increased 16d disorder, and improved room-temperature conductivity (mid-10^-6 S/cm). The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as the XRD refines to a spinel (Fd-3m) phase (1.0 weight fraction) but with several unindexed/missing peaks and a moderate Rwp of 10.22%, indicating structural mismatch or minor unidentified features, and the measured room-temperature ionic conductivity is only 9.41e-08 S/cm, far below the targeted mid-10^-6 S/cm and lower than prior Mg–Nb or Cu2+-co-doped references.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of using V3+ alone in Li1.8Mg0.8V0.2Cl4 to introduce ~0.2 Li vacancies while preserving a largely disordered single-phase spinel (Fd-3m) and achieving improved room-temperature ionic conductivity without the phase separation observed in V3+ + Nb5+ co-doping. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as XRD shows the spinel phase is dominant (spinel (Fd-3m) 0.8099 wt fraction) but a significant Li6VCl8 (Fm-3m) secondary phase remains (0.1901), with extra/missing peaks suggesting structural deviations or ordering; the room-temperature ionic conductivity is 1.05e-06 S/cm, which is modest—slightly higher than Cr3+-doped benchmarks but below In3+- and Y3+-containing compositions—indicating only limited performance gains and incomplete suppression of phase separation.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of combining a small Sn2+ (lone-pair) fraction to frustrate Li/M ordering in the inverse-spinel Li2−yM1±xCl4 matrix while using Y3+ to deliberately form a limited Li3YCl6 boundary network, thereby creating moderate Li vacancies and improving room-temperature Li+ conductivity. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as XRD shows a dominant spinel (Fd-3m) phase (0.8764) with a minority Li3YCl6 (P-3m1) phase (0.1236) and no LiCl detected, and the ionic conductivity at 25 °C is 1.32e-05 S/cm—consistent with the observed trend that Li3YCl6 presence correlates with higher σ and roughly an order of magnitude above Li3YCl6-suppressed 400 °C products; note that several unindexed and model-extra peaks (Rwp 9.57%) indicate structural deviations/disorder in the spinel that merit further structural refinement but do not contradict the intended phase/transport design.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of pairing small Bi3+ and Zr4+ substitutions in the inverse spinel Li2−yM1±xCl4 framework (Li1.4Mg0.6Bi0.2Zr0.2Cl4) to generate high Li-vacancy content and cation-site disorder that suppress ordering and yield a phase-pure spinel with room-temperature conductivity in the few 10^-6 S/cm range. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as XRD shows a majority spinel (Fd-3m, ~67.4 wt%) but with substantial secondary phases (LiCl ~29.6 wt%, ZrCl2 ~3.0 wt%), moderate fit quality (Rwp 12.57%), and missing/extra peaks indicating unmodeled order/distortions; the room-temperature ionic conductivity is 1.4e-06 S/cm—within the 10^-6 range but below the targeted improvement and lower than the Bi-only benchmark (~3.1e-06 S/cm). This suggests the co-doping did not achieve phase-pure disordered spinel or enhanced σ at 400 °C.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of applying mixed-valence co-doping (In3+ + Ta5+) to a Co-based inverse spinel chloride, Li1.6Co0.8In0.1Ta0.1Cl4, to stabilize a disordered Fd-3m spinel without low-angle ordering while introducing y~0.4 Li vacancies to maintain a 3D vacancy network and achieve ~1e-5 to 2e-5 S/cm at room temperature (synthesized at 400 C). The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as XRD shows a majority spinel (Fd-3m, 85.6 wt%) with good refinement (Rwp 2.93%) and no explicit low-angle (~15 deg) superstructure features, indicating the targeted framework largely forms, but the presence of LiCl impurity (~14.4 wt%) and several unindexed weak peaks suggest deviations/secondary phases, and the room-temperature ionic conductivity is only 1.29e-06 S/cm, about an order of magnitude below the targeted range, so the conductivity enhancement aspect is not supported.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of extending the mixed Y3+ + In3+ (total 0.5 per f.u.) aliovalent substitution strategy to an Fe2+-host inverse spinel, Li1.5Fe0.5Y0.25In0.25Cl4, to stabilize a single Fd-3m spinel with frustrated cation ordering and a vacancy-rich Li network (y≈0.5) for high room-temperature Li+ conductivity while suppressing Li3YCl6/Li6In2−xCl12 formation. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as XRD reveals a multiphase product with only 69.75 wt% spinel (Fd-3m) alongside 18.34 wt% Li3YCl6 (P-3m1), 9.89 wt% LiCl (Fm-3m), and 2.03 wt% FeCl3 (P-3) (Rwp 3.79%); an extra low-angle peak (15.82°) and several missing peaks indicate deviations/possible ordering relative to the ideal Fd-3m model; and the room-temperature ionic conductivity is 9.48e-05 S/cm, below the high-conductivity regime expected for a single-phase, highly disordered inverse spinel.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of achieving high room-temperature Li-ion conductivity by setting Li ≈ 1.7 (y ≈ 0.3 vacancies) and using a mixed Mg2+/Mn2+/V3+ M-sublattice in Li1.7Mg0.35Mn0.35V0.3Cl4 to retain a disordered inverse-spinel framework that promotes fast Li transport. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as XRD after 400 °C synthesis indexes to a spinel (Fd-3m) phase at 100 wt% with good Rwp (6.21%), indicating the targeted framework forms, but several unindexed/missing peaks and a strong extra low-angle peak (~14.98° 2θ) imply deviations from ideal Fd-3m (likely cation/vacancy ordering or subtle distortions). Critically, the measured room-temperature ionic conductivity is 2.87e-06 S/cm, an order of magnitude below the ≥10^-5 S/cm benchmarks for comparable Li-deficient, aliovalently doped spinel chlorides, so the high-conductivity aspect of the hypothesis is not achieved under these conditions.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of using multi-aliovalent co-doping (Y3+, Ta5+, Sn2+, with Ta5+) to set y ≈ 0.3 Li vacancies in Li1.7Fe0.62Sn0.2Ta0.06Y0.12Cl4, thereby maximizing Li/M disorder, softening the chloride lattice, suppressing cation/vacancy ordering, and achieving a single-phase inverse spinel with enhanced room-temperature ionic conductivity. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as XRD shows a majority spinel (Fd-3m) phase (86.77 wt%) but with LiCl impurity (13.23 wt%) and several weak unindexed peaks (Rwp 4.10%), indicating incomplete single-phase formation; the room-temperature ionic conductivity is 3.64e-05 S/cm—respectable and comparable to prior Y- or Ta-doped spinels but not higher than the best Fe-rich reference (≈6.16e-05 S/cm). This supports the vacancy-targeting strategy for maintaining moderate-to-high σ, but does not demonstrate a clear conductivity gain from Sn/Y/Ta co-doping and suggests possible solubility/segregation (e.g., LiCl formation), so the single-phase/ordering-suppression aspect of the hypothesis is not fully realized.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Bi3+ at x=0.10 in Li1.9Fe0.9Bi0.1Cl4 exceeding spinel solid solubility and/or partially volatilizing at 400 °C, driving LiCl secondary-phase formation that suppresses σRT; lowering the synthesis temperature to 350 °C should suppress chloride loss, yield single-phase spinel, and restore σRT toward typical Fe-based inverse-spinel values. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.9Fe0.9Bi0.1Cl4 synthesized at 350 °C refines as 100 wt% spinel (Fd-3m; Rwp=5.60%) with no LiCl detected by XRD and σRT increases from 1.49e-07 S/cm (400 °C) to 1.19e-05 S/cm—comparable to Li2FeCl4 (1.14e-05 S/cm) and Li1.95Fe0.95Bi0.05Cl4 (7.68e-06 S/cm). Several unindexed/extra peaks remain, indicating some mismatch between the reference model and the data, but the removal of LiCl and ≥2-order conductivity recovery are consistent with the temperature-mitigated volatility/solubility explanation.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of low-temperature synthesis (250 °C) of Li2Zn0.5Mg0.5Cl4 freezing a more ordered Li/M distribution and leaving residual ZnCl2, which suppress Li+ transport; raising the synthesis temperature to 350 °C should increase Li/M-site disorder within the spinel and consume ZnCl2 without strongly promoting Li2ZnCl4 formation, yielding ≥5× higher σRT and improved XRD fit versus the 250 °C product. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as the 350 °C sample shows σRT = 3.35e-07 S/cm (~33× higher than 1.0e-08 S/cm at 250 °C), a lower Rwp (9.75% vs 12.85%), no ZnCl2 detected, and a majority spinel fraction (spinel (Fd-3m) = 0.6225). However, substantial Li2ZnCl4 phases are present (Pnma 0.2351 and Fd-3m 0.1424, totaling 0.3775), and multiple missing peaks remain, indicating that formation of non-spinel Li2ZnCl4 persists at 350 °C contrary to the “without strongly promoting Li2ZnCl4” expectation.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of abnormally low σ in Li2Zn0.5Mg0.5Cl4 stemming from a vacancy-poor, cation-ordered spinel, and that introducing 10% excess divalent metal to form Li1.8Zn0.55Mg0.55Cl4 at 350 °C would create Li vacancies, disrupt ordering, and substantially raise σRT with a cleaner spinel XRD signature (target ≥1e-6 S/cm or ≥10× vs the 400 °C sample). The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as the 350 °C product shows spinel (Fd-3m) 0.5681 with substantial secondary phases (Li2ZnCl4 Pnma 0.2498; LiCl Fm-3m 0.1821), increased unindexed/extra features (12 missing peaks and 5 extra peaks vs 6/0 at 250 °C), and σRT = 5.28e-07 S/cm—only ~2.8× higher than the 400 °C sample (1.88e-07 S/cm) and below the ≥1e-6 S/cm target and spinel benchmarks—indicating the intended vacancy introduction at 350 °C did not yield the predicted structural simplification or conductivity gain.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of using an Fe‑rich Mn–V inverse spinel host with light In3+ (0.1) heterovalent substitution to introduce Li vacancies/disorder, preserve a predominantly spinel phase, and achieve Mn–V-like high Li+ conductivity while avoiding Li3InCl6 segregation. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.5V0.2Mn0.2In0.1Fe0.6Cl4 synthesized at 400 °C is 96.3% spinel (Fd-3m) with only 3.7% LiCl (Rwp 4.24%; a few weak unindexed peaks) and shows 1.29e-05 S/cm at 25 °C—comparable to the best Mn–V spinels—indicating maintained spinel framework and high conductivity without evident Li3InCl6 formation.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of stabilizing an inverse-spinel Li chloride via a Mn-rich backbone (Mn 0.6) with Mg2+ (0.3) to preserve the spinel framework, a small V3+ dose (0.1) to introduce vacancies/disorder without Ni/Zn liabilities, and a small Fe2+ component (0.1) to diversify the octahedral field, while using a moderate vacancy level (Li=1.7; y=0.3) to maintain Li percolation and phase robustness. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as XRD shows a predominantly spinel phase (spinel (Fd-3m) 97.87%) with only minor LiCl (2.13%) and a good refinement (Rwp 5.43%), with only low-intensity unindexed peaks, indicating successful spinel formation and phase robustness; the room-temperature ionic conductivity is 3.64e-06 S/cm, consistent with the proposed “moderate” conductivity and comparable to Mg-stabilized benchmarks, while the small LiCl impurity aligns with the anticipated risk of slight phase segregation at this composition.

This sample Li1.4Zr0.1In0.2Y0.2Mn0.5Cl4 is made in order to test the hypothesis of using Y3+ (z≈0.2) to seed a minor Li3YCl6 boundary phase while retaining a spinel-majority host, and co-doping with Zr4+ and In3+ (with Mn2+ as the divalent anchor) to tune average M charge and Li-vacancy concentration to achieve ~1e-5 S/cm conductivity. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as XRD shows a spinel (Fd-3m) majority (0.6434) with a Li3YCl6 minority (0.1575), though an additional In-rich halide (Li6In2.12Cl12, 0.1991) also formed; refinement is good (Rwp 5.34%) with only small missing peaks, and the room-temperature ionic conductivity is 5.82e-05 S/cm—exceeding the target and consistent with boundary-phase-assisted transport, indicating Zr did not depress σ in this co-doped formulation.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of increasing Y to 0.3 to boost ionic conductivity via a spinel + percolative Li3YCl6 composite while using Fe co-doping (with Zr) to retain an Fd-3m spinel majority and suppress Zr-related ordering/impurities in Li1.3Mn0.1Zr0.2Y0.3Fe0.4Cl4. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as the XRD shows a strong spinel (Fd-3m) majority (0.7691, Rwp 6.17%) and the room-temperature ionic conductivity reached 2.01e-05 S/cm, but Li3YCl6 is not detected; instead, ZrFeCl6 (0.1557) and ZrCl3 (0.0752) form with multiple unindexed peaks, indicating the intended Li3YCl6-driven percolation mechanism and impurity suppression were not realized.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of replacing Zr4+ with low-level Hf4+ while co-doping with Fe2+, Mg2+, and Mn2+ (and excluding Ni) in Li1.4Hf0.1Mg0.3Fe0.5Mn0.3Cl4 would stabilize a spinel-only phase and yield mid-10^-6 S/cm ionic conductivity by enhancing octahedral-site disorder and Li-vacancy concentration, thereby generalizing the Zr–Fe stabilization/σ-improvement pattern to Hf. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as XRD refines to a single spinel (Fd-3m) phase at 100 wt% with low Rwp = 5.32% (noting a few missing/extra peaks indicating subtle deviations), and the measured room-temperature ionic conductivity is 5.17e-06 S/cm, matching the predicted mid-10^-6 range and exceeding prior Ni–Hf results.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of combining near‑optimal Li‑vacancy content (y ≈ 0.2 at Li ≈ 1.8) with Zr4+–Mn2+ co‑substitution and low Mg2+ to increase cation disorder and thereby enhance Li+ conductivity in the inverse spinel chloride framework. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.8Mn0.2Fe0.6Mg0.1Zr0.1Cl4 synthesized at 400 °C refines to an average spinel (Fd-3m) phase (Rwp 4.15%) but shows several unindexed/missing peaks, and delivers a room‑temperature ionic conductivity of 5.24e-06 S/cm—well below the Fe‑only y ≈ 0.2–0.3 benchmarks and prior Zr–Mn examples—indicating the anticipated conductivity enhancement was not realized under these conditions (possibly due to residual ordering/structural deviations at 400 °C).

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of combining moderate Ta5+ (0.1), substantial Mn2+ (0.4), and slight Mg2+ (0.1) in Li1.5Mg0.1Mn0.4Ta0.1Fe0.5Cl4 to raise Li-vacancy content and promote Li/M site disorder in an inverse spinel chloride, thereby achieving room-temperature ionic conductivity in the ~1–4×10^-5 S/cm range while keeping a largely spinel phase. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as the 400 °C synthesis yielded predominantly spinel (Fd-3m, 0.9808 wt fraction) with only minor LiCl (0.0192), a good refinement (Rwp 4.19%) and just one weak unindexed peak, and the measured 25 °C ionic conductivity is 2.31×10^-5 S/cm—within the targeted band and comparable to prior Ta- and Mn-containing benchmarks—indicating the designed vacancy/disorder strategy achieved high σ without significant phase segregation.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of maintaining the y ≈ 0.2 Li-vacancy inverse-spinel framework while introducing 10% Cu2+ into the Fe2+/Y3+ matrix so that Cu2+ Jahn–Teller distortions frustrate cation/vacancy ordering and thereby preserve a disordered spinel and enhance room-temperature Li+ conductivity relative to the Y3+-only baseline. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as XRD shows a majority spinel (Fd-3m) phase (0.8456) but also a significant ordered/low-symmetry component indexed as Li2FeCl4 (Imma) (0.1544) with numerous missing/extra peaks, indicating residual ordering/phase heterogeneity rather than fully suppressed ordering; the room-temperature ionic conductivity is 2.13e-05 S/cm, which remains in the expected 10^-5 S/cm regime but is lower than the Li1.8Fe0.8Y0.2Cl4 benchmark (3.82e-05 S/cm), indicating Cu2+ did not improve conductivity and may have promoted phase/ordering effects that offset the intended disordering benefit.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of co-doping V3+ and Hf4+ in the inverse spinel chloride framework at Li≈1.7 (Li vacancies y≈0.3) to promote Li/M site disorder and achieve ≳1e-5 S/cm conductivity in a spinel phase. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.7Fe0.8V0.1Hf0.1Cl4 synthesized at 400 °C refines predominantly as spinel (Fd-3m, 1.0 weight fraction, Rwp 3.41%) and delivers 1.14e-05 S/cm at 25 °C; minor unindexed peaks suggest subtle impurities or ordering, but the targeted high conductivity in a spinel matrix is achieved.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of using a high-vacancy inverse spinel chloride at Li=1.3 with a multivalent octahedral cation mix (V3+, Mn2+, Fe2+, Zr4+) to frustrate cation/vacancy ordering, retain single-phase spinel, and thereby increase room-temperature Li+ conductivity relative to Mn–V benchmarks, without introducing V-related impurity phases. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.3Zr0.2V0.5Fe0.1Mn0.1Cl4 formed a two-phase mixture (spinel (Fd-3m) 0.8035, VCl3 (R-3) 0.1965; Rwp 6.47%) with several unindexed and model-mismatched peaks, and exhibited low ionic conductivity (2.05e-07 S/cm), which is ~20–75× lower than the cited Mn–V high-vacancy compositions; thus neither the anticipated phase purity nor enhanced conductivity was achieved.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of introducing a small amount of Ta5+ into a vacancy-rich Mn–V–Fe inverse spinel chloride (Li1.4Mn0.1Ta0.1V0.5Fe0.2Cl4) to frustrate cation/vacancy ordering, retain the Fd-3m spinel framework at high Li deficiency, and enhance room-temperature Li+ conductivity. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as XRD shows a multiphase product with only ~62.8% spinel alongside FeCl3 (~22.2%) and Li2FeCl4 (~15.0%), plus several unindexed/mismatched peaks (Rwp 5.95%), indicating segregation/ordering rather than a single, disordered spinel, and the measured ionic conductivity is low (1.82e-07 S/cm). Ta incorporation is not confirmed (no identifiable Ta-bearing phase), consistent with the lack of conductivity enhancement.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of transferring the high-V, vacancy-optimized inverse-spinel motif from Mn–V to Fe–V—i.e., that increasing V3+ content (and Li-vacancy concentration, y≈0.6) in Li1.4Fe0.4V0.6Cl4 will enhance Li+ conductivity by improving 8a–16c–8a percolation and suppressing Li/M ordering, largely independent of the M2+ species. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as XRD shows a multiphase product with only 0.6329 spinel (Fd-3m) alongside significant FeCl3 (P312, 0.2153) and LiCl (Fm-3m, 0.1518), plus missing/extra peaks indicating additional unidentified or structurally mismatched components; correspondingly, the room-temperature ionic conductivity is 6.37e-09 S/cm, orders of magnitude below Mn–V benchmarks and even below lower-vacancy Fe–V, indicating that the targeted vacancy-driven enhancement was not realized under these conditions.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of stabilizing a predominantly inverse-spinel Li2−yM1±xCl4 framework using a Mn-rich backbone (Ni/Zn/Cr-free) with small Mg/Fe disorder and modest aliovalent Y3+ (0.1) and Ta5+ (0.1) to create controlled Li vacancies (y≈0.2) and Li/M site disorder that preserve the spinel field (avoid Li3YCl6) and lift room-temperature Li+ conductivity into the ~10^-5 S/cm range. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as XRD shows a dominant spinel phase (94.71%) with only minor LiCl (5.29%) and no Li3YCl6, a good refinement (Rwp 5.05%) with only two weak unindexed peaks, and the measured ionic conductivity is 8.17e-06 S/cm—higher than prior low-Y spinel baselines—consistent with modest conductivity gains from vacancy/disorder at y=0.2.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of using a Mn-rich inverse spinel chloride with very high Li vacancy content (Li1.2Mn0.6Zr0.2Fe0.1Co0.2Mg0.1Cl4) where Zr4+ and minor Fe/Co/Mg promote octahedral-site disorder and retain a disordered spinel framework, thereby enhancing Li+ transport without V and aiming for conductivities approaching Mn–V analogs. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as XRD shows the spinel (Fd-3m) framework as the dominant phase (0.9212 wt fraction, Rwp 4.46%) with a minor ZrCl2 impurity (0.0788) and some unindexed peaks, indicating mostly successful spinel formation but some Zr segregation; the room-temperature ionic conductivity (5.59e-06 S/cm) exceeds Zr-in-Co-only baselines (~2e-07 S/cm) but remains below the Mn–V benchmark (~1.5e-05 S/cm), and no LiCl was identified by XRD.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of using In3+ co-doping, together with Fe2+/Mn2+/Mg2+ and Nb5+, to stabilize a single inverse-spinel Li2−yMCl4 framework in Li1.5Fe0.3Nb0.1Mn0.1In0.2Mg0.3Cl4, creating Li vacancies and multi-cation disorder that yield intrinsic room-temperature conductivity ≥1e−5 S/cm without relying on Li3YCl6-type boundary phases. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as XRD shows a single spinel (Fd-3m) phase at 1.0 weight fraction with good refinement (Rwp 5.30%), no extra peaks and only one very weak unindexed peak (50.01°, 0.06), and the ionic conductivity is 2.36e-05 S/cm at 25 °C—exceeding the ≥1e−5 S/cm target and outperforming Mg-only baselines, with no evidence of Li3InCl6 formation.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of leveraging Y3+ to induce a minority Li3YCl6 phase within a spinel chloride matrix so that grain-boundary/dual-phase transport elevates room-temperature conductivity (~1e-5–2e-5 S/cm), while Fe/Mn/Mg stabilize the spinel and Cu’s potential penalty is offset by the Li3YCl6 contribution. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as XRD shows a majority spinel (Fd-3m, 77.46 wt%) with a substantial Li3YCl6 (P-3m1, 22.54 wt%) minority and good refinement (Rwp 4.98%); the measured conductivity is 1.13e-05 S/cm, squarely in the targeted range. Minor missing/extra peaks indicate some disorder or unmodeled features but do not detract from the intended phase assemblage and performance.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of leveraging Y≈0.2 in the Li2−yM1±xCl4 inverse-spinel framework—now on a Co–Mn host with added Nb5+—to reproducibly form a spinel-majority + Li3YCl6 mixture that yields ~1e-5 S/cm at room temperature via vacancy-enabled Li transport and interfacial/secondary-phase-assisted conduction. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.5Co0.2Nb0.1Mn0.4Cu0.1Y0.2Cl4 synthesized at 400 °C forms 81.98 wt% spinel (Fd-3m) with 18.02 wt% Li3YCl6 (P-3m1), Rwp = 4.00%, no missing/extra peaks, and exhibits σRT = 2.01e-05 S/cm—consistent with the targeted mixed-phase regime and demonstrating transferability of the Y=0.2 strategy beyond Mg-based systems.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of anchoring the Li=1.4/Nb=0.2 inverse-spinel chloride motif while adding small Zr4+ and Ni2+ (with Mn2+/Fe2+ mixing) to enhance 16d configurational disorder, preserve a clean spinel phase, and maintain or surpass the ~2.63e-05 S/cm benchmark conductivity of Li1.4Mn0.8Nb0.2Cl4. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.4Mn0.3Zr0.1Ni0.1Nb0.2Fe0.2Cl4 refines mainly to spinel (Fd-3m, 1.0 wt%, Rwp 4.49%) but shows several missing peaks indicative of unmodeled features, and its room-temperature ionic conductivity is 7.44e-06 S/cm—about 3.5× lower than the benchmark.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of a composite/interfacial origin for the high σRT in Li2Cr0.5Mn0.5Cl4 at 400 °C—specifically, that coexistence of spinel with LiCl and Li2CrCl4 creates vacancy-rich spinel regions and heterointerfaces that elevate conductivity, and that driving the reaction to single-phase spinel at 450 °C would reduce σ toward the 10^-8–10^-7 S/cm range typical of Cr-containing spinels. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as Li2Cr0.5Mn0.5Cl4 synthesized at 450 °C refines as single-phase spinel (Fd-3m, 1.0 weight fraction; Rwp = 5.24%) yet exhibits σRT = 2.47e-05 S/cm (≥1e-5), exceeding the predefined threshold and remaining far above the Cr-spinel cohort. Extra/missing low-angle features persist (e.g., extra at 14.99°), but no LiCl or Li2CrCl4 are detected; thus, elevated conductivity persists without secondary phases, contradicting the composite/interfacial mechanism and indicating the enhancement is likely intrinsic to the Mn–Cr spinel or its defect/ordering state.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of low-temperature structural heterogeneity (ordering and/or minor secondary features) causing the abnormally low σ in Li1.6Mg0.6Cu0.2Nb0.2Cl4 at 400 °C, with the expectation that synthesizing at 450 °C would reduce unindexed reflections and raise σ to ≥1e-6 S/cm. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.6Mg0.6Cu0.2Nb0.2Cl4 at 450 °C shows spinel (Fd-3m) 0.8384 with LiCl (Fm-3m) 0.1616, retains unindexed features (missing peaks at 24.44°, 29.63°, 34.36° and an extra peak at 15.02°; Rwp 8.80%), and exhibits σRT = 8.71e-08 S/cm—essentially unchanged and far below the ≥1e-6 S/cm target and 450 °C spinel benchmarks (~3–6e-06 S/cm).

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Ca2+ co-doping with Bi3+ at 450 °C stabilizing cation/Li-vacancy ordering (deviations from ideal Fd-3m) in Li1.8Bi0.2Ca0.2Mg0.6Cl4, which lowers σ; removing Ca at the same temperature (Li1.8Bi0.2Mg0.8Cl4) should suppress these ordering signatures and restore higher σ. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.8Bi0.2Mg0.8Cl4 (450 °C) is single-phase spinel (Fd-3m, 1.0), shows no extra peaks (the low-angle extra at ~14.74° seen with Ca is absent), has fewer missing peaks (8 vs 15 for the Ca-containing sample at 450 °C) with improved Rwp (8.93% vs 13.43%), and exhibits σRT = 4.51e-06 S/cm, which is >40× higher than the Ca-containing analogue at 450 °C (1.11e-07 S/cm) and exceeds the Li2MgCl4 baseline at 450 °C (3.16e-06 S/cm). Residual missing peaks remain, but the predefined decision rule (fewer/absent missing peaks and σ ≥ ~1e-06 S/cm) is met, indicating Ca co-doping was the key contributor to the low-σ anomaly.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Y-driven Li3YCl6 formation at 450 °C being the primary cause of the conductivity drop in Y/In-doped inverse spinels, with the prediction that reducing Y while keeping Σ(M3+) = 0.5 (Li1.5Mn0.5Y0.1In0.4Cl4 at 450 °C) would suppress Li3YCl6, retain a predominantly disordered spinel, and yield σRT ≈ 1e-4 S/cm. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as Li3YCl6 is absent but an In-rich Li6In2.03Cl12 (C12/m1) secondary phase is present (spinel (Fd-3m) 0.8384; Li6In2.03Cl12 0.1616; Rwp 6.41%), and the room-temperature ionic conductivity is low (8.65e-06 S/cm), even below the 450 °C Y-containing reference that did form Li3YCl6 (Li1.5Mn0.5Y0.25In0.25Cl4, 0.3024 Li3YCl6; σRT 3.98e-05 S/cm). This indicates that suppressing Li3YCl6 alone did not preserve high conductivity at 450 °C, pointing to other factors (e.g., temperature-driven structural changes and/or formation of other secondary phases) controlling transport in this regime.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of abnormally low σRT in Li2Zn0.5Mn0.5Cl4 at 400 °C arising from persistent cation ordering (inferred from a strong low-angle extra peak near 14.7° relative to Fd-3m) and residual Li2ZnCl4 (~18 wt%), with the expectation that synthesizing at 450 °C would suppress the ~14.7° feature, dissolve Li2ZnCl4 into a single spinel solid solution (>95% spinel), and raise σRT by ≥5×. The hypothesis is refuted by the experiment outcome as the 450 °C product remains biphasic with spinel (Fd-3m) 0.7991 and Li2ZnCl4 (Fd-3m) 0.2009, the low-angle extra peak persists at 14.81° (relative intensity 0.3; reduced but not eliminated), and σRT is 3.53e-07 S/cm—slightly lower than at 400 °C (4.16e-07 S/cm) and far from the targeted ≥5× improvement.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of the high conductivity in Li1.5Mg0.6In0.3Zr0.1Cl4 originating from the fixed Li=1.5 vacancy level together with In3+-driven multi-cation disorder within an inverse-spinel framework, with Zr4+ not being essential; thus, removing Zr while keeping Li=1.5 (Li1.5Mg0.5In0.5Cl4) should still yield a spinel-dominant XRD and conductivity near or above ~1e-05 S/cm. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.5Mg0.5In0.5Cl4 synthesized at 400 °C refines as single-phase spinel (Fd-3m, 1.0 weight fraction; Rwp 9.37%) with several missing but no extra peaks, and shows a room-temperature ionic conductivity of 1.55e-05 S/cm—exceeding the predefined threshold (~8e-06 S/cm), surpassing the original outlier (1.03e-05 S/cm), and lying well above the spinel-only baseline band (~2e-06–6e-06 S/cm). This indicates that high conductivity can be achieved without Zr4+ at fixed Li vacancy, consistent with In3+-driven disorder; the XRD misfit features reflect deviations from the ideal model, with no additional crystalline phase identified by XRD.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Li3YCl6-driven high conductivity in Li1.6Mg0.6Y0.4Cl4 at 450 °C, namely that suppressing Li3YCl6 by synthesizing at 400 °C would markedly reduce its fraction and lower σ toward spinel-only baselines. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as the 400 °C sample refines to spinel (Fd-3m) 1.0 with no Li3YCl6 reported (Rwp = 8.00%; numerous missing/extra peaks indicate model/sample mismatch but do not identify Li3YCl6), and σRT drops from 2.52e-05 S/cm (450 °C) to 4.38e-06 S/cm—now comparable to spinel baselines (e.g., Li2MgCl4: 3.16e-06 S/cm)—consistent with conductivity being enhanced by Li3YCl6 in the higher-temperature sample.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of low-temperature cation/Li-vacancy ordering in Li1.4Mg0.8Ta0.2Cl4 suppressing ionic conductivity at 400 °C, and that isovalent mixing on the high-valent site (Ta0.1Nb0.1) at fixed Li content would frustrate this ordering, remove low-angle XRD misfit features, and increase σ at the same synthesis temperature. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.4Mg0.8Ta0.1Nb0.1Cl4 (400 °C) shows only a slight Rwp improvement (11.29% vs 12.51% for Li1.4Mg0.8Ta0.2Cl4 at 400 °C) and absence of the prior low-angle missing peaks, but its σRT decreases to 3.94e-08 S/cm (vs 6.8e-08 S/cm). Moreover, the XRD refines as two Fd-3m phases (spinel (Fd-3m) 0.6644 and Li13.52Mg9.28Cl32 (Fd-3m) 0.3356) with remaining high-angle misfit features, so the key conductivity criterion is not met and the phase mixture complicates attribution to ordering frustration.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of an Nb-dependent V solubility/ordering boundary at 400 °C in Li2−y(Mn,V,Nb)Cl4: specifically, that reducing Nb from 0.05 to 0.04 at fixed V=0.15 will suppress Li6VCl8 formation and recover ~1e-5 S/cm room-temperature ionic conductivity. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.73Mn0.81Nb0.04V0.15Cl4 (400 °C) shows ≥95 wt% spinel (Fd-3m 0.9591) with no Li6VCl8 detected (only minor LiCl 0.0233 and Nb3Cl8 0.0177; Rwp 4.96%; no extra peaks), and σRT = 7.93e-06 S/cm—substantially higher than the abnormal 400 °C product (9.98e-07 S/cm) but below the predefined ≥1e-5 S/cm success criterion and lower than the 400 °C Nb=0.03 analogue (1.63e-05 S/cm).

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of using an Ni/Zn/Cr-free Mn–V inverse spinel host co-doped with small amounts of Ta5+ and Hf4+ to raise the average M charge, introduce substantial Li vacancies (Li=1.4; y≈0.6), frustrate cation ordering, suppress V-rich impurities, and thereby retain a spinel framework with ~10^-5 S/cm Li+ conductivity. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.4V0.1Ta0.1Hf0.1Fe0.4Mn0.3Cl4 synthesized at 400 °C refines as single-phase spinel (Fd-3m, Rwp 4.80%) with no indexed Li6VCl8 or other secondary phases, and exhibits room-temperature ionic conductivity of 8.08e-06 S/cm; several low-intensity missing peaks and one low-angle extra peak indicate subtle structural deviations but do not contradict the spinel, vacancy-enabled conduction pathway.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of designing a Ni/Zn/Cr-free, Mn–V–based inverse spinel chloride (Li1.6Ta0.1V0.1Fe0.1Mn0.4Mg0.3Cl4) where small Ta5+ addition and multi-cation disorder set y≈0.4 Li vacancies and preserve the spinel framework to achieve 10^-6–10^-5 S/cm at room temperature while avoiding Li6VCl8 formation. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as XRD shows a dominant spinel (Fd-3m) phase (0.9378) with minor LiCl impurity (0.0622) and no Li6VCl8 signatures, good refinement (Rwp 5.03%) with only one weak unindexed peak, and the ionic conductivity is 6.0e-06 S/cm at 25 °C, within the targeted range.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Zn2+-induced cation redistribution/disorder intrinsically boosting Li+ conductivity in Li1.6Ni0.4V0.4Zn0.2Cl4 at fixed vacancy level (y≈0.4), independent of the NiCl2 impurity present at 450 °C. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as the 500 °C synthesis yields a single-phase spinel (Fd-3m 1.0; Rwp 7.27%) with NiCl2 eliminated, yet the room-temperature ionic conductivity drops to 1.55e-07 S/cm from 2.5e-06 S/cm in the 450 °C sample (which contained 0.1539 NiCl2), satisfying the predefined decision rule that a collapse to ~10^-7 S/cm upon removing NiCl2 argues against an intrinsic Zn-driven enhancement.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of a 1:1 Mn:Sc ratio at 500 °C promoting Li/M octahedral ordering that degrades Li+ transport, whereas moving off 1:1 and increasing Sc (thus Li-vacancy concentration) frustrates ordering and enhances conductivity; the unusually high σRT in Li1.4Mn0.4Sc0.6Cl4 was attributed to this synergy. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.45Mn0.45Sc0.55Cl4 (500 °C) refines as single-phase spinel (Fd-3m, 1.0 wt; Rwp 7.32%) with only a few moderate-intensity missing peaks and no extra_peaks, and exhibits σRT = 1.44e-04 S/cm—meeting the predefined ≥8e-05–1e-04 criterion, comparable to Li1.4Mn0.4Sc0.6Cl4 (1.28e-04 S/cm) and far above Li1.6Mn0.6Sc0.4Cl4 (3.45e-05 S/cm) and Li1.5Mn0.5Sc0.5Cl4 at 500 °C (2.2e-06 S/cm)—consistent with enhanced transport off 1:1 and with higher vacancy content at 500 °C.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of the unusually high σRT in Li1.7Fe1.15Cl4 arising primarily from an optimal Li-vacancy fraction near y≈0.30 in the inverse-spinel framework rather than from Fe over-stoichiometry, by holding Li at 1.7 (y≈0.30) and reducing total M content via partial Y3+ substitution (Li1.7Fe0.85Y0.2Cl4). The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.7Fe0.85Y0.2Cl4 (500 °C) refined as spinel (Fd-3m, 1.0 wt; Rwp 4.35%) with several weak missing peaks and no extra peaks, and exhibited σRT = 7.64e-05 S/cm—higher than Li1.7Fe1.15Cl4 (6.16e-05 S/cm) and above Y-doped references—indicating that high conductivity persists (and even improves) when metal over-stoichiometry is reduced at fixed Li content. While the missing peaks suggest minor unmodeled features, no secondary phases were identified by the refinement, consistent with a vacancy-dominated conductivity enhancement.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Mn2+-enabled multi-cation disorder being the primary driver of the abnormally high σRT in Li1.4Fe0.8Mn0.3Zr0.1Cl4 at 500 °C; specifically, removing Mn while holding Li (1.4), Zr (0.1), and total M-excess (1.2) constant (Li1.4Fe1.1Zr0.1Cl4) should significantly reduce σRT and alter the ~15° 2θ extra reflection if Mn-driven disorder is essential. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.4Fe1.1Zr0.1Cl4 synthesized at 500 °C refines as a single spinel (Fd-3m, 1.0 wt%, Rwp 3.64%) and shows σRT = 4.87e-05 S/cm—comparable to Li1.4Fe0.8Mn0.3Zr0.1Cl4 (5.35e-05 S/cm) and much higher than Li1.6Fe0.8Zr0.2Cl4 (2.95e-06 S/cm); moreover, the pronounced extra low-angle ~15° peak seen in the Mn-containing sample is absent (extra_peaks = []), with only several weak unindexed peaks present, indicating high conductivity persists without Mn.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of the abnormally high σRT in Li1.5Fe0.5Y0.25In0.25Cl4 being dominated by a Li3YCl6 secondary phase; suppressing Li3YCl6 at fixed Li-vacancy level (y = 0.5) by shifting to Li1.5Fe0.5Y0.2In0.3Cl4 at 500 °C should lower σ into the spinel-only range. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.5Fe0.5Y0.2In0.3Cl4 retains substantial Li3YCl6 (P-3m1) at 0.2102 with spinel (Fd-3m) 0.7656 and minor FeCl2 (R-3m) 0.0242 (Rwp 4.46%), and shows σRT = 7.16e-05 S/cm—higher than single-phase/near-single-phase spinel benchmarks at 500 °C (3.82e-05–4.23e-05). Because Li3YCl6 was not suppressed, the test does not isolate the intrinsic spinel conductivity; the elevated σ alongside persistent Li3YCl6 is consistent with, but does not definitively prove, the hypothesis.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of vacancy-optimized conductivity in Li2−y(Co,Fe,Sc)Cl4 spinels at 500 °C, specifically that the abnormally high σRT for Li1.8Co0.4Fe0.4Sc0.2Cl4 arises from near‑optimal Li‑vacancy content at y≈0.2, and that increasing Sc to y=0.25 (Li1.75Co0.375Fe0.375Sc0.25Cl4) will not further improve σRT and may introduce deviations from the ideal spinel (e.g., secondary phases/misfit peaks). The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.75Co0.375Fe0.375Sc0.25Cl4 (500 °C) shows σRT = 1.39e-05 S/cm—comparable to Li1.8Co0.4Fe0.4Sc0.2Cl4 (1.21e-05 S/cm) and not ≥1.5× higher—while XRD remains spinel-dominant (spinel (Fd-3m) 0.977) with a minor LiCl (Fm-3m) secondary phase (0.023) and several unindexed peaks (e.g., 24.79°), indicating a conductivity plateau near y≈0.2 with emerging deviations/secondary phase at 25% Sc under these conditions.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of using V3+ ≈ 0.1 with Li deficiency (Li=1.8) and Nb5+ (0.1), combined with Fe/Co/Mn 2+ mixing, to suppress Li6VCl8 formation, stabilize a disordered Fd-3m inverse spinel, and achieve ~10^-5 S/cm room-temperature conductivity. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.8Nb0.1Fe0.4V0.1Co0.1Mn0.2Cl4 forms predominantly spinel (Fd-3m, 0.9708) with only minor Nb3Cl8 (R3m, 0.0292) and no Li6VCl8 detected (Rwp 3.93%), but the room-temperature ionic conductivity is 6.54e-06 S/cm—below the targeted 1–3e-05 S/cm—and several weak unindexed peaks suggest subtle structural deviations or minor unidentified phases.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Y3+/In3+ co-doping at Li ≈ 1.5 in the inverse spinel chloride framework (Li1.5Mn0.25Fe0.25Y0.25In0.25Cl4) to stabilize a (near) single-phase spinel and deliver ~10^-4 S/cm room-temperature ionic conductivity. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as XRD after 400 °C synthesis shows a dominant spinel (Fd-3m) phase at 81.34 wt% but with a 18.66 wt% Li3YCl6 (P-3m1) side phase and minor missing/extra peaks (Rwp 4.64%), while the measured ionic conductivity is 1.36e-4 S/cm, matching the targeted σ but not achieving single-phase spinel (the Li3YCl6 impurity may also contribute to σ).

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of a Ni/Zn-free, vacancy-rich inverse spinel chloride where a Fe-based backbone lightly alloyed with Mn and V and heterovalently doped with In3+ and Nb5+ (Li1.3In0.1Fe0.7Mn0.1V0.1Nb0.1Cl4) will stabilize a predominantly spinel (Fd-3m) phase and, via Li-vacancy creation and M-site disorder, deliver elevated room-temperature Li+ conductivity. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as XRD at 400 °C refinement gives a single spinel (Fd-3m) phase at 1.0 weight fraction with good fit (Rwp 5.02%), showing only minor deviations (unindexed peaks near 32.6–34.8° and 49.9–50.3°, and a calculated-but-absent reflection at 14.86°) consistent with subtle ordering/distortion rather than secondary phases, and the room-temperature ionic conductivity reaches 3.12e-05 S/cm, exceeding the cited Mn–V benchmarks and aligning with the proposed vacancy/disorder-enhanced transport.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of creating moderate Li-vacancy content (Li≈1.7) in a Co/Fe inverse-spinel chloride host and enhancing 16d cation disorder by co-doping small Nb5+ with isovalent Mg2+ and Mn2+ (while avoiding Ni/Zn) to raise room-temperature Li+ conductivity toward ~1e-5 S/cm. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.7Co0.2Mg0.2Fe0.3Nb0.1Mn0.2Cl4 forms predominantly spinel (Fd-3m, ~95 wt%) with minor LiCl and Nb3Cl8 impurities (Rwp 3.54%), and exhibits σRT = 1.22e-05 S/cm—an order-of-magnitude higher than prior Nb-only Co hosts and comparable to Sc-doped Co/Fe systems—despite some unindexed/extra peaks suggesting subtle structural deviations or minor residual phases.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of leveraging high Li-vacancy (y ~ 0.4) and multi-cation configurational disorder (Co/Fe/Mn with small Cu and Zr4+) in the inverse spinel chloride Li1.6Co0.2Zr0.1Cu0.2Mn0.3Fe0.4Cl4—while avoiding Ni/Zn—to frustrate cation ordering and raise room-temperature Li+ conductivity toward ~1e-5 S/cm. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as XRD shows a predominant spinel phase (spinel (Fd-3m) 90.74%) with minor LiCl (9.26%) and good refinement (Rwp 3.82%), but the measured conductivity is 1.78e-06 S/cm—higher than Zr4+-only and many Ni/Zn-containing baselines yet below the targeted high-conductivity regime; unindexed weak peaks and a strong extra calculated peak indicate structural deviations (e.g., residual ordering or secondary phases) that may limit σ.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of using high Li-vacancy content (Li = 1.4; y ≈ 0.6) and mixed aliovalent co-doping (Hf4+/Zr4+ with Mg2+) in an inverse spinel chloride to maximize cation/charge disorder and thereby raise room-temperature ionic conductivity beyond single 4+/5+ doped Co spinels, without the degradation seen with Ni/Zn. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.4Co0.1Mg0.4Hf0.1Fe0.2Zr0.2Cl4 forms predominantly a spinel phase (Fd-3m, 98.98 wt%) with only a minor Zr0.667Cl2 impurity (~1 wt%), but XRD shows a strong low-angle extra peak and multiple missing peaks indicative of cation ordering/symmetry deviation from the reference model; the room-temperature ionic conductivity is 4.61e-06 S/cm—higher than typical single-dopant baselines and prior mixed-dopant examples, yet still below the best vacancy-rich systems (~1e-5 S/cm), and no LiCl impurity is detected.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of using In3+-centered multi-cation/aliovalent co-doping (In3+ plus a small Nb5+ with divalent Co/Mn/Fe) in Li1.3In0.4Co0.1Nb0.1Mn0.3Fe0.1Cl4 to create a vacancy-rich, highly disordered inverse-spinel that boosts room-temperature Li+ conductivity while avoiding Ni/Cu/Zn-induced degradation, ideally as a single-phase spinel. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as XRD shows a predominant spinel (Fd-3m) phase at 0.8923 wt with a minor LiCl (Fm-3m) impurity at 0.1077 wt (consistent with the anticipated risk at y=0.7), and the sample exhibits elevated ionic conductivity of 2.08e-05 S/cm (exceeding prior In3+-containing references), with a good refinement quality (Rwp 3.82%) and only one weak unindexed peak, indicating the designed vacancy/disorder effectively enhanced σ despite not being strictly single-phase.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of using In3+ at 0.5 to stabilize a spinel chloride host while limiting V3+ to 0.1 and incorporating Mg2+/Fe2+/Mn2+ to maximize Li vacancies and Li/M disorder, thereby avoiding Li6VCl8 formation and achieving ~10^-5 S/cm room-temperature Li+ conductivity in Li1.2Mn0.1V0.1Mg0.3Fe0.1In0.5Cl4. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as XRD refines to a spinel (Fd-3m) model at 100 wt% with reasonable Rwp (7.50%), but several unindexed/missing peaks and one extra calculated peak indicate minor unidentified phases or cation-ordering/lower-symmetry deviations from ideal spinel; importantly, no clear Li6VCl8 is observed. The room-temperature ionic conductivity is 7.71e-06 S/cm, higher than V-rich analogs and near (but below) the targeted ~1e-5 S/cm, consistent with improved but not best-in-class transport.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis that Li1.9V0.1Mn0.1Zr0.1Mg0.5Fe0.1Cl4, a low‑vacancy inverse spinel, will use Fe2+ to stabilize Zr4+ in a predominantly spinel framework while a small V3+ fraction introduces beneficial charge disorder without forming V-driven impurity phases, thereby achieving Mg–Zr-like conductivity improvements with minimal impurities. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as XRD shows a mostly spinel product (spinel (Fd-3m) 96.75 wt% with only 3.25 wt% Zr6FeCl15, Rwp 6.74%) and no Li6VCl8; however, minor missing peaks indicate additional unidentified traces. The room-temperature ionic conductivity is 2.77e-06 S/cm, modest but slightly higher than the prior Fe–Mg–Zr benchmark (≈1.96e-06 S/cm), consistent with Fe-assisted Zr spinel stabilization and small V3+ not inducing the Li6VCl8 impurity, yet gains are limited by the low vacancy level and residual impurity.

This sample, Li1.4Mg0.2Cu0.1In0.2Fe0.2Mn0.5Cl4, is made in order to test the hypothesis of using a Y-free, Li≈1.4 inverse-spinel chloride with modest In3+ (0.2) to create Li vacancies and multi-2+ cation mixing (Mg/Cu/Fe/Mn) to retain octahedral disorder in Fd-3m, thereby suppressing parasitic phases and enabling ~1e-4 S/cm room-temperature ionic conductivity comparable to Sc/Y+In analogs. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as XRD at 400 °C shows a majority spinel (Fd-3m, 81.1 wt%, Rwp=5.41%) consistent with the targeted framework and no Y-containing phases, but an In-rich Li6In2.12Cl12 side phase (18.9 wt%) formed despite the modest In level, several minor peaks remained unindexed, and the ionic conductivity is 1.19e-05 S/cm—about an order of magnitude below the targeted ~1e-4 S/cm.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of using a divalent-only, metal-excess (x≈+0.2) inverse spinel chloride to introduce Li vacancies and maximize cation configurational disorder (Fe/Ni/Co/Cu/Mg) on 16d, thereby preserving the spinel framework while avoiding Li3MCl6-type side phases and achieving mid-10^-5 S/cm ionic conductivity. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.6Mg0.1Cu0.1Co0.2Ni0.2Fe0.6Cl4 synthesized at 400 °C refines as single-phase spinel (Fd-3m, 100 wt%, Rwp 3.21%) with a few minor missing/extra peaks suggesting subtle deviations, yet the room-temperature ionic conductivity is 1.88e-06 S/cm—well below the targeted mid-10^-5 S/cm and lower than the Li1.8Mn1.1Cl4 benchmark—despite the absence of obvious secondary phases.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of using Ta5+ (~0.2) to create Li vacancies while Mn2+, Mg2+, and a small Sn2+ addition frustrate cation ordering and enhance configurational disorder, enabling a disordered inverse-spinel Li network that maintains >=1e-5 S/cm even at low Li (~1.2). The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.2Mn0.4Sn0.1Ta0.2Mg0.3Fe0.1Cl4 synthesized at 400 °C refined as predominantly spinel (Fd-3m, 100 wt%) with good Rwp (6.03%), only a few low-intensity unindexed peaks (34.2°, 34.94°, 50.37°), and achieved room-temperature ionic conductivity of 1.53e-05 S/cm, meeting the targeted conductivity and indicating a largely disordered, vacancy-rich spinel with minor deviations/possible minor secondary features.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of combining the Mn+Zr co-doping motif with modest Ta5+-induced Li vacancies and a small amount of Co2+ in Li1.3Mn0.2Fe0.3Zr0.2Ta0.1Co0.2Cl4 to suppress cation ordering (especially the ~15° 2θ superstructure) and, via enhanced vacancy concentration and cation-state disorder, exceed ~5e-05 S/cm room-temperature ionic conductivity. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as the XRD at 400 °C refines predominantly to spinel (Fd-3m, Rwp 3.32%) but shows several unindexed/missing reflections (e.g., at 35.07° and 50.4° 2θ) and extra calculated peaks, indicating deviations (possible minor impurity or ordering), and the measured room-temperature ionic conductivity is 5.54e-06 S/cm—well below the targeted and benchmark Mn–Zr values—despite no flagged low-angle (~15° 2θ) superstructure peak.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Zn2+-driven cation-site disorder, kinetically stabilized at 450 °C, being responsible for the abnormally high room-temperature conductivity in Li1.6Ni0.4V0.4Zn0.2Cl4; specifically, at fixed y = 0.4, increasing Zn (Li1.6Ni0.3V0.4Zn0.3Cl4) at 450 °C should maintain a dominant spinel phase and raise σRT to ≥2.5e-06 S/cm. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as XRD shows a dominant spinel framework (spinel (Fd-3m) 0.9362; NiCl2 (R-3m) 0.0638; Rwp 7.17%), but the measured σRT is 1.6e-07 S/cm—over an order of magnitude lower than Li1.6Ni0.4V0.4Zn0.2Cl4 at 450 °C (2.5e-06 S/cm) and comparable to Ni-based baselines—indicating that increasing Zn from 0.2 to 0.3 at 450 °C does not reproduce or enhance the high-conductivity state.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of disorder-driven high conductivity in Li1.5Mg0.5In0.5Cl4: the 400 °C product’s elevated σRT (1.55e-05 S/cm) arises from Li/M and Li-vacancy disorder preserved at lower temperature, so synthesizing at 450 °C should reduce disorder (clearer match to Fd-3m) and lower σRT. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.5Mg0.5In0.5Cl4 at 450 °C shows a marked conductivity drop to 2.48e-06 S/cm—now comparable to spinel-only baselines Li2MgCl4 (3.16e-06 S/cm) and Li1.6Mg1.2Cl4 (4.55e-06 S/cm)—but the XRD does not unambiguously improve toward a single-phase Fd-3m model: a secondary LiCl (Fm-3m) phase appears at 0.2876 weight fraction (spinel (Fd-3m) 0.7124), Rwp worsens from 9.37% to 13.04%, and unindexed features persist (6 missing and 4 extra peaks). Thus, while the conductivity behavior is consistent with the temperature/disorder hypothesis, the emergence of LiCl and lack of clearer structural convergence introduce a confounding factor, preventing attribution of the σ drop solely to reduced disorder.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Zn-driven cation ordering combined with too few Li vacancies causing the abnormally low σ in Li2Fe0.5Zn0.5Cl4, and that introducing ~10% Li vacancies at fixed Fe:Zn (Li1.9Fe0.525Zn0.525Cl4) would increase σRT toward ~1e-5 S/cm and reduce XRD superstructure-related mismatches. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.9Fe0.525Zn0.525Cl4 (450 °C) refines as spinel (Fd-3m, 1.0; Rwp 5.31%) and shows σRT = 5.21e-06 S/cm—higher than Li2Fe0.5Zn0.5Cl4 at 250 °C (3.25e-08 S/cm) and 500 °C (3.05e-06 S/cm)—but still below Li2FeCl4 (1.14e-05 S/cm) and Li2Mg0.5Fe0.5Cl4 (1.04e-05 S/cm); moreover, XRD retains multiple missing peaks and a strong extra peak at 15.07° (relative intensity 0.8), indicating structural discrepancies relative to the Fd-3m model persist rather than clearly decreasing.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of percolation-limited low conductivity in Li1.6Zn0.8Zr0.2Cl4—i.e., that increasing Zr4+ to Li1.5Zn0.75Zr0.25Cl4 at 450 °C would increase Li-vacancy concentration and stabilize a majority inverse-spinel (Fd-3m) phase, yielding ≥100× higher σ if percolation were the limiting factor. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as XRD shows Li2ZnCl4 (Pnma) remains the majority (0.747) with only 0.253 spinel (lower than 0.3565 in Li1.6Zn0.8Zr0.2Cl4), alongside notable model mismatches (Rwp 10.01% with numerous missing/extra peaks), and the room-temperature ionic conductivity increases only to 1.44e−07 S/cm (~14× over 1e−08), below the predefined ≥100× threshold; thus no majority spinel is achieved and the data do not validate a percolation-limited explanation under these conditions.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of vacancy- and Li/M-disorder–driven high conductivity in Li1.5Mg0.6In0.3Zr0.1Cl4 (y≈0.5 from charge neutrality) that does not rely on the low-angle extra reflection (~15.31°) seen at 400 °C; increasing synthesis temperature to 500 °C should suppress that extra peak while maintaining or improving σ (≥1.0e-05 S/cm). The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.5Mg0.6In0.3Zr0.1Cl4 synthesized at 500 °C remains spinel-only (Fd-3m, 1.0) with the previous ~15.31° extra peak absent (extra_peaks = []), Rwp slightly worsened (12.21% vs 11.66%), and the room-temperature ionic conductivity drops to 2.86e-06 S/cm—well below the 400 °C value (1.03e-05 S/cm) and within baseline spinel ranges—indicating that removal of the low-angle feature coincides with reduced σ, contrary to the vacancy+disorder-alone explanation.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of the exceptionally low σRT in Li1.4Mg0.8Ta0.1Nb0.1Cl4 at 400 °C being caused by low-temperature-stabilized phase separation into two Fd-3m-derived phases and associated cation/Li-vacancy ordering, and that increasing the synthesis temperature to 500 °C would promote a single-phase inverse spinel and markedly increase σRT. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.4Mg0.8Ta0.1Nb0.1Cl4 synthesized at 500 °C refines to a dominant spinel (Fd-3m) 0.9038 with only LiCl (Fm-3m) 0.0962 (the secondary Fd-3m phase seen at 400 °C is absent), shows improved Rwp (7.72% vs 11.29%) with no missing/extra peaks, and its σRT increases from 3.94e-08 S/cm to 4.4e-06 S/cm (>100×), meeting the predefined decision criteria.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of a 1:1-specific Li/M cation ordering at 500 °C in Li1.5Mn0.5Sc0.5Cl4 that collapses σRT, and that introducing a slight total-M excess at fixed Mn:Sc=1:1 (targeting Li1.45Mn0.51Sc0.51Cl4) would frustrate the ordering, restore higher conductivity, and yield a more self-consistent Fd-3m spinel fit. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as the 500 °C product for Li1.45Mn0.51Sc0.51Cl4 refines to non-spinel phases—Li3ScCl6 (C12/m1, 0.8625) + Sc7Cl12 (R-3, 0.1375) with Rwp 6.98% and residual misfits—so the intended structural test within Fd-3m could not be assessed; although σRT = 1.2e-4 S/cm is much higher than the collapsed 2.2e-06 S/cm at 1:1, it is measured on a different phase assemblage and therefore does not demonstrate restoration of disordered spinel transport.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of whether the anomalously high ionic conductivity in Li1.7Fe1.15Cl4 is primarily governed by the Li-vacancy fraction (y≈0.30) independent of how vacancies are introduced, such that Li1.7Fe0.7In0.3Cl4 (same y) should reproduce a similar σ and spinel XRD fingerprint. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.7Fe0.7In0.3Cl4 (500 °C) refines as single-phase spinel (Fd-3m, 1.0; Rwp 4.81%; two weak missing peaks at 11.17° and 50.24°; no extra peaks) but exhibits σRT = 2.1e-05 S/cm—approximately 66% lower than Li1.7Fe1.15Cl4 (6.16e-05 S/cm) synthesized at the same temperature—indicating that the Li-vacancy fraction alone does not set the conductivity and that the vacancy-introduction route (and associated cation distribution/disorder) also influences transport.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Mn2+-induced cation-disorder being the key driver of the abnormal σ in Li1.4Fe0.8Mn0.3Zr0.1Cl4 at fixed Li = 1.4, Zr = 0.1, and Mtotal = 1.2, such that increasing Mn to Li1.4Fe0.65Mn0.45Zr0.1Cl4 (at 500 °C) would further increase σ and reduce the low-angle intensity mismatch. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.4Fe0.65Mn0.45Zr0.1Cl4 shows σRT = 5.27e-05 S/cm, slightly lower than Li1.4Fe0.8Mn0.3Zr0.1Cl4 at 500 °C (5.35e-05 S/cm), and XRD remains single-phase spinel (Fd-3m 1.0) but the pronounced extra low-angle peak persists with similar intensity (~14.93° at 0.58) and the refinement quality (Rwp = 4.31%) does not improve versus the 0.3 Mn case (Rwp = 3.79%); additional missing peaks are also present. Thus, increasing Mn from 0.3 to 0.45 at fixed Li/Zr/Mtotal does not enhance conductivity nor alleviate the low-angle model–data mismatch.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of the abnormally high σRT in Li1.5Fe0.5Y0.25In0.25Cl4 synthesized at 400 °C arising primarily from the Li3YCl6 secondary phase (~18 wt%) providing parallel Li+ transport; increasing the synthesis temperature to 500 °C should suppress Li3YCl6 and lower σRT toward the spinel-only range observed in peers. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as the 500 °C product remains multiphase with Li3YCl6 present (0.1197) alongside spinel (0.7781) and LiCl (0.1022), and σRT stays essentially unchanged at 9.31e-05 S/cm (vs 9.48e-05 S/cm at 400 °C), still above spinel-only references (≈3.82e-05–7.64e-05 S/cm), consistent with persistent Li3YCl6 sustaining the elevated conductivity.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of vacancy-threshold–driven conductivity in Li2−y M1±x Cl4 spinels: the abnormally high σ in Li1.9Co0.45Fe0.45Sc0.1Cl4 arises from reaching y≈0.10 and suppressing the extra ~24.8°/39.4° features seen in Li2Co0.5Fe0.5Cl4, and σ should primarily scale with the Li-vacancy concentration y independent of whether y is introduced by Sc3+ or by slight M-excess; thus, creating y=0.20 at fixed Sc (Li1.8Co0.475Fe0.475Sc0.1Cl4) should yield σ comparable to the 20% Sc sample. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.8Co0.475Fe0.475Sc0.1Cl4 (500 °C) refines as spinel (Fd-3m, 1.0 weight fraction, Rwp 3.32%) without reappearance of the ~24.8°/39.4° unindexed features (only low-intensity unindexed peaks at 10.04° and 81.61°), and σRT = 7.03e-06 S/cm—higher than Li1.9Co0.45Fe0.45Sc0.1Cl4 (4.8e-06 S/cm) but below both the ≥1.0e-05 S/cm decision threshold and the 15–20% Sc cases (1.17e-05–1.21e-05 S/cm)—indicating vacancies enhance σ but conductivity does not scale solely with y under these conditions.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of Zn-driven cation ordering at Co:Zn = 1:1 causing a strong ~15° model–sample XRD misfit and very low σRT in Li2Co0.5Zn0.5Cl4, and that increasing Li-vacancy content at fixed Co:Zn (Li1.8Co0.55Zn0.55Cl4) would suppress the ~15° feature and raise σRT. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.8Co0.55Zn0.55Cl4 still shows a prominent low-angle mismatch (extra_peak at 15.25° with relative intensity 0.78 and a missing peak at 15.32° with 0.13), alongside CoCl2 (R-3m) at 0.1151 wt fraction; its room-temperature ionic conductivity is 2.77e-08 S/cm, only modestly above Li2Co0.5Zn0.5Cl4 (1.32e-08 S/cm at 500 °C) and below both the ≥1e-07 S/cm decision threshold and Li1.9Co0.525Zn0.525Cl4 (9.98e-08 S/cm).

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of low-temperature cation/Li-vacancy ordering in Li1.4Mg0.8Ta0.2Cl4 suppressing Li+ transport, and that multi-cation mixing (Fe co-substitution) at the same 400 °C synthesis temperature would frustrate this ordering, reduce low-angle XRD misfit features, and restore higher σRT. The hypothesis is partially supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.4Fe0.2Mg0.6Ta0.2Cl4 (400 °C) refines as single-phase spinel (Fd-3m, 1.0) with improved Rwp (8.41% vs 12.51% for Li1.4Mg0.8Ta0.2Cl4 at 400 °C) and shows σRT = 5.07e-06 S/cm (~75× higher than 6.8e-08 S/cm and above the ≥1e-06 target), but low-angle misfit features persist (a strong extra peak at 14.9° (0.55) and missing peaks at 30.09° (0.31) and 34.92° (0.31)), indicating that while conductivity is restored and overall fit improved, the anticipated reduction of low-angle anomalies is not fully achieved.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of mixed Y3+/In3+ co-doping in Li1.5Mn0.5Y0.25In0.25Cl4 uniquely stabilizing a single-phase spinel at 400 °C and suppressing Li3YCl6, thereby enabling the abnormally high σRT; conversely, the Y-only counterpart Li1.5Mn0.5Y0.5Cl4 at 400 °C should exhibit Li3YCl6 and a lower σRT (~10^-5 S/cm). The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.5Mn0.5Y0.5Cl4 synthesized at 400 °C shows spinel (Fd-3m) 0.5797 and Li3YCl6 (P-3m1) 0.4203 (Rwp 6.93%) with σRT = 1.59e-05 S/cm, markedly lower than Li1.5Mn0.5Y0.25In0.25Cl4 at 400 °C (single-phase spinel, σRT = 1.19e-04 S/cm), consistent with Li3YCl6 persistence without In and reduced conductivity.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of a composite-conduction origin for the abnormal σRT at 400 °C in Li1.5Mn0.3Fe0.2Y0.25In0.25Cl4, specifically that a percolative In-based Li–halide secondary phase (indexed as Li6In2.12Cl12) primarily boosts conductivity; therefore, reducing In to Li1.5Mn0.3Fe0.2Y0.35In0.15Cl4 at 400 °C should suppress Li–In chloride in XRD and lower σRT by ≥30–40%, whereas maintaining ≥1.1×10^-4 S/cm without Li–In chloride would argue against this mechanism. The hypothesis is not supported by the experiment outcome as XRD for Li1.5Mn0.3Fe0.2Y0.35In0.15Cl4 at 400 °C shows no Li–In chloride (phases: spinel (Fd-3m) 0.6168, Li3YCl6 (P-3m1) 0.3317, FeCl2 (Pa-3) 0.0515; Rwp 5.19%), yet σRT remains high at 1.11×10^-4 S/cm—only ~21% below 1.4×10^-4 S/cm for the abnormal sample and above the ≥1.1×10^-4 S/cm threshold—indicating that an In-based secondary phase is not required to achieve the high conductivity. Because Li3YCl6 persists, the result does not isolate intrinsic spinel transport, but it contradicts the specific In-based composite-boost hypothesis.

This sample is made in order to test the hypothesis of the abnormally low room-temperature conductivity in Li1.9Fe0.9Bi0.1Cl4 synthesized at 400 °C being caused by Bi loss (volatility) that leads to LiCl secondary-phase formation; providing a slight Bi excess at the same temperature (Li1.88Fe0.88Bi0.12Cl4) should suppress LiCl and restore conductivity. The hypothesis is supported by the experiment outcome as Li1.88Fe0.88Bi0.12Cl4 synthesized at 400 °C refines as 1.0 spinel (Fd-3m; Rwp 4.31%) with no LiCl detected by XRD and achieves σRT = 1.48e-05 S/cm—comparable to Li2FeCl4 (1.14e-05 S/cm) and far above Li1.9Fe0.9Bi0.1Cl4 at 400 °C (1.49e-07 S/cm). This indicates that compensating Bi loss removes the LiCl impurity and restores σ; while minor missing peaks suggest some model mismatch, the data support a volatility-driven impurity origin rather than a strict solubility limit at the target Bi level under these conditions.
